learning_objectives: Define a computer and distinguish data from information.
Describe the features of a computer system and its application areas.
Identify the common input devices and what each is for.
Explain the CPU, its components and the instruction cycle.
Describe the motherboard and the role of the data bus.
Distinguish primary from secondary memory, and RAM from ROM.
Describe output devices and the difference between soft and hard copy.
Classify software and give examples of each kind.

blocks.text: The word computer comes from the Latin computare, which means to calculate — to find the result of some operation on values, numeric or not. That etymology is a reminder that calculation was the original job, and everything else the machine now does grew from it.
A multipurpose, programmable, electronic data processing device that accepts input, processes it, produces information as output, and can store it if necessary.
Data and information
These two words are not interchangeable, and the difference is the point of the whole exercise.

head: Data
Information
rows: A collection of unorganised facts and figures
Data that has been organised and processed
No — it carries no pattern or context
Yes — it is meaningful and can be acted on
The average temperature for three days
blocks.caption: Data versus information

blocks.text: A computer does not create information; it converts data into information. Because that is now so easy, and because the internet carries the result anywhere, the world has become what is often called a global village.
A computer system

A computer system is an integrated set of hardware and software designed to perform a variety of tasks. Hardware is the electronic and electromechanical components — the parts you can touch. Software is the collection of programs that tell the hardware what to do.

A computer system typically has an input/output (I/O) unit, a central processing unit (CPU), and a memory unit. Hardware without software does nothing; software without hardware has nothing to run on. The system is the two together.
Features of a computer system

items: Speed — billions of instructions per second, measured in hertz (Hz).
Accuracy — very high, though errors still occur if the data or instructions are wrong. Bad input gives bad output: GIGO, Garbage In Garbage Out.
Word length — the number of bits processed at once in parallel: commonly 8, 16, 32 or 64. The longer the word, the faster the machine.
Automation — once given a program and data, it works without the user intervening.
Diligence — it repeats work at the same speed and accuracy without becoming bored or tired.
Reliability — consistent results for the same data and instructions.
Versatility — different programs make it a different machine.
Storage/memory — a huge amount of data can be held and retrieved at high speed.

blocks.text: How speed is measured

head: Unit of frequency
Equals
Unit of time
blocks.caption: Frequency and the time it corresponds to

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: The frequency and time columns are the same fact written two ways: a higher frequency means a shorter time for one operation. If you learn the pairing you can answer either kind of question.
Application areas
Computers are used in education, business, office, communication, banking, hospitals, industry, the military, aviation, robotics and computer-aided design, among others.

blocks.caption: A computer used as a teaching tool (CAI).

blocks.text: Education. Learning with a computer has proved more successful, and new teaching methods have been developed around it. In institutions it serves as a teaching tool (Computer Aided Instruction, CAI), as an information resource, and as a means of computing and research. It is also used to prepare documents, reports and presentations.

Business. Used in shopping malls, hotels and retail centres to process sales and issue receipts at a Point of Sale (POS) terminal, and to update sales records and inventory control. E-commerce is buying, selling and exchanging products or services over an electronic medium, with payment made electronically.
Office. Preparing reports, letters, contracts, forms, notes and notices; storing, retrieving and displaying text. It automates office work across departments.
Communication. Email, social media, and online conferencing — computer conferencing, teleconferencing, audio or video conferencing — over the internet.

Bank. Handling transactions, maintaining the ledger, issuing deposit receipts, making withdrawals and deposits, and giving customers online access to balances and statements. Online banking performs these transactions over the internet.

blocks.caption: Computers in diagnosis and medical imaging.

blocks.text: Hospital. Helping doctors diagnose, find information about diseases and treatments, and keep patient records. Doctors can consult distant data banks and expert systems, and discuss cases by teleconferencing. Importantly, machines such as MRI, CT scanners, eye-testing and ultrasonic machines have computers built into them.

Industry. Automatic control of machines and processes, and measurement and display of electrical and physical quantities: the temperature of a heating system, motor speed, generator voltage, boiler pressure. If a fault occurs the system alarms and isolates the faulty part.

Military. Modern tanks, missiles and fighter planes use internal computers. A guided missile holds a detailed map of the target area in memory, and compares photographs of the area against it before striking. Such craft fly faster and turn more quickly than manned aircraft, and can enter dangerous zones without risking a pilot.

Aviation. Stores flight numbers, routes, distances, seats available in each class and fares, so a counter clerk can tell at once whether a seat is free on a given flight. It prints and issues tickets, informs customers of departure and arrival times, and controls take-off and landing to reduce risk. It also runs RADAR and other communication devices.
Robotics. A robot is a computer-controlled programmable machine with a mechanical body and optical sensors for vision. It can walk, move, place devices, spray paint, weld, pack and stack cartons.
Computer-Aided Design (CAD). Used for simulations, design and automation — producing and testing designs on screen before anything is built.
An input device takes what a person supplies and converts it into a form the computer can use. Without one, a computer cannot be told anything.

blocks.caption: A mouse — the standard pointing device.

blocks.text: Mouse — a pointing device that moves a pointer on screen to select and drag in a graphical interface.

blocks.caption: A keyboard — the standard text input device.

blocks.text: Keyboard — provides textual input; each key closes a circuit that the keyboard's own controller converts to a code.
Joystick — a lever reporting direction and tilt, used in games, simulators and for controlling machinery.
Microphone — captures sound, converting speech or other audio into digital form.

blocks.caption: A scanner converts paper into a digital image.

blocks.text: Scanner — captures digital images of documents and photographs.

blocks.caption: A webcam captures images and video.

blocks.text: Webcam — captures images and video, mainly for video calls.

blocks.caption: A touch screen: display and input in one.

blocks.text: Touch screen — detects where a finger or stylus touches the display, so the screen is both output and input device.

blocks.caption: A touch pad, common on laptops.

blocks.text: Touch pad — a flat, touch-sensitive surface found on laptops, replacing the mouse where there is no desk.
Bar code reader — reads information from the printed black-and-white stripes of a bar code, as at a shop till.
QR code scanner — reads a Quick Response (QR) code, a two-dimensional code holding far more data than an ordinary bar code.
The primary component responsible for executing instructions and processing data. It performs arithmetic, logic, control and input/output operations specified by the instructions in a program.
Modern CPUs are typically multi-core, so they can carry out several tasks at once. The two main manufacturers are Intel and AMD (Advanced Micro Devices). Speed is measured in hertz.
Functions of the CPU

items: It gives commands to all parts of the computer system.
It controls the sequence of operations, and controls the storage of data.
It performs arithmetic calculations such as addition and subtraction.
It supervises and controls the input/output devices.

blocks.text: The instruction cycle
A complete cycle has five steps, and the machine repeats them billions of times a second.

items: Fetch — the CPU fetches the next instruction from memory.
Decode — it works out what operation is needed.
Execute — it carries out the decoded instruction.
Write back — it stores the result back in memory.
Update program counter — the counter is advanced to point at the next instruction.

blocks.text: Components of the CPU

items: Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU) — performs arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) and logical operations (AND, OR, NOT) plus relational comparisons (=, >, <, >=, <=). Arithmetic does the calculating; logic and comparison provide decision-making.

Control Unit (CU) — controls all components using control signals. It instructs the rest of the system how to carry out a program's instructions and directs the movement of electronic signals between components.

Registers — small, high-speed storage locations inside the CPU that hold the data, instructions and addresses being worked on at this instant. They work closely with the CU and ALU, holding data, intermediate results and instructions fetched from RAM.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Registers are faster than RAM because they sit inside the CPU itself — no bus journey is involved. That is the whole answer to "why are registers faster than RAM?".
The main circuit board of a computer, acting as a central hub connecting the CPU, RAM, storage devices, expansion cards and peripherals.

blocks.caption: A motherboard with its labelled parts.

blocks.text: It provides communication pathways through buses, slots and connectors, houses the chipsets that manage data flow, and carries built-in ports for external connections such as USB, HDMI and Ethernet. For these reasons it is called the backbone of the computer.
Functions of the motherboard

items: It coordinates the various devices and maintains an interface among them.
It carries the non-volatile memory chips — the system firmware or BIOS chip.
It distributes power from the power supply to the components.

blocks.text: Roles of the motherboard

items: It is the central hub where the CPU, memory, storage and peripherals connect.
It provides the CPU socket, giving the processor its electrical connections.
It has slots for RAM modules.
It has PCIe (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express) expansion slots for graphics, sound and network cards.
It provides storage connectors, such as SATA ports for hard drives and SSDs, so the CPU can read and write to them.
It distributes power from the power supply.
It houses the BIOS (Basic Input/Output System) or UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface), which initialises hardware during booting.

blocks.text: The data bus

A communication system that transfers data between components inside a computer, or between computers. It is a set of wires or traces on the motherboard carrying data signals, and it may be parallel or serial.

items: It transfers data between the CPU, memory and peripherals so they can communicate.
It operates by defined protocols that specify how data is formatted, transmitted and received.
It keeps transfer efficient and delay low, which maintains performance.
It lets the CPU, RAM and storage work together — it is the backbone of the system.
It often includes error-checking, so data arrives accurately and integrity is preserved.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: A bus is a communication pathway, not a storage device and not a processor. Questions offering those as alternatives are testing exactly that distinction.
The part of the computer that stores data, instructions and programs, either temporarily or permanently.
Functions of memory

items: Data storage and retrieval — holds temporary data (RAM) and permanent data (hard disk), letting the CPU reach what it needs.
Data processing — RAM supplies the CPU with the information it needs for calculations and program execution.
Program execution — holds the currently running programs and their data.
Buffering and caching — acts as a buffer for transfers between devices, and provides cache memory for frequently used data.

blocks.text: Units of measurement

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: A kilobyte is 1024 bytes, not 1000, because memory is counted in binary. 8 bits make a byte, and 4 bits make a nibble — the small unit that questions like to ask about.
Types of memory
A digital computer has two kinds: primary and secondary.
Primary memory

Also called system or internal memory, it is the processor's working area — the main memory. It holds data and instructions during processing and is the only memory the CPU can address directly. It is fast but expensive and small. Examples: RAM, ROM, cache memory.
RAM (Random Access Memory) is the read/write memory. The CPU can reach any location in any order without passing through the others. It needs power to hold data.

items: SRAM (Static RAM) — holds data as long as the machine is on. Expensive but faster than DRAM, storing data as voltage and using less power. Used for cache memory.
DRAM (Dynamic RAM) — loses its data after a few milliseconds even while the machine is on, so it needs a refreshing circuit. Cheaper but slower than SRAM, storing data as charge and using more power.

blocks.text: RAM is volatile: its contents are lost when power is off. It is fast, and it is what makes multitasking possible.

ROM (Read Only Memory) cannot be written to in normal use. It is non-volatile — the contents survive power being cut — and it holds the permanent programs, including the firmware and the instructions needed to start the machine.
ROMs are either mask-programmed, burnt at the factory by the chip manufacturer, or user-programmed: PROM, EPROM and EEPROM can be programmed by the user.

head: RAM
ROM
rows: Volatile — lost when power is off
Holds data and instructions being processed
Holds the programs a device needs to operate
blocks.caption: RAM versus ROM

blocks.text: Secondary memory
Secondary memory holds data for the long term. It is not directly accessible to the CPU and is cheaper per bit, but slower.

blocks.caption: The inside of a hard disk drive.

blocks.text: Hard Disk Drive (HDD) — magnetic storage on spinning platters.
Pen drive — flash memory; files can simply be dragged onto it, no harder than attaching a file to an email.
Solid State Drive (SSD) — stores data on instantly-accessible memory chips rather than spinning disks, replacing mechanical hard disks with flash-based memory that is significantly faster.

items: Low access time; files transfer faster.
Low power requirements, so better battery life in laptops and tablets.
Shock resistant, reducing data loss if a device is dropped.
Preferred for gaming, because levels and files load faster.

head: SSD
HDD
rows: Semiconductor, NAND flash, no moving parts
Susceptible to damage from moving parts
blocks.caption: SSD versus HDD

blocks.text: Flash memory is used in memory chips and cards. Magnetic tape — thin plastic ribbon — is used mainly for audio, video and backup; it needs a tape drive and accesses data sequentially.
Cloud storage

Cloud storage keeps data on remote servers reached over the internet, managed by a third-party provider. Capacity is effectively large and depends on the plan; access speed depends on the connection. It is used for backup, file sharing and collaboration, and lets a business scale without buying hardware.

head: Primary memory
Secondary memory
rows: Not direct — needs primary memory as a go-between
Hard disk, CD, DVD, pen drive
blocks.caption: Primary versus secondary memory

blocks.text: Output devices translate processed information into a form people can understand. The computer works in 0s and 1s; a person needs words, numbers or pictures.
Soft copy and hard copy

head: Soft copy
Hard copy
rows: The electronic version, held in memory
No — it is a virtual copy
Yes — it is on paper or transparency
blocks.caption: Two kinds of output
A CRT monitor, and how it works.

blocks.text: Types of monitor

CRT (Cathode Ray Tube) works much like a television set. An electron gun sends a beam at a positively charged, phosphor-coated screen. The phosphor is arranged as a grid of dots, and the smallest dot the gun can focus on is a pixel. When the electrons strike the phosphor it gives off visible light. The gun scans every pixel from the top-left, moving right then dropping down a line at a time; varying the beam's intensity builds the picture. A colour CRT uses three guns for red, green and blue, which is why colour monitors are called RGB monitors.

items: Comparatively cheaper than other monitors.
Better brightness.
A larger viewing angle, almost 180 degrees.

blocks.text: LCD (Liquid Crystal Display) uses liquid crystals whose alignment controls how light passes through, with a backlight behind them. Thin and low-power.
LED (Light Emitting Diode) monitors use light-emitting diodes for backlighting, giving better contrast and lower power than an LCD.
Printers
Dot matrix is an impact printer — it strikes the paper through an inked ribbon, building each character from a grid of pins.
Inkjet is a non-impact printer that sprays tiny droplets of ink onto the page.
Laser printers are non-impact: a laser draws the image as static charge on a drum, which picks up toner, and heat fuses the toner to the paper. Fast and sharp.
3D printers build a three-dimensional object layer by layer rather than putting marks on paper.
Speakers produce audio output. A USB device can serve as an output destination as well as an input source.
A collection of computer programs that tell the hardware what to do.
Software is usually divided into system software, which runs the machine (operating systems, device drivers, utilities), and application software, which does a job for the user.
Utility software

Utilities maintain and look after the computer: antivirus, disk cleanup, backup, file compression and similar. They are not the point of owning a computer, but without them it slowly stops working well.
Open source software

Open source software is released under a licence that lets anyone see, modify and share the source code. The opposite is proprietary software, where the source is kept secret and the program is licensed rather than sold.
Mobile applications
Apps written for phones and tablets. They are usually distributed through an app store, run inside a sandboxed environment, and are designed for touch input and a small screen.
Web-based applications

Applications that run in a browser rather than being installed. The advantages are that there is nothing to install, everyone is always on the current version, and the same application works on any operating system. The corresponding limitation is that it needs an internet connection.

mcq.q: What type of input device is a mouse?
mcq.teacher_note: A mouse reports position and clicks — it points. It does not scan, process or store.

mcq.q: What type of input does a keyboard primarily provide?
mcq.teacher_note: Textual input. Other devices handle audio (microphone), images (scanner) and motion (joystick).

mcq.q: A microphone is primarily used for:
mcq.teacher_note: A microphone captures sound. Displaying is output, scanning is a scanner's job, and processing is the CPU's.

mcq.q: What is the primary function of a scanner?
mcq.teacher_note: A scanner captures a digital image of a physical document. Storing is memory, displaying is a monitor, and sound is a speaker.

mcq.q: A webcam is mainly used for:
mcq.teacher_note: A webcam captures images and video, chiefly for video calls.

mcq.q: A touchpad is commonly found in:
mcq.teacher_note: Laptops — a touch pad replaces the mouse where there is no desk to push one across.

mcq.q: A barcode reader is used to:
mcq.teacher_note: It reads the data encoded in the stripes of a bar code.

mcq.q: What does QR in QR code stand for?
mcq.teacher_note: Quick Response — the code was designed to be read quickly.

mcq.q: In which sector are computers used for simulations, design and automation?
mcq.teacher_note: Manufacturing — this is computer-aided design and computer-aided manufacturing.

mcq.q: What is the primary function of the CPU in a computer system?
mcq.teacher_note: The CPU executes instructions, and the operations it performs are arithmetic and logical. Input is a device's job, storage is memory's, and graphics rendering belongs to the GPU.

mcq.q: Which component of a computer system is responsible for executing instructions?
mcq.teacher_note: The CPU executes instructions. RAM and the hard drive hold data; the monitor displays it.

mcq.q: The CPU is also known as the:
mcq.teacher_note: The brain of the computer — it does the thinking. The heart is sometimes used for the power supply or the clock, but the established phrase is "brain".

mcq.q: The speed of a CPU is measured in:
mcq.teacher_note: Hertz — cycles per second. Bits and bytes measure data; joules measure energy.

mcq.q: What is the role of registers in the CPU?
mcq.teacher_note: Registers are temporary, high-speed storage inside the CPU — the fastest memory in the machine.

mcq.q: The ALU is responsible for:
mcq.teacher_note: The ALU performs arithmetic and logical operations. Controlling flow is the Control Unit's job.

mcq.q: The main function of the CU is to:
options: Increase the speed of the computer
mcq.teacher_note: The Control Unit fetches, decodes and sees instructions executed. Logical comparisons are the ALU's.

mcq.q: The CU directs the flow of:
options: Data and instructions within the CPU
Electrical signals in the power supply
mcq.teacher_note: It directs the flow of data and instructions between the components of the system.

mcq.q: What is the role of the motherboard in a computer system?
options: Connect all hardware components and provide communication between them
mcq.teacher_note: The motherboard connects the components and lets them communicate. It distributes power but does not manage the supply; executing is the CPU's job and permanent storage is the disk's.

mcq.q: The motherboard is also known as the:
mcq.teacher_note: The main circuit board — the backbone everything else plugs into.

mcq.q: Which slot on the motherboard is used to install a graphics card?
mcq.teacher_note: PCIe is the expansion slot for a graphics card. SATA and IDE are for storage; DIMM is for RAM.

mcq.q: The data bus is responsible for:
options: Transferring data between components inside a computer
Managing power distribution inside the CPU
mcq.teacher_note: A bus transfers data between components. It is a pathway, not a store.

mcq.q: Which of the following best describes a bus in computer architecture?
options: A communication pathway for transferring data
mcq.teacher_note: A bus is a communication pathway. Watch for the storage-device distractor — it appears often.

mcq.q: The smallest unit of memory in a computer is:
mcq.teacher_note: The bit — a single 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte.

mcq.q: 1 Kilobyte (KB) =
mcq.teacher_note: 1024 bytes. It is not 1000, because memory is counted in binary: 2<sup>10</sup> = 1024.

mcq.q: Which of the following is the largest memory unit?
mcq.teacher_note: Petabyte — the order runs KB, MB, GB, TB, PB, EB.

mcq.q: What is the main function of RAM in a computer system?
options: To store temporary data for quick access
To connect the computer to the internet
mcq.teacher_note: RAM holds temporary data for fast access while the machine is on. Permanent storage is the disk's job.

mcq.q: Which of the following types of RAM is faster?
mcq.teacher_note: SRAM is faster than DRAM — but costlier, which is why DRAM is used for main memory and SRAM for cache. ROM is not a type of RAM at all.

mcq.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of ROM?
mcq.teacher_note: ROM is non-volatile: its contents survive power being removed.

mcq.q: Which of the following types of ROM can be erased and rewritten?
mcq.teacher_note: Both EPROM and EEPROM. PROM can be written once only. EPROM is erased with ultraviolet light; EEPROM electrically.

mcq.q: Cache memory is used to:
mcq.teacher_note: Cache holds frequently accessed data close to the processor, so the CPU is not left waiting for main memory.

mcq.q: Which type of RAM requires constant refreshing?
mcq.teacher_note: DRAM leaks its charge and must be refreshed constantly. SRAM does not.

mcq.q: Which of the following is an example of secondary memory?
mcq.teacher_note: The hard disk is secondary memory. RAM, ROM and cache are all primary.

mcq.q: SSDs are faster than HDDs because:
options: They use a magnetic storage system
mcq.teacher_note: No moving parts means no waiting for a disk to spin and a head to seek — access is nearly instant.

mcq.q: The main disadvantage of SSDs compared to HDDs is:
mcq.teacher_note: Higher cost per GB. SSDs are faster, have fewer moving parts (none) and are available in large capacities — they just cost more.

mcq.q: Computers can perform different tasks in different circumstances because of which characteristic?
mcq.teacher_note: Versatility — the program decides the job, so changing the program changes what the machine does. Reliability is about consistency, accuracy about correctness, and storage capacity about how much it can hold.

mcq.q: A computer does not suffer from fatigue or boredom, making it capable of continuous operation. This feature is known as:
mcq.teacher_note: Diligence is the ability to keep working without tiring. Do not confuse it with reliability, which is about producing the same result consistently.

mcq.q: Which characteristic of a computer ensures that it provides the correct output if given correct input?
mcq.teacher_note: Accuracy — and note the condition in the question: correct input AND a correct program. Wrong input gives a wrong answer, which is what GIGO describes.

mcq.q: Which fraction of a second is equivalent to one billionth of a second?
mcq.teacher_note: One nanosecond is 10<sup>-9</sup> s. Milli is 10<sup>-3</sup>, micro is 10<sup>-6</sup>, pico is 10<sup>-12</sup>.

mcq.q: Which is the term used to describe the concept where incorrect input leads to incorrect output?
mcq.teacher_note: GIGO — Garbage In, Garbage Out. FIFO (first in, first out) and LIFO (last in, first out) are queue and stack orders, not error terms.

mcq.q: The function of an output device is to:
mcq.teacher_note: Output devices present the results of processing to the user. Processing is the CPU, storage is memory or disk, and taking input is the job of an input device.

mcq.q: The most commonly used output device for visual display is:
mcq.teacher_note: The monitor is the standard visual display. A printer produces paper, a mouse is an input device and a speaker produces sound.

mcq.q: Which of the following is used for hardcopy output?
mcq.teacher_note: Hard copy means a permanent physical copy, which only the printer produces. The others are soft-copy or audio output.

mcq.q: The full form of CRT is:
mcq.teacher_note: Cathode Ray Tube — the vacuum tube technology used in older televisions and monitors, in which a beam of electrons is fired at a phosphor screen.

mcq.q: Which display technology uses liquid crystals?
mcq.teacher_note: LCD — Liquid Crystal Display. Note that many screens sold as LED are actually LCD panels with LED backlighting.

mcq.q: Which of the following has the lowest power consumption?
mcq.teacher_note: LED is the most efficient. CRT and plasma are the heaviest users, which is one reason plasma screens disappeared.

mcq.q: Which of the following is an impact printer?
mcq.teacher_note: The dot matrix printer strikes an inked ribbon against the paper, which is what makes it an impact printer. Laser, inkjet and thermal are all non-impact.

mcq.q: Which printer is best for producing high-quality text documents?
mcq.teacher_note: A laser printer gives the sharpest text and is fastest for long documents. Inkjet is better for photographs; dot matrix is lowest quality.

mcq.q: Which type of printer uses a toner cartridge?
mcq.teacher_note: Laser printers use a toner cartridge containing dry powder. Inkjet uses liquid ink; dot matrix uses an inked ribbon; thermal uses heated paper.

mcq.q: A common application of impact printers is:
mcq.teacher_note: Because the print head physically strikes the paper, an impact printer can press through several layers at once, so it is used for multi-part forms such as invoices and delivery notes. Receipts are now mostly printed on thermal printers; impact printers cannot do high-resolution images.

mcq.q: Which device is used for audio output?
mcq.teacher_note: The speaker converts the electrical audio signal into sound. A scanner is an input device.

mcq.q: What is the function of a sound card in a computer?
mcq.teacher_note: The sound card converts digital audio to an analogue signal for output, and analogue input to digital. Storing files is storage; amplifying is the job of an amplifier, usually inside powered speakers.

mcq.q: Which port is commonly used for connecting external storage devices?
mcq.teacher_note: USB connects external drives, flash drives and most other peripherals. HDMI and VGA carry video; Ethernet carries network traffic.

mcq.q: Which USB port is reversible and supports high-speed data transfer?
mcq.teacher_note: USB Type-C has a symmetrical connector that goes in either way, and supports the highest transfer rates and power delivery of the common USB connectors.

mcq.q: Which port is primarily used to connect a computer to a monitor?
mcq.teacher_note: Both VGA and HDMI connect a computer to a monitor — that is exactly why the "both" option is correct and the single-answer ones are traps. HDMI is the modern standard; VGA is the older one.

mcq.q: HDMI ports are used for:
mcq.teacher_note: HDMI carries digital video and audio on one cable, which is why it replaced the separate VGA plus audio leads.

mcq.q: Which connector is mostly used for wired internet connections?
mcq.teacher_note: Ethernet. The others carry data, video or power, not network traffic.

mcq.q: Which port has mostly replaced VGA for connecting displays?
mcq.teacher_note: HDMI replaced VGA because it is digital, carries audio as well, and gives a sharper picture.

mcq.q: Computer software refers to:

options.text: A collection of programs and data

mcq.teacher_note: Software is the programs and their data. Physical components are hardware, and software is not limited to system programs — applications count too.

mcq.q: Software that directly interacts with computer hardware and provides a platform for other software is called:
mcq.teacher_note: That is the definition of system software. Application software needs a platform rather than providing one.

mcq.q: Which of the following is an example of system software?
mcq.teacher_note: Windows is an operating system, so it is system software. The others are application software that runs on top of an operating system.

mcq.q: The primary function of an operating system is to:
mcq.teacher_note: The OS manages the processor, memory, files and devices, and provides the platform applications run on. The rest are things it helps with, not its primary function.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT an operating system?
mcq.teacher_note: Chrome is a web browser — an application. Windows, Linux and macOS are all operating systems.

mcq.q: Which of these is an example of an open-source operating system?
mcq.teacher_note: Linux is open source: its source code is published and anyone may modify and share it. The others are proprietary.

mcq.q: Which operating system is used in Apple Mac computers?
mcq.teacher_note: Apple Macs run macOS. Android is Google mobile OS, iOS is Apple mobile OS.

mcq.q: The operating system that runs on smartphones is:
mcq.teacher_note: Android is the mobile operating system here; the others are desktop or legacy systems.

mcq.q: A compiler converts:

options.text: High-level code into machine code at once
Code line by line during execution

mcq.teacher_note: A compiler translates the whole high-level program in one go. Converting assembly is the assembler; line-by-line is the interpreter.

mcq.q: An interpreter executes programs:

options.text: By converting into binary code first

mcq.teacher_note: An interpreter reads and runs one statement at a time, without producing a separate machine-code file first.

mcq.q: Which language translator converts assembly language into machine code?
mcq.teacher_note: The assembler handles assembly language. A debugger finds faults; it does not translate.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT a utility software?
mcq.teacher_note: A video player is application software — it does a task for the user. The others maintain the computer, which is what utilities do.

mcq.q: The function of a device driver is to:

options.text: Enable hardware components to communicate with the OS

mcq.teacher_note: A driver is the translator between the operating system and one piece of hardware — a printer, a graphics card — so the OS does not need to know the details of every device.

mcq.q: Which of the following software is used to detect and remove viruses?
mcq.teacher_note: Antivirus software. A compiler translates programs, a driver talks to hardware, and the OS manages the system.

mcq.q: Application software is designed to:
mcq.teacher_note: Application software does the job the user actually wants — writing, calculating, browsing. The others are system-software functions.

mcq.q: Which of the following is an example of application software?
mcq.teacher_note: Word is an application. Windows is an OS, Disk Defragmenter is a utility and a printer driver is system software.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of application software?
mcq.teacher_note: Managing hardware is the operating system job. The others are tasks applications do.

mcq.q: Tailored software is:
mcq.teacher_note: Tailored (bespoke) software is written for one organisation particular requirements. Packaged software is the opposite.

mcq.q: Which of the following is an example of package software?
mcq.teacher_note: Microsoft Office is sold to millions of customers unchanged. The other three are all bespoke, written for one organisation.

mcq.q: Which of the following is an open-source software?
mcq.teacher_note: Linux is open source. Office, Windows and Photoshop are all proprietary.

mcq.q: Proprietary software is software that:

options.text: Has a source code available to the public
Is owned and licensed by a company

mcq.teacher_note: Proprietary means owned: the source code is closed and you hold only a licence to use it.

mcq.q: Which of these is NOT a characteristic of open-source software?
mcq.teacher_note: Requiring paid licences is a proprietary trait. Open source is normally free to obtain, though paid support is often sold alongside it.

mcq.q: Which software is specifically designed to run on mobile devices?
mcq.teacher_note: Mobile applications are built for phones and tablets. Web apps run in a browser; desktop and server software run elsewhere.

mcq.q: Which of these is an example of a mobile application?
mcq.teacher_note: Google Maps on a phone is a mobile app. The others are desktop software or an operating system.

mcq.q: Which app store is used to download iOS mobile applications?
mcq.teacher_note: Apple App Store for iOS. Google Play is for Android.

mcq.q: Which of the following is an example of a web-based application?
mcq.teacher_note: Google Docs runs in a browser over the internet. The others are installed on the machine.

mcq.q: Web applications require:

options.text: A web browser and internet connection

mcq.teacher_note: A web app needs a browser and a connection; nothing is installed locally, which is the whole point of it.

mcq.q: Which technology is commonly used to develop web-based applications?
mcq.teacher_note: HTML, CSS and JavaScript are the standard trio for web applications. Python is often used on the server, but the front end is these three.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a web-based application?

options.text: Can run on any device with a browser
Requires installation on a local machine

mcq.teacher_note: Requiring local installation is the opposite of a web app: the defining feature is that you do NOT install it.

short.q: List the three components of the CPU.
short.a: The Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU), which performs arithmetic and logical operations; the Control Unit (CU), which directs the other components using control signals; and registers, the small high-speed storage locations inside the CPU.

short.q: What are the main functions of a CPU?
short.a: It gives commands to all parts of the system; controls the sequence of operations and the storage of data; performs arithmetic such as addition and subtraction; and supervises and controls the input and output devices.

short.q: What is the Control Unit?
short.a: The Control Unit is the part of the CPU responsible for controlling all the components of the computer. It uses control signals to tell the components how to carry out a program's instructions, and directs the movement of electronic signals between them.

short.q: Define the role of registers.
short.a: Registers are small, high-speed storage locations inside the CPU. They hold the data, instructions and addresses the CPU needs at this instant, working closely with the CU and the ALU to hold data, intermediate results and instructions fetched from main memory.

short.q: Identify two common manufacturers of CPU.
short.a: Intel and AMD (Advanced Micro Devices).

short.q: List the five steps involved in the instruction cycle of the CPU.
short.a: Fetch — get the next instruction from memory. Decode — work out what operation is needed. Execute — carry it out. Write back — store the result in memory. Update program counter — point at the next instruction.

short.q: Why are registers considered faster storage or execute than RAM?
short.a: Because they are inside the CPU itself. Reading RAM means a journey across the bus and a wait for the memory controller; a register is already there. Registers are also built from the fastest (and most expensive) memory technology, which is why there are so few of them.

short.q: Compare arithmetic operations with logical operations performed by the ALU.
short.a:
Arithmetic operations — addition, subtraction, multiplication, division — produce a numeric result and are used for calculation.

Logical operations — AND, OR, NOT, together with relational comparisons such as =, >, <, >=, <= — produce a true/false result. They are used for comparison, and they are what give the machine the ability to make decisions.

short.q: What is the primary function of the motherboard in a computer system?
short.a: To connect all the hardware components and provide communication between them. It is the central hub carrying the CPU socket, memory slots, expansion slots, storage connectors and external ports, and it distributes power.

short.q: List three components that are directly connected to the motherboard.
short.a: The CPU (in its socket), RAM modules (in their slots), and storage devices (through SATA ports). Others include graphics and network cards in PCIe slots, and the power supply.

short.q: What is the primary function of a data bus in a computer system?
short.a: To transfer data between the CPU, memory and peripheral devices so that they can communicate. It is the communication pathway — the backbone — of the system.

short.q: List two types of slots found on a motherboard.
short.a: PCIe slots (for expansion cards such as graphics, sound and network cards) and DIMM slots (for RAM modules). SATA connectors for storage drives are also commonly given.

short.q: Explain why the motherboard is often called the "backbone" of a computer.
short.a: Because every component connects to it and communicates through it. The CPU, memory, storage and peripherals all plug into the motherboard, and the buses and chipsets on it carry the data between them. Remove the motherboard and the parts have no way to work together — exactly what a backbone does.

short.q: What role does the data bus play in data transfer?
short.a: It carries the data itself between components, following defined protocols for how data is formatted, transmitted and received. Its width and speed determine how much can be transferred at once and how quickly, and it often includes error-checking so that what arrives is what was sent.

short.q: Define primary memory.
short.a: Primary memory — also called main, internal or system memory — is the working area for the processor. It holds the data and instructions currently being processed and is the only memory the CPU can address directly. It is fast but expensive and relatively small. Examples: RAM, ROM and cache memory.

short.q: Give two examples of primary memory.
short.a: RAM (Random Access Memory) and ROM (Read Only Memory). Cache memory and registers are also primary memory.

short.q: What type of memory is directly accessible by the CPU?
short.a: Primary memory — RAM, ROM and cache. Secondary memory cannot be addressed directly; its contents must be brought into primary memory first.

short.q: Define secondary memory.
short.a: Secondary memory — also called auxiliary, external or backup memory — holds data and programs for future use. It is non-volatile, much cheaper per bit, slower, and not directly accessible to the CPU. Examples: hard disk, SSD, CD, DVD and pen drive.

short.q: List four examples of secondary memory.
short.a: Hard disk drive (HDD), solid state drive (SSD), pen drive (flash memory) and optical disc (CD, DVD, Blu-ray). Magnetic tape is another.

short.q: What is the purpose of a pen drive?
short.a: To carry data between computers. It is a small, portable flash-memory device: files can be dragged onto it and carried away, no harder than attaching a file to an email. It is non-volatile, so it needs no power to keep the data.

short.q: Explain why primary memory is called volatile.
short.a: Because it loses its contents when the power is switched off. RAM stores data as electrical charge or voltage, and without a supply that state disappears. That is why work held only in RAM is lost in a power cut, and why data you want to keep must be saved to secondary storage. ROM is the exception among primary memories — it is non-volatile.

short.q: What is the purpose of ROM in a computer?
short.a: ROM stores the firmware and the essential instructions the machine needs to start up. Because it is non-volatile, those instructions are still there when the power comes back, which is what allows the computer to boot before anything has been loaded from disk. It also holds permanent system data that does not change.

short.q: If you need to store a large amount of data permanently, which type of memory would you choose and why?
short.a: Secondary memory — a hard disk or SSD. Primary memory is volatile, so the data would be lost at switch-off, and it is far too expensive per gigabyte for large volumes. Secondary memory is non-volatile and much cheaper per bit, so it is the only practical choice for permanent bulk storage.

short.q: Define computer. List any two features of a computer system.
short.a:
A computer is a multipurpose, programmable, electronic data processing device that accepts input, processes it, produces information as output, and can store it if necessary.

Any two of: speed (billions of instructions per second), accuracy, diligence (repeat work without tiring), versatility, automation, reliability, storage and word length.

short.q: What is the difference between soft copy and hard copy output?
short.a: A soft copy is the electronic version of a document, held in the computer's memory and shown on screen — it is a virtual copy you cannot touch. A hard copy is the printed version on paper or transparency, which you can touch.

short.q: Differentiate between impact and non-impact printers.
short.a:
An impact printer strikes the paper through an inked ribbon, as a dot matrix printer does with its pins. It is noisy and slower, but it can print through carbon paper to make multi-part forms.

A non-impact printer marks the page without contact — inkjet sprays droplets, a laser printer fuses toner with heat, a 3D printer builds in layers. These are quiet and faster, but cannot produce carbon copies.

short.q: Write the full forms: GIGO, CAI, POS, MRI, CT, CAD, ns, I/O, CPU, Hz, KHz, MHz, GHz, THz, PHz, EHz, bit, E-commerce, IPOS.
short.a: GIGO — Garbage In, Garbage Out — if you feed a computer wrong data it will produce wrong results. CAI — Computer-Aided Instruction, learning that uses the computer as a tutor. POS — Point of Sale, the place where a retail transaction is completed. MRI — Magnetic Resonance Imaging, a scanning technique used in hospitals. CT — Computed Tomography, an X-ray scan that builds a cross-section of the body. CAD — Computer-Aided Design, drawing and modelling on a computer. ns — nanosecond, one billionth of a second. I/O — Input/Output. CPU — Central Processing Unit. Hz — Hertz, one cycle per second. KHz — Kilohertz, one thousand cycles per second. MHz — Megahertz, one million cycles per second. GHz — Gigahertz, one thousand million cycles per second. THz — Terahertz, one million million cycles per second. PHz — Petahertz, one thousand million million cycles per second. EHz — Exahertz, one thousand million million million cycles per second. bit — binary digit, a single 0 or 1 — the smallest unit of data. E-commerce — Electronic commerce, buying and selling over the internet. IPOS — Input, Process, Output, Storage — the cycle every computer follows.

short.q: Write the full forms: BCR, QR Code, USB.
short.a: BCR — Bar Code Reader. QR Code — Quick Response Code, the square two-dimensional barcode read by a phone camera. USB — Universal Serial Bus.

short.q: Write the full forms: CPU, CU, ALU.
short.a: CPU — Central Processing Unit. CU — Control Unit, the part of the CPU that directs the other parts. ALU — Arithmetic and Logic Unit, the part of the CPU that does the calculations and comparisons.

short.q: Write the full forms: BIOS, PCIe, UEFI.
short.a: BIOS — Basic Input/Output System. PCIe — Peripheral Component Interconnect Express, the slot a graphics card plugs into. UEFI — Unified Extensible Firmware Interface, the modern replacement for the BIOS.

short.q: Write the full forms: RAM, ROM, SRAM, DRAM, GB, EPROM, EEPROM, SSD, HDD, CD, DVD, BD.
short.a: RAM — Random Access Memory. ROM — Read Only Memory. SRAM — Static Random Access Memory, fast and expensive, used for cache. DRAM — Dynamic Random Access Memory, slower and cheaper, used for main memory. GB — Gigabyte, roughly one thousand million bytes. EPROM — Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory, erased with ultraviolet light. EEPROM — Electrically Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory, erased with an electric signal. SSD — Solid State Drive. HDD — Hard Disk Drive. CD — Compact Disc. DVD — Digital Versatile Disc. BD — Blu-ray Disc.

short.q: Write the full forms: CRT, LED, VGA, LCD, 3D.
short.a: CRT — Cathode Ray Tube, the technology inside older televisions and monitors. LED — Light Emitting Diode. VGA — Video Graphics Array, a display standard and the connector it uses. LCD — Liquid Crystal Display. 3D — Three-Dimensional.

short.q: Write the full forms: GPL, ERP.
short.a: GPL — General Public License, the licence Linux and much other open-source software is released under. ERP — Enterprise Resource Planning, software that runs all of a company's departments from one database.

short.q: Self Test 1.1: Define computer.
short.a: A computer is an electronic device that takes in data, processes it according to a set of instructions, produces output, and stores the results for later use. It works through the IPO cycle — input, process, output — with storage alongside.

short.q: Self Test 1.1: What is memory?
short.a: Memory is the part of the computer that holds data and instructions so the processor can reach them quickly. It is divided into primary memory — RAM and ROM, which the CPU works on directly — and secondary memory, such as a hard disk, which holds data permanently.

short.q: Self Test 1.1: List any two features of computer system.
short.a:
1. Speed — it carries out millions of operations a second.
2. Accuracy — it does not tire or make careless slips; errors almost always come from the data or the instructions it was given.
Others: diligence, versatility, large storage capacity, and automation.

short.q: Self Test 1.2: List any three application areas of computers.
short.a: Any three of: education (online classes, research, learning software); medicine (patient records, scanners, diagnosis support); banking (ATMs, online banking, card payments). Others include communication, business, industry, the military, entertainment, aviation and computer-aided design.

short.q: Self Test 1.2: What is CAD?
short.a: CAD — Computer-Aided Design — is the use of a computer to create, modify and check designs. Engineers and architects use it to draw precisely, to test a design before anything is built, and to change it quickly. Examples include AutoCAD and SolidWorks.

short.q: Self Test 1.3: List the types of mouse.
short.a: The common types are the mechanical mouse (with a rolling ball), the optical mouse (which tracks movement with a light — the usual kind now), the laser mouse (more precise, works on more surfaces), the wireless mouse (no cable) and the trackball, where the ball is on top and the body stays still.

short.q: Self Test 1.3: What is the purpose of a keyboard?
short.a: A keyboard is the main device for entering text and commands. Pressing a key sends a code to the computer, which displays or acts on the character. It is also used for shortcuts and for controlling programs — the arrow keys and function keys do more than type.

short.q: Self Test 1.3: Define touchpad.
short.a: A touchpad is a flat, touch-sensitive surface used instead of a mouse, mostly on laptops. Sliding a finger across it moves the pointer, and tapping or clicking the built-in buttons selects. It does the same job as a mouse in far less space.

short.q: Self Test 1.3: What is a scanner?
short.a: A scanner is an input device that converts a physical image or document into a digital file. It works by shining light on the page and recording what is reflected. Scanners are used for photographs, documents, and — with OCR software — for turning printed text into text that can be edited.

short.q: Self Test 1.4: What is CPU?
short.a: The CPU — Central Processing Unit — is the part of the computer that carries out instructions. It is often called the brain of the computer. It fetches an instruction from memory, works out what it means, and executes it, repeating that cycle millions of times a second.

short.q: Self Test 1.4: Write the functions of CPU.
short.a:
1. Fetch — get the next instruction from memory.
2. Decode — work out what the instruction means.
3. Execute — carry it out, doing any calculation in the ALU.
4. Store — write the result back to memory.
5. Control — direct and coordinate the rest of the hardware.

short.q: Self Test 1.4: What is CU?
short.a: The Control Unit is the part of the CPU that directs operations. It does not process data itself — it fetches instructions, decodes them, and sends control signals telling the other parts what to do, keeping everything in step. It manages the fetch–decode–execute cycle.

short.q: Self Test 1.5: What is a motherboard?
short.a: The motherboard is the main circuit board of the computer. Everything connects to it — the CPU, memory, storage and expansion cards. It carries the data buses that let those parts communicate, and it supplies power and the connections for peripherals.

short.q: Self Test 1.5: What is a data bus?
short.a: A data bus is a set of parallel wires on the motherboard that carries data between the CPU, memory and other components. Its width — 32-bit, 64-bit — is how many bits it can carry at once, which is a large part of what determines how fast the system feels.

short.q: Self Test 1.5: Write down two importance of a data bus.
short.a:
1. It is the pathway for all data — without it, the parts of the computer could not communicate at all.

2. Its width determines performance: a wider bus moves more data per transfer, so the system runs faster.

short.q: Self Test 1.6: Write the importance of primary memory.
short.a: Primary memory is where the CPU keeps the data and instructions it is working on right now. Nothing can be executed before it is loaded into primary memory, so without it the processor would have nothing to work on. Its speed is what keeps the CPU supplied — a processor is only as fast as the memory feeding it.

short.q: Self Test 1.6: Why is secondary memory required?
short.a: Primary memory is fast but expensive, and it loses everything when the power goes. Secondary storage solves both problems: it is cheap enough for large amounts of data, and it keeps data permanently. It is also how programs survive being switched off.

short.q: Self Test 1.6: Write the characteristics of primary memory.
short.a: It is fast — far quicker than any disk. It is directly accessible by the CPU. Most of it, RAM, is volatile. It is more expensive per unit than secondary storage, so machines have less of it. And it is limited in capacity compared with a hard disk.

short.q: Self Test 1.6: What is volatile memory?
short.a: Volatile memory loses its contents when the power is switched off. RAM is the standard example — which is why unsaved work disappears in a power cut. It is used for data the computer needs only while it is running.

short.q: Self Test 1.6: Define non-volatile memory.
short.a: Non-volatile memory keeps its contents without power. ROM, flash memory, hard disks and SSDs are all non-volatile — the data is still there after the machine is switched off and on again.

short.q: Self Test 1.7: Define output device.
short.a: An output device is any piece of hardware that presents the results of processing to the user — turning data the computer holds into something a person can see, hear or touch. A monitor, a printer and a speaker are all output devices.

short.q: Self Test 1.7: Write any two advantage of LED monitor.
short.a:
1. It uses less power than older LCD or CRT screens.
2. It gives better brightness and contrast, with more accurate colour. It is also thinner and lasts longer than a CCFL-backlit display.

short.q: Self Test 1.7: What is LCD monitor?
short.a: An LCD — Liquid Crystal Display — monitor is a flat-panel screen that forms the picture using liquid crystals that change how they let light through. It does not emit light itself, so it needs a backlight. It replaced the CRT because it is thin, light and uses far less power.

short.q: Self Test 1.8: What is a printer?
short.a: A printer is an output device that produces a permanent copy of what is on screen — text or images — on paper. It is the standard way to get a hard copy of a document.

short.q: Self Test 1.8: What is an inkjet printer?
short.a: An inkjet printer makes an image by spraying tiny droplets of liquid ink onto the page from a moving print head. It is cheap to buy and good at photographs and colour, but the ink is expensive and printing is slow compared with a laser printer.

short.q: Self Test 1.8: What is a laser printer?
short.a: A laser printer uses a laser beam and toner powder rather than liquid ink. The laser draws the image on a drum, toner sticks to the charged areas, and heat fuses it to the paper. It is faster and cheaper per page than an inkjet, and produces sharp text — but costs more to buy.

short.q: Self Test 1.8: What is VGA?
short.a: VGA — Video Graphics Array — is a standard for connecting a computer to a monitor, and the connector used for it. It carries an analog video signal. It has largely been replaced by digital connections such as HDMI and DisplayPort.

short.q: Self Test 1.8: What is USB?
short.a: USB — Universal Serial Bus — is the standard connector for attaching peripherals to a computer: keyboards, mice, printers, storage, phones. It is "universal" in that one port type serves many devices, and it usually supplies power as well as carrying data.

short.q: Self Test 1.9: Define software.
short.a: Software is a collection of programs and instructions that tell the computer what to do. Unlike hardware, it cannot be touched. It falls mainly into system software, such as the operating system, and application software, such as a word processor.

short.q: Self Test 1.9: List the types of computer software.
short.a:
1. System software — the operating system, device drivers and utility programs that run the machine.
2. Application software — programs that do a job for the user, such as word processors, spreadsheets, browsers and games.
A third group sometimes given is programming software — compilers, interpreters and editors, used to write other programs.

short.q: Self Test 1.9: Define open-source software.
short.a: Open-source software is software whose source code is published, so anyone can read, change and share it. It is usually free. Linux, Firefox and LibreOffice are examples. The opposite is proprietary software, where the code is kept secret and use is licensed.

short.q: Self Test 1.9: Write the purpose of a device driver.
short.a: A device driver is a small program that lets the operating system talk to a particular piece of hardware. It translates the operating system's general requests into the specific commands that device understands. Without the right driver, the hardware simply does not work.

short.q: Self Test 1.9: Define language translator.
short.a: A language translator is system software that converts a program written in an assembly or high level language into machine code the computer can execute. The three kinds are the assembler, the compiler and the interpreter.

short.q: Self Test 1.10: Define mobile application.
short.a: A mobile application — usually shortened to an app — is software designed to run on a phone or tablet. It is installed onto the device and typically uses its features, such as the camera, GPS and touchscreen.

short.q: Self Test 1.10: List any two features of the mobile application.
short.a:
1. It is built for touch — large targets, swipes, pinch to zoom.
2. It can use the device's own hardware: camera, GPS, accelerometer. It is also usually designed for small screens and can often work offline.

short.q: Self Test 1.10: What is a web-based application?
short.a: A web-based application is software you use through a browser rather than installing. The program and its data live on a server; the browser is just the window onto it. Web mail and online document editors are typical examples.

short.q: Self Test 1.10: Write features of web based applications.
short.a:
1. No installation — you open it in a browser and it works.
2. It is platform independent, running on any device with a browser.
3. Updates happen on the server, so everyone is on the same version.
4. Data is stored centrally, so it can be reached from anywhere and is easier to back up.
5. It generally needs an internet connection.

short.q: Define data in the context of computer system.
short.a:
Data is the raw material a computer works on: unprocessed facts and figures such as 45, Kathmandu or 2024. On their own they do not tell you much — 45 could be an age, a temperature or a score.

Data is what is entered into the computer through an input device and what it stores. It becomes useful only after it has been processed.

short.q: Define information in the context of computer system.
short.a:
Information is data that has been processed, organised or put into context so that it carries meaning. "The temperature in Kathmandu was 45 °C today" is information; 45 on its own is only data.

That is the point of the IPOS cycle — the computer takes data in, processes it, and puts information out. Information is what lets a person make a decision, which the raw figures on their own do not.

short.q: What do you mean by accuracy of a computer?
short.a:
Accuracy means a computer gives the correct result whenever it is given correct input and a correct program. It is a matter of exactness rather than of judgement: the machine does not round, guess or have an off day.

Accuracy has one important limit, summed up by GIGO — Garbage In, Garbage Out. A computer will faithfully process wrong data and produce a wrong answer, so accuracy depends on the input and the program, not on the machine alone.

short.q: What do you mean by versatility of a computer?
short.a:
Versatility is the ability to turn your hand to completely different kinds of work. The same machine can write a letter, play music, work out a spreadsheet, control a factory robot or render a film.

This is possible because a computer is a general-purpose device: it does whatever the program it is currently running tells it to do. Change the program and you change the machine's job, without changing any hardware.

short.q: What does the term GIGO stand for in computing?
short.a:
GIGO — Garbage In, Garbage Out.

It is the reminder that a computer does exactly what it is told, including when it is told something wrong. If the data or the instructions are faulty, the output will be faulty too, and no amount of processing power will rescue it. The machine has no way of noticing that its input was nonsense.

short.q: Why is the computer referred to as a reliable device?
short.a:
Two reasons. First, it gives the same result every time the same input and the same program are used, so its output can be depended on. Second, it can run for long periods without failing, because it has no moving parts in its processing and memory to wear out in the way a mechanical device does.

Reliability here means consistency, not infallibility — the result is reliable only as long as the input and the program are sound.

short.q: Explain how the computer has impacted everyday life.
short.a:
Communication — email, messaging and video calls make keeping in touch instant and nearly free.

Education — online lessons, reference material and simulations let people learn at their own pace and from anywhere.

Banking and shopping — most payments, transfers and purchases can now be done without visiting a branch or a shop.

Medicine — scanners, patient records and research all depend on computing, so diagnoses are faster and better informed.

Work — documents, accounts, design and manufacturing are all done faster and with fewer errors than by hand.

short.q: Explain why diligence is considered a significant characteristic of computers.
short.a:
Diligence means a computer does not tire, lose concentration or get bored. It can repeat the same calculation millions of times with exactly the same care on the millionth occasion as on the first.

A person doing a repetitive task makes more mistakes as they tire; a computer does not. That is why it is trusted for work that is too long or too monotonous for a person — checking a million records, or running the same test overnight.

short.q: Name two fields where robotics is commonly used.
short.a:
1. Manufacturing — welding, painting and assembly on production lines, especially car plants.

2. Medicine — surgical robots and rehabilitation devices.

Others include agriculture, warehouse logistics, space exploration and defence.

short.q: Explain how computers are used as a teaching tool in education.
short.a:
Through CAI — Computer-Aided Instruction — the computer acts as a tutor. It presents material, sets questions, marks them and adapts to how the student is doing.

It also supports learning by simulation, so a student can run an experiment that would be too expensive, too slow or too dangerous to do for real, and by giving access to reference material, video and interactive diagrams.

short.q: Define the term input device.
short.a:
An input device is any piece of hardware used to get data and instructions from the outside world into the computer, where the processor can work on them.

Input can be text from a keyboard, a position from a mouse, sound from a microphone or an image from a scanner. Whatever the device, its job is the same: to convert what a person does or what the environment provides into the binary signals the computer can store and process.

short.q: What is the main purpose of a mouse?
short.a:
To point at things on screen and select them. Moving the mouse moves a pointer; clicking and dragging let you choose, open, move or resize what is under it.

It is a pointing device, and its purpose is to make interaction direct — you act on the thing you can see, instead of typing a command to describe it.

short.q: What type of input does a microphone capture?
short.a:
Sound — that is, audio. The microphone converts the varying air pressure of speech or music into a continuously varying electrical signal, which the sound card then samples and converts into digital values the computer can store or transmit.

So the input is analogue in nature and is converted to digital, which makes the microphone an important example of the difference between the real world and what the computer stores.

short.q: List any four input devices.
short.a:
1. Keyboard
2. Mouse
3. Scanner
4. Microphone

Others include a webcam, joystick, touchpad, touch screen, bar code reader (BCR) and QR code scanner.

short.q: Explain keyboard and joystick.
short.a:
Keyboard — the main device for entering text. Each key sends a code unique to that key, so the computer knows exactly which character was pressed. It is still the fastest way to get words and numbers into a machine.

Joystick — a stick that tilts in different directions, used to control movement in games, simulators and sometimes machinery such as a crane or a wheelchair. Where a mouse reports a position, a joystick reports a direction and often how far it is being pushed, which suits continuous steering better than pointing.

short.q: How does a scanner differ from a webcam in the type of data it captures?
short.a:
A scanner captures a still, flat image — it converts a physical document or photograph into a digital image file, one line at a time, at high resolution.

A webcam captures moving images — it takes a sequence of frames many times a second, so it records video rather than a single picture.

Both produce pictures, but the scanner is for reproducing documents faithfully while the webcam is for capturing live action.

short.q: List two types of output provided by output devices.
short.a:
1. Soft copy — output shown on a screen, such as a monitor or projector. It is temporary: it disappears when the power goes off or the file is closed.

2. Hard copy — output on paper or another permanent medium, such as a printed page. It can be read without a computer and handed to someone else.

A third, worth remembering, is audio — sound from a speaker or headphones, which is neither soft nor hard copy.

short.q: Define softcopy output.
short.a:
Soft copy is output that exists only in electronic form and is viewed on a screen — a document on a monitor, a projected slide or an e-book.

It can be edited, copied and searched instantly and costs nothing to produce, but it cannot be read without a device and is lost when the power is removed unless it has been saved.

short.q: Define hardcopy output.
short.a:
Hard copy is output produced on a physical, permanent medium — most often paper from a printer, but also film, plastic or a plotter drawing.

It needs no device to read, can be signed, filed and handed over, and survives a power cut. It costs paper and ink, takes time, and cannot be searched or edited once printed.

short.q: What is the difference between a monitor and a printer?
short.a:
A monitor produces soft copy — a temporary, electronic display you look at. A printer produces hard copy — a permanent physical page.

MonitorPrinter
Type of outputSoft copyHard copy
PermanenceTemporary, needs powerPermanent
Running costElectricity onlyPaper, ink or toner
Can be handed overNo, it stays on the screenYes
Can be edited after outputYesNo

short.q: How does a speaker function as an output device?
short.a:
The sound card or audio chip turns the digital audio data held by the computer into a continuously varying electrical signal. The speaker takes that signal and uses it to move a cone back and forth, which pushes the air and creates the sound waves you hear.

So a speaker is an output device because it converts information inside the machine into something a person can sense. It is also a conversion in the other direction from a microphone: digital data becomes analogue sound.

short.q: Which output device would be most suitable for displaying a digital presentation? Explain why.
short.a:
A projector, because it throws the image onto a large screen so a whole room can see it at once.

A monitor would be the choice for one or two people, but in a classroom or meeting the picture has to be big enough for everyone. If no projector is available, a large monitor is the fallback; for very large rooms a wall of screens or an LED panel is used instead.

short.q: Which output device is used for printing high-quality images, and justify your choice?
short.a:
An inkjet printer. It sprays extremely fine droplets of liquid ink onto the paper and can blend several colours at each point, so it produces smooth photographic gradation and a wide colour range.

A laser printer gives sharper text and is faster and cheaper per page, but its strength is text rather than photographs. A dot matrix printer cannot produce photographic quality at all. So for a photograph or a colour poster, inkjet on photo paper is the right choice.

short.q: What is the primary function of an Ethernet port?
short.a:
To connect the computer to a wired local area network, and through it to the internet, using an Ethernet cable.

It carries data between the computer and the network much faster and more reliably than Wi-Fi, with less interference and lower delay, which is why it is preferred for desktop machines, servers and online gaming.

short.q: What is computer software?
short.a:
Software is the set of programs, data and instructions that tells the hardware what to do. It is the part of a computer system you cannot touch.

Hardware on its own does nothing useful — a machine with no program is just metal and silicon. Software is what turns it into a word processor, a calculator or a game. The two depend on each other: hardware carries out the instructions, software supplies them.

short.q: Define system software.
short.a:
System software is the software that runs and manages the computer itself, rather than doing a task for the user. It works in the background and provides the platform that everything else runs on.

It has three main kinds:

1. Operating systems — Windows, Linux, macOS, Android — which manage memory, files, devices and the processor.

2. Utility software — antivirus, disk cleanup, file compression — which keeps the machine running properly.

3. Language translators — compiler, interpreter, assembler — which turn the programs people write into machine code.

short.q: Name four examples of application software.
short.a:
1. Microsoft Word — word processing
2. Microsoft Excel — spreadsheets
3. Google Chrome — web browsing
4. VLC Media Player — playing video

Others include Photoshop, Tally, Zoom and PowerPoint. What they have in common is that each does a task the user actually wants done, as opposed to system software, which exists to keep the machine running.

short.q: How does a utility software support system operation?
short.a:
Utility software looks after the computer rather than producing work of its own. It keeps the machine healthy, fast and safe.

Antivirus finds and removes malicious software. Disk cleanup and defragmentation reclaim space and tidy files so access is quicker. Backup tools copy data so it can be recovered after a failure. File compression reduces what files take up on disk and over a network. Disk repair tools find and fix errors in the file system.

Without utilities the operating system would still run, but it would gradually get slower, fuller and more exposed.

short.q: Why is software essential for computer functionality?
short.a:
Because hardware has no purpose of its own. A processor can only fetch an instruction and obey it — it needs the sequence of instructions, and that sequence is software.

Without an operating system the machine cannot start, recognise its keyboard or disk, or run anything. Without application software it cannot do anything a user would find useful. In short, hardware is the body and software is what gives it something to do.

short.q: Explain the concept of proprietary software in your own words.
short.a:
Proprietary software is software that belongs to someone — a company or an individual — who decides how it may be used. You buy or accept a licence to use it, but you do not own it and you do not get to see or change how it works.

In practice this means: you usually pay for it; you get the finished program but not the source code; you may not copy it for others, modify it or resell it; and you depend on the owner for updates and support. Windows, Microsoft Office and Adobe Photoshop are all proprietary.

The opposite is open-source software, where the source code is published and anyone may read, change and share it.

long.q: Explain the roles of the Control Unit (CU) and the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) in the CPU.
long.a:
The two units divide the work of the CPU between them: one decides what happens, the other does it.

The Control Unit. It is responsible for controlling all the components of the computer. It issues control signals, instructs the rest of the system how to carry out a program's instructions, and directs the movement of electronic signals between the components. It manages the fetch–decode–execute sequence. It processes no data itself.

The ALU. It performs the actual operations. Arithmetic operations — addition, subtraction, multiplication and division — produce numeric results. Logical operations — AND, OR, NOT — together with relational comparisons such as =, >, <, >=, <=, produce true/false results. Arithmetic is used for calculating; logic and comparison are what give the machine the ability to decide.

How they work together. The CU fetches an instruction and decodes it. If the instruction is a calculation or a comparison, the CU routes the operands to the ALU and tells it which operation to perform. The ALU returns the result, and the CU sees it written to the right place. Neither is useful alone: without the CU the ALU has no instructions; without the ALU the CU has nothing to execute.

long.q: Explain how the CPU interacts with both primary and secondary memory during data retrieval.
long.a:
The key fact is that the CPU can only address primary memory directly. Secondary memory is not wired to the CPU's address lines at all.

Primary memory. To fetch data, the CPU places the address on the address bus and signals a read on the control bus. The data comes back along the data bus and is held in a register. Cache and registers sit closest and are fastest; main RAM is a step away, across the bus.

Secondary memory. If the data is on disk, the CPU cannot read it directly. It instructs the disk controller to transfer the required block, and the data goes into RAM first — usually by direct memory access, so the CPU is not tied up during the transfer. Only then can the CPU access it. This is why opening a large file takes a moment the first time: the delay is the disk, not the processor.

Why it is built this way. Secondary storage is thousands of times slower than RAM. If the CPU waited on the disk for every byte it would be idle almost all of the time, so the memory hierarchy — registers, cache, RAM, disk — keeps a copy of what is likely to be needed close to the processor.

long.q: Explain the functions of the data bus in a computer system.
long.a:
A data bus is a communication system — a set of wires or traces on the motherboard — that transfers data between the components of a computer. Its functions:

1. Its primary function is to facilitate the transfer of data between the CPU, memory and peripherals so they can communicate effectively.

2. It operates according to defined protocols that specify how data is formatted, transmitted and received, so that two components agree on what the signals mean.

3. It keeps transfer efficient and delay low, maintaining performance in computing tasks.

4. It lets the components work together — CPU, RAM and storage — acting as the backbone of the whole system.

5. It often includes error-checking, so that data is transmitted accurately and the integrity of what is being processed is preserved.

Its width (how many bits travel at once) and speed are what determine how much data moves and how fast, and they are major factors in overall system performance.

long.q: Explain the roles of the motherboard in a computer system.
long.a:
The motherboard is the main circuit board and the backbone of the computer. Its roles:

1. It is the central hub where the CPU, memory, storage and peripherals connect.

2. It provides the CPU socket, giving the processor a secure mounting and the electrical connections it needs to talk to everything else.

3. It has slots for RAM, allowing main memory to be installed.

4. It provides PCIe expansion slots for graphics, sound and network cards.

5. It provides storage connectors such as SATA ports, letting the CPU read and write to hard drives and SSDs.

6. It distributes power from the power supply to the connected components.

7. It houses the BIOS or UEFI, the firmware that initialises hardware during booting.

Its functions can be summarised as coordinating the devices and maintaining an interface among them, holding the firmware chip, and distributing power. Without it, the components are separate parts with no way to work together.

long.q: You are tasked with transferring data from one computer to another. Which type of memory would be most suitable for this, and why?
long.a:
Secondary memory — specifically a portable device such as a pen drive or an external SSD, or else cloud storage.

Why secondary. Primary memory cannot be used at all: RAM is volatile, so its contents vanish the moment the first machine is switched off, and it is not removable in any case. Secondary memory is non-volatile, so the data survives the journey, and it is physically (or, in the cloud's case, logically) transportable.

Choosing between the options. A pen drive is the simplest answer: small, cheap, needs no network, and files are dragged onto it. An external SSD is better for large amounts of data, being much faster. Cloud storage suits the case where the two computers are in different places and both have internet access — nothing physical is carried, and both parties can reach the data — but the transfer speed depends entirely on the connection.

For most school answers, the pen drive is the expected choice, with the reason being that it is portable and non-volatile.

long.q: Differentiate between SRAM and DRAM.
long.a:
