SRAM (Static RAM) holds its data as voltage for as long as the machine is on, with no refreshing needed. It is expensive but faster to read and write, and it consumes relatively little power. It is used for cache memory.

DRAM (Dynamic RAM)

The trade-off is the point: SRAM is better but dearer, so a machine uses a little of it for cache and a lot of DRAM for main memory. That combination is what makes fast memory affordable.

long.q: Differentiate between RAM and ROM with examples.
long.a:
RAM (Random Access Memory) allows both reading and writing, is volatile — contents lost when power is switched off — and usually has a larger capacity. It holds data and instructions while they are being processed. Types: SRAM and DRAM.

ROM (Read Only Memory) allows reading only, is non-volatile — contents survive without power — and usually has a smaller capacity. It holds the programs a device needs in order to operate, such as the boot firmware. Types: PROM, EPROM, EEPROM.

ROM is slower than RAM but faster than a hard disk. In short: RAM is the working area that is cleared at switch-off; ROM is the permanent store that tells the machine how to start.

long.q: Differentiate between volatile and non-volatile memory with examples.
long.a:
Volatile memory requires power to retain its contents. When the supply is removed, the data is lost. Example: RAM — both SRAM and DRAM. This is why unsaved work disappears in a power cut.

Non-volatile memory retains its contents without power. Examples: ROM, hard disks, SSDs, pen drives, optical discs and magnetic tape.

Both are necessary. Volatile memory is fast, which the processor needs; non-volatile memory is permanent, which the user needs. The machine constantly moves data between the two — loading from disk into RAM to work on it, and saving back to disk to keep it.

long.q: Describe the features of a computer system and its application areas.
long.a:
Features. Speed — billions of instructions per second, measured in hertz. Accuracy — very high, though wrong data or instructions still produce wrong output (GIGO). Word length — the number of bits processed at once, commonly 8, 16, 32 or 64. Automation — once given a program and data, it works without intervention. Diligence — it repeats work without tiring. Reliability — consistent results for the same input. Versatility — different programs make it a different machine. Storage — a huge amount of data held and retrieved at speed.

Application areas. Education — teaching (CAI), research, documents. Business — point of sale, inventory, e-commerce. Office — reports, letters, automation. Communication — email, social media, conferencing. Banking — transactions, ledgers, online banking. Hospitals — diagnosis, records, MRI and CT imaging. Industry — process control and measurement. Military — guided missiles and aircraft. Aviation — reservations and air-traffic control. Robotics — programmable machines. CAD — design and simulation.

What links the features to the applications is that each feature makes a class of work possible: diligence makes repetitive industrial control practical, speed makes air-traffic control possible, and versatility is why one machine serves all these fields.

long.q: Justify the statement: a computer can perform different tasks depending on the programs fed to it.
long.a:
A computer's hardware is general purpose. The processor fetches instructions, carries them out and fetches the next; it has no idea whether those instructions add a column of figures, draw a letter or steer a robot arm. What the machine does is decided entirely by the software running on it.

That is why the same laptop can be a word processor in the morning and a video editor in the afternoon. Nothing inside it changed except the program.

The contrast is with a fixed-purpose machine. A calculator can only calculate; a washing machine can only wash. Their function is built into their wiring. A computer's function is not built in — it is supplied, and resupplied, as instructions in memory.

This is the property called versatility, and it is the reason a single machine has replaced so many single-purpose ones.

long.q: Draw a table that compares the measuring units for processing speed in terms of frequency and time.
long.a:
Frequency measures how many cycles happen each second; period is the time one cycle takes. They are reciprocals: period = 1 / frequency.

UnitCycles per secondPeriod (one cycle)
1 hertz (Hz)11 second
1 kilohertz (KHz)1031 millisecond
1 megahertz (MHz)1061 microsecond
1 gigahertz (GHz)1091 nanosecond
1 terahertz (THz)10121 picosecond
1 petahertz (PHz)10151 femtosecond
1 exahertz (EHz)10181 attosecond

A clock speed of 3 GHz therefore means about three thousand million cycles each second, each one lasting roughly a third of a nanosecond. Clock speed alone does not tell you how fast a computer is, because different processors do different amounts of work per cycle.

long.q: Explain BCR, QR code scanner and touch screen.
long.a:
BCR — Bar Code Reader. It shines light at the black and white stripes of a bar code and measures how much is reflected back. Dark stripes absorb light, light stripes reflect it, so the pattern of reflections reads back as the pattern of stripes, which the computer translates into the product number. You see them at every supermarket checkout and in libraries.

QR code scanner. A QR (Quick Response) code is a two-dimensional square pattern rather than a line of stripes, so it holds far more data — a web address, a payment detail, a boarding pass. The scanner is usually just a phone camera plus software that finds the three corner markers, works out the orientation and decodes the grid.

Touch screen. A display you can also use as an input device — it detects where a finger or stylus touches it. Most use a capacitive layer: the finger slightly changes the electrical charge at that point and the screen works out the position from the change. Because the output surface and the input surface are the same, no separate pointing device is needed, which is why touch screens dominate phones and tablets.

long.q: Explain webcam, scanner and touch pad.
long.a:
Webcam. A small digital camera that feeds live video into the computer. It captures a series of still frames quickly enough to look like continuous movement, and is used for video calls, recording and sometimes for face recognition to sign in.

Scanner. A device that makes a digital copy of a physical page or picture by moving a light and a sensor across it and recording the brightness and colour point by point. The result is a still image file rather than a stream, and it is used to digitise documents, photographs and artwork.

Touch pad. The flat, touch-sensitive rectangle below the keyboard of a laptop. Sliding a finger across it moves the pointer, tapping clicks, and two-finger gestures scroll or zoom. It does the same job as a mouse in a space too small for one, and works by sensing the change in capacitance where the finger touches.

long.q: Draw a diagram that shows how the motherboard connects the CPU, RAM, and storage devices.
long.a:
Think of the motherboard as the computer's transport system: it does not do the computing itself, but nothing can talk to anything else without it.

        +-------------------- MOTHERBOARD --------------------+
        |                                                     |
        |   +----------+        buses         +-----------+   |
        |   |   CPU    |<==================>|    RAM    |   |
        |   | (socket) |   address / data /   |  (DIMM    |   |
        |   +----------+      control          |   slots)  |   |
        |        |                             +-----------+   |
        |        |                                             |
        |        |  (chipset: northbridge / southbridge)        |
        |        |                                             |
        |        v                                             |
        |   +----------------+          +------------------+   |
        |   |  Storage: SSD  |          |  Expansion slots |   |
        |   |  HDD (SATA /   |          |  PCIe (graphics, |   |
        |   |  NVMe)         |          |  sound, network) |   |
        |   +----------------+          +------------------+   |
        |                                                     |
        |   +----------+   +-----------+   +--------------+    |
        |   |  BIOS /  |   |  Power    |   |  I/O ports:  |    |
        |   |  UEFI    |   |  connector|   |  USB, HDMI,  |    |
        |   |  chip    |   |           |   |  Ethernet    |    |
        |   +----------+   +-----------+   +--------------+    |
        +-----------------------------------------------------+

How the parts are joined

1. The CPU sits in a socket on the board. Every other part communicates with it through the board's copper tracks.

2. RAM plugs into DIMM slots close to the CPU. It is connected by the memory bus, made of an address bus (which location), a data bus (what is being carried) and a control bus (read or write).

3. Storage — SSD or HDD — connects through a SATA or NVMe interface. It is much slower than RAM, so the CPU does not read directly from it: data is copied into RAM first, then used.

4. The chipset manages traffic between the CPU, memory, storage and peripherals, so the processor is not burdened with low-level housekeeping.

5. The board also carries the BIOS/UEFI chip that starts the machine, the power connector that feeds every part, and the I/O ports on the back panel.

That is why the motherboard is called the backbone: it supplies both the physical mounting and the electrical paths that let the parts work as one system.

long.q: What is the function of a VGA port in connecting a computer to a monitor?
long.a:
VGA (Video Graphics Array) carries the picture from the computer to the monitor. Its job is to take the image the graphics card has produced and send it, as continuously varying voltages, down a cable to the display.

How it works

VGA is an analogue standard. It sends the picture as three separate signals — red, green and blue — whose voltages rise and fall with the brightness of each colour, plus horizontal and vertical synchronising signals that tell the monitor when to start a new line and a new frame.

What this means in practice

Because the signal is analogue, it degrades over a long cable: the picture can look soft, washed out or ghosted. The computer's graphics card produces a digital picture, so it has to be converted to analogue to leave a VGA port, and the monitor converts it back — two conversions, each of which loses a little quality.

Why it has been replaced

HDMI, DisplayPort and DVI send the picture digitally, so there is no conversion and no degradation, and the same cable can carry sound as well. That is why VGA is now mainly found on older equipment and projectors, though adapters are still common.

long.q: How would you apply tailored software to improve business processes in a retail store?
long.a:
Tailored software — also called bespoke or custom software — is written for one particular organisation, so it fits the way that business already works instead of forcing the business to change.

What I would build for a retail store

1. Sales and billing — a till system that matches the store's own receipts, tax rules and discount schemes.

2. Stock control — levels update automatically as goods are sold, and the system reorders when a line runs low, which prevents both running out and over-ordering.

3. Customer records — purchase history so regular customers can be recognised and offered what they actually buy.

4. Reporting — daily and monthly figures in the shape the owner wants, rather than a generic report that has to be reworked in a spreadsheet.

5. Integration — links to the store's existing accounts and supplier systems, so numbers are entered once.

The trade-off

Tailored software is expensive to write, takes months to deliver and must be maintained — but it fits exactly, gives an advantage competitors using the same packaged program do not have, and can be changed as the business grows. Packaged software is far cheaper and available immediately, but the store has to adapt to it.

long.q: Determine which type of mobile app would be best for an online shopping platform.
long.a:
Three kinds of app are possible, and the choice depends on what matters most.

1. Native app — written specifically for Android or for iOS. Fastest and most reliable, has full access to the camera, GPS, fingerprint login and push notifications, and works offline. But it must be built twice, once per platform, so it costs the most.

2. Web app — runs in a browser. One codebase works everywhere, updates are instant and there is no app-store approval. But it needs a connection, is slower, and cannot use device features as deeply.

3. Hybrid app — one codebase wrapped in a native shell. Cheaper than native and reaches both platforms, but performance and access to device features sit between the other two.

Recommendation. For an online shopping platform, a native app is the best choice if the business can afford it. Shopping depends on speed, a smooth checkout, trustworthy payment and push notifications about orders — all of which native does best, and a slow or clumsy checkout loses sales directly.

If the budget is limited, start with a web app to prove the idea, then move to native once the platform has enough customers to justify it. Many real shops run both: a web app for reach, a native app for regular buyers.

long.q: Compare and contrast open source and proprietary software in terms of customization and cost.
long.a:
Open-sourceProprietary
Cost to obtainUsually free to download and use; you pay, if at all, for supportLicence fee — a one-off purchase or a subscription
Source codePublished; you can read and change itClosed; you get only the finished program
CustomisationAlmost unlimited — change anything, or pay anyone to change itLimited to the settings the vendor allows; you cannot alter the program itself
Who can customiseAnyone with the skill, or any contractor Only the vendor, and usually for a fee
Hidden costsStaff time to install, configure and support itLicence renewals, per-user fees, upgrade charges
SupportCommunity forums and documentation; paid support from some vendorsContractual support from the vendor
ExamplesLinux, LibreOffice, Firefox, PythonWindows, Microsoft Office, Photoshop

The honest summary. Open-source wins on cost and freedom to customise — if you need a program to do something unusual, open-source lets you make it do that. Proprietary wins on convenience and accountability: someone is contractually obliged to support it, and it usually needs less technical skill to run.

But "free" does not mean zero cost. Open-source software still has to be installed, configured, secured and maintained, and that takes skilled people. The right choice depends on whether the organisation has those people or would rather pay a vendor to take the problem away.

long.q: Assess the advantages and disadvantages of using packaged software in a large organisation.
long.a:
Packaged software — often called off-the-shelf — is a ready-made product sold to many customers, such as Microsoft Office or Tally.

Advantages

1. Available immediately — no development wait.

2. Much cheaper — the development cost is shared across every customer.

3. Proven and well tested — thousands of other users have found the faults already.

4. Supported and updated — the vendor fixes faults and issues new versions.

5. Staff already know it — little training needed, and new hires often arrive knowing it.

6. Documented — manuals, courses and a community of users exist.

Disadvantages

1. It will not fit exactly — the organisation must change its processes to suit the software, not the other way round.

2. Unwanted features — you pay for a lot you never use.

3. Missing features — anything specific to the business may not exist, and you cannot add it.

4. Ongoing licence cost — per user, per year, forever; over ten years this can exceed the cost of building something.

5. Vendor dependence — if the vendor raises prices, drops the product or goes out of business, the organisation is exposed.

6. Integration problems — it may not talk cleanly to existing systems.

Assessment. For a large organisation the sensible approach is nearly always packaged software for standard jobs — word processing, accounts, email — because the work is the same everywhere and the savings are large. Tailored software is justified only where the process is genuinely distinctive and gives a competitive advantage worth paying for. Most big organisations end up with a mix of both.

long.q: Examine the importance of language translators in system software.
long.a:
A processor obeys machine code — patterns of binary digits — and nothing else. People cannot write machine code at any useful scale, so programs are written in languages that look something like English or mathematics. Language translators are the bridge, and without them no software could be written at all.

The three translators

1. Assembler — turns assembly language, which uses short mnemonics such as MOV and ADD, into machine code. One assembly instruction becomes one machine instruction.

2. Compiler — reads the whole high-level program at once and translates it into a complete machine-code file. The translation happens once; after that the program runs fast. Faults are reported in a batch after compilation. Used for C, C++ and similar languages.

3. Interpreter — reads and executes the program one line at a time, translating each as it comes to it. Nothing is stored as machine code, so it runs more slowly, but a fault stops the program at that line, which makes it much easier to learn with. Python is interpreted.

Why they matter

They are what makes programming possible in a language a human can think in. They let the same program be written once and run on different processors, because only the translator has to be rewritten for each machine. And they are the tools that shape how a language feels to use — whether you wait for a compile or see a result immediately.

They belong to system software rather than application software because they do not do a task for an end user; they support the creation of other software.

practical.q: Draw an IPO block diagram of a computer on chart paper and display it in the classroom.
practical.a:
IPO stands for Input – Process – Output, and it is the simplest useful model of what a computer does.

Draw three blocks in a row, with arrows pointing left to right:

Input — the devices that put data in: keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone.

Process — the CPU doing the work. Worth splitting this block in your diagram into the three parts that do the processing: the ALU (arithmetic and logic), the Control Unit (directing operations) and Memory (holding data and instructions).

Output — the devices that show the result: monitor, printer, speakers.

Add a fourth block for storage with arrows running both ways, because storage is both a source and a destination for data — unlike input and output, which only go one way.

practical.q: Prepare a collection showing the use of computers in education, communication, banking, medicine and entertainment.
practical.a:
Note: the textbook's wording for this item is partly illegible in the source used, so the task has been reconstructed from the readable fragment — the five fields listed are exactly as printed.

Take one field per page and give each a concrete example:

Education — online classes, learning software, research.

Communication — email, messaging, video conferencing.

Banking — ATMs, online banking, card payments.

Medicine — patient records, scanners, diagnosis support.

Entertainment — streaming, games, digital music.

Add a picture or a short cutting to each page. The point of the exercise is to see that the same machine serves completely different purposes depending on the software it runs.

practical.q: In four groups, prepare and present on: characteristics of computers; importance of computers in daily life; the block diagram of a digital computer; and the IPO cycle.
practical.a:
One topic per group. Each group should produce a chart-paper or multimedia presentation.

Characteristics — speed, accuracy, diligence, versatility, storage capacity, and the lack of any intelligence of its own. That last point is worth stressing: a computer follows instructions, it does not understand them.

Importance in daily life — pick real examples from the five fields above rather than generalities.

Block diagram — show input, the CPU with its three parts, memory, storage and output, with arrows showing which way data flows.

IPO cycle — walk one concrete example all the way through, such as typing two numbers, adding them, and seeing the total. Following one real example is far more convincing than describing the cycle in the abstract.

practical.q: Search for information on "use of the computer in different sectors or fields", and display one application per page.
practical.a:
Search for each sector, then write up one application per page with three things on it: what the computer does in that field, what the benefit is, and one real example you can name.

Check the source and date of what you find, and prefer a second source for anything you intend to rely on.

practical.q: Learning Workshop 1 activity: Computer System Scavenger Hunt
practical.a:
Learning outcome: students understand the parts of a computer system, what each one does, the storage devices available and the difference between system and application software, by handling and sorting real examples rather than only reading about them.

Materials needed: flashcards naming computer components, memory types and storage devices; chart paper and markers; printed pictures of computer hardware; sticky notes for group work.

How to run it

1. Prepare two sets of cards beforehand — one set naming a component (RAM, hard disk, CPU, monitor, ROM, cache, SSD, keyboard), the other set describing what it does ("holds the programs you are running right now", "keeps your files when the power is off").

2. Hide the cards around the room before the class arrives.

3. Send students out in teams of three or four to find them. A team scores only when it can pair a name card with the correct function card.

4. Each team sticks its matched pairs on chart paper and labels the group — input, output, processing, storage, or software.

5. Walk around while they match and ask a team to justify any pairing that looks wrong; that is where the real learning happens.

What it teaches: the IPO model and the memory hierarchy. Teams almost always confuse RAM with storage, so finish by asking which card would still hold its contents after you switch the computer off — that single question settles the difference.

units.title: Chapter 2 — Number System
units.overview: How numbers are written and converted between the decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal systems, and the arithmetic and complements that go with them.
units.summary: Chapter 2 — Number System. Review the chapter summary for definitions and key points.

detailed.heading: Chapter 2 — Number System
detailed.note: Detailed teaching notes for Number System, written from the textbook and illustrated with the book's own figures.
learning_objectives: Define a number system and explain base (radix).
Describe the applications of number systems.
Name and describe the four positional number systems.
Explain why computers use binary rather than decimal.
Convert between decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
Carry out binary addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.

blocks.text: A way of representing numbers using digits, together with a base (radix) that fixes how many digits there are and what each position is worth.

Number systems have been around for thousands of years, and the diversity survives today. The common system is based on ten, but binary (base 2), ternary (base 3), quaternary (base 4), quinary (base 5), octal (base 8), decimal (base 10), duodecimal (base 12) and hexadecimal (base 16) are all in use.
Base or radix
The base of a number system is the number of different digits it uses. Decimal uses ten digits (0–9), so its base is 10. The base is written as a subscript after the number.

head: Number
Reads as
blocks.caption: How the subscript shows the base

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: The subscript is not decoration — it is the whole point. (11)<sub>2</sub> is three, (11)<sub>8</sub> is nine, and (11)<sub>10</sub> is eleven. The same digits, three different values.
Applications of the number system

items: Computing and digital electronics — binary (base 2) is fundamental: computers process, calculate and store using 0 and 1.
Programming — binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal are used for memory addressing, colour coding in graphics, IP addresses in networking, and data representation.
Mathematics — arithmetic, algebra, calculus and other advanced work.
Data representation — ASCII for text, BCD (binary-coded decimal), and Unicode; essential for compression and encoding.
Signal processing — DSP relies on binary representation to analyse and modify audio and video for transmission and storage.
Engineering — circuit design, control systems and simulation in electrical, mechanical and civil engineering.

blocks.text: Types of positional number system

items: Decimal (base 10) — ten digits, 0–9.
Binary (base 2) — two digits, 0 and 1.
Octal (base 8) — eight digits, 0–7.
Hexadecimal (base 16) — sixteen symbols, 0–9 and A–F.

blocks.text: Decimal or denary
The most popular system in daily life. It has ten digits (0–9), so it is base 10, subscripted 10 or D. Example: (123)<sub>10</sub>.
Binary
The number system of the computer — its mother language. It has two digits, 0 and 1, is base 2, and is subscripted 2 or B. Example: (101)<sub>2</sub>.
Why computers use binary rather than decimal

items: It suits the two-state nature of the components: a transistor conducting or not, a pulse present or absent, a magnetic material magnetised one way or the other.
It is hard to keep a device that recognises ten distinct levels reliable; it is easy to build one that is reliably either ON (1) or OFF (0).
Binary is much simpler — just 0 and 1.
Operations are performed more rapidly.

blocks.text: The one disadvantage is that binary needs a large number of digits to express a given number — (255)<sub>10</sub> becomes (11111111)<sub>2</sub>.
Octal

Computers struggle with long binary strings, so octal and hexadecimal were introduced to make numbers shorter and easier to handle. Octal has eight digits (0–7), is base 8, and is subscripted 8 or O. Example: (126)<sub>8</sub>.

head: Octal
Decimal
Binary
blocks.caption: Octal, decimal and binary — one octal digit is exactly three bits

blocks.text: Hexadecimal
Hexadecimal has sixteen symbols: the digits 0–9 and the letters A–F, standing for 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15. It is base 16, subscripted 16 or H. Example: (A26)<sub>16</sub>.

head: Hexadecimal
Decimal
Binary
blocks.caption: Hexadecimal, decimal and binary — one hex digit is exactly four bits

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: The grouping is worth memorising: three bits make one octal digit, four bits make one hexadecimal digit. That single fact turns conversion between binary and either base into grouping rather than arithmetic.
Decimal to binary, octal and hexadecimal
The method is the same for all three: divide repeatedly by the target base and read the remainders upwards.

items: Divide the given number by the target base.
Write the quotient underneath; it becomes the new number.
Write the remainder at the right.
Repeat until the quotient is 0.
The remainders, read from bottom to top, give the answer.

blocks.text: Decimal to binary — (43)<sub>10</sub>
Reading the remainders from the bottom up: (43)10 = (101011)2.
Decimal to octal — (123)<sub>10</sub>
Reading the remainders from the bottom up: (123)10 = (173)8.
Decimal to hexadecimal — (423)<sub>10</sub>
Reading the remainders from the bottom up: (423)10 = (1A7)16.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: In hexadecimal, a remainder of 10 is written A, 11 is B, 12 is C, 13 is D, 14 is E and 15 is F. Forgetting to convert a remainder of 10–15 into its letter is the commonest error in this topic.
Binary, octal and hexadecimal to decimal
Expand by place value: write each digit as the base raised to a power, counting from 0 at the right, then add.
Binary to decimal. (1011)2 = 1×23 + 0×22 + 1×21 + 1×1 = (11)10
Octal to decimal. (213)8 = 2×82 + 1×81 + 3×1 = (139)10
Hexadecimal to decimal. (1A8)16 = 1×162 + A×161 + 8×1 = (424)10
Binary to hexadecimal and to octal

Method I — group the bits, four at a time for hexadecimal and three at a time for octal, working from the right and padding with zeros on the left if needed. Method II — convert to decimal first, then to the target base.
Example (binary → hexadecimal): (1011001011)2. Grouping from the right in fours: 10 1100 1011 → 0010 1100 1011 = (2CB)16.
Example (binary → octal): the same number grouped in threes: 1 011 001 011 → 001 011 001 011 = (1313)8.
Octal to binary
Take each octal digit on its own and write it as three bits.
So (3367)8 = (011011110111)2.
Octal ↔ hexadecimal
Neither converts directly — go through binary (or decimal).
Octal to hexadecimal: (517)8 = (101 001 111)2; regroup in fours from the right: (0001 0100 1111)2 = (14F)16.
Hexadecimal to octal: (A7C5)16 = (1010 0111 1100 0101)2; regroup in threes: (001 010 011 111 000 101)2 = (123705)8.
Binary addition

items: Align the numbers by their least significant bits.
Add each column from the right.
Carry whenever a column sums to 2 or more: write the low bit and carry the high bit left.
Continue through each column, including any carry.
Write the final result, including a carry left over at the end.

blocks.text: Example — (1011)2 + (1101)2. From the right: 1+1 = 0 carry 1; 1+0+1 = 0 carry 1; 0+1+1 = 0 carry 1; 1+1+1 = 1 carry 1. Reading the result with the final carry: (11000)2 — which is 11 + 13 = 24, as it should be.
Binary subtraction
Example — (1101)2 − (1011)2. From the right: 1−1 = 0; 0−1 needs a borrow, giving 10−1 = 1 and reducing the next column; 0−0 = 0; 1−1 = 0. Result: (0010)2 — that is 13 − 11 = 2.
Binary multiplication
Multiplication is simply repeated shifting and adding, because there are only two possible digits. For each 1 in the multiplier, write the multiplicand shifted by that position, then add the rows.
Binary division
Division works as long division, comparing and subtracting. Dividing by zero is not defined, exactly as in decimal.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Every binary answer can be checked by converting to decimal, doing the arithmetic there and converting back. If you have time in an exam, do it — it catches nearly every slip.

mcq.q: The number system that uses only two digits (0 and 1) is called:
mcq.teacher_note: Binary — base 2, using only 0 and 1.

mcq.q: The decimal number system is based on which radix (base)?
mcq.teacher_note: Decimal is base 10 — ten digits, 0 to 9.

mcq.q: How many digits are used in the octal number system?
mcq.teacher_note: Octal uses 8 digits: 0 to 7.

mcq.q: The hexadecimal number system consists of how many symbols?
mcq.teacher_note: Hexadecimal has 16 symbols: 0–9 and A–F.

mcq.q: In hexadecimal, the decimal number 15 is represented as:
mcq.teacher_note: The letters run A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, so 15 is F.

mcq.q: What is the sum of (1011)<sub>2</sub> + (1101)<sub>2</sub>?
mcq.teacher_note: 11 + 13 = 24, and 24 in binary is 11000. Working it out column by column gives the same result.

mcq.q: What is the result of (1101)<sub>2</sub> − (1010)<sub>2</sub>?
mcq.teacher_note: 13 − 10 = 3, and 3 in binary is 11, written as 0011 with four digits. Note the printed options are inconsistent here, so convert to decimal, subtract, and convert back — that never fails.

mcq.q: Which of the following binary additions is correct?
The decimal number 25 is represented in binary as:
mcq.teacher_note: 25 = 16 + 8 + 1, so bits 4, 3 and 0 are set: 11001.

mcq.q: The decimal number 35 is represented in octal as:
mcq.teacher_note: 35 ÷ 8 = 4 remainder 3, then 4 ÷ 8 = 0 remainder 4. Reading up: 43.

mcq.q: The decimal number 47 is represented in hexadecimal as:
mcq.teacher_note: 47 ÷ 16 = 2 remainder 15, and 15 is F. So 2F.

mcq.q: Convert (10110)<sub>2</sub> to decimal:
mcq.teacher_note: 16 + 4 + 2 = 22.

mcq.q: Convert (101100)<sub>2</sub> to octal:
mcq.teacher_note: Group in threes from the right: 101 100 = 5 4, so 54 in octal.

mcq.q: Convert (100101)<sub>2</sub> to hexadecimal:
mcq.teacher_note: Group in fours from the right: 0010 0101 = 2 5, so 25 in hexadecimal.

mcq.q: Convert (57)<sub>8</sub> to decimal:
Convert (36)<sub>8</sub> to binary:
mcq.teacher_note: 3 = 011 and 6 = 110, so 011110 — that is, 11110.

mcq.q: Convert (30)<sub>16</sub> to decimal:
mcq.teacher_note: 3×16 + 0 = 48.

mcq.q: Convert (1A)<sub>16</sub> to binary:
mcq.teacher_note: 1 = 0001 and A = 1010, so 00011010 — that is, 11010.

short.q: What do you mean by number system?
short.a: A number system is a way of representing numbers using digits, together with a base (radix) that fixes how many digits there are and what each position is worth. The same digits mean different things in different bases, which is why the base is written as a subscript.

short.q: Define binary number system.
short.a: The binary number system has only two digits, 0 and 1, so its base is 2. It is the number system of the computer — its mother language — because two states are what electronic components can represent reliably.

short.q: What is octal number system?
short.a: The octal number system has eight digits, 0 to 7, so its base is 8. It was introduced to make long binary strings shorter and easier to handle, since one octal digit is exactly three bits.

short.q: What is decimal number system?
short.a: The decimal (or denary) number system has ten digits, 0 to 9, so its base is 10. It is the most widely used system in everyday life.

short.q: Define hexadecimal number system.
short.a: The hexadecimal number system has sixteen symbols: the digits 0–9 and the letters A–F, standing for 10 to 15. Its base is 16, and one hexadecimal digit is exactly four bits.

short.q: List the types of number system.
short.a: The four positional number systems are decimal (base 10, digits 0–9), binary (base 2, digits 0 and 1), octal (base 8, digits 0–7) and hexadecimal (base 16, digits 0–9 and A–F).

short.q: Convert the decimal number (106)<sub>10</sub> into binary.
short.a: 106 ÷ 2 = 53 r 0; 53 ÷ 2 = 26 r 1; 26 ÷ 2 = 13 r 0; 13 ÷ 2 = 6 r 1; 6 ÷ 2 = 3 r 0; 3 ÷ 2 = 1 r 1; 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r 1. Reading the remainders from the bottom up: (1101010)2.

short.q: Convert the decimal number (63)<sub>10</sub> into octal.
short.a: 63 ÷ 8 = 7 r 7; 7 ÷ 8 = 0 r 7. Reading up: (77)8. Check: 7×8 + 7 = 63.

short.q: Convert the binary number (1011001)<sub>2</sub> into decimal.
short.a: 64 + 16 + 8 + 1 = 89. (The bits set are positions 6, 4, 3 and 0, counting from 0 at the right.)

short.q: Convert the binary number (1011001011)<sub>2</sub> into octal.
short.a: Group the bits in threes from the right, padding on the left: 1 011 001 011 → 001 011 001 011. That is 1 3 1 3, so (1313)8.

short.q: Write the full forms: BIT, IP address, DSP, ASCII, BCD, UNICODE.
short.a: BIT — Binary Digit. IP address — Internet Protocol address. DSP — Digital Signal Processing. ASCII — American Standard Code for Information Interchange. BCD — Binary-Coded Decimal. UNICODE — a universal character encoding standard (not an acronym in the usual sense, though sometimes expanded as Universal Code).

short.q: Self Test 2.1: Define decimal number system.
short.a: The decimal number system has ten digits, 0 to 9, so its base is 10. It is the system used in everyday life. Each position is worth a power of 10 — units, tens, hundreds — so in 423 the 4 means 4 hundreds, the 2 means 2 tens and the 3 means 3 units.

short.q: Self Test 2.1: List different types of positional number system.
short.a: Four: decimal (base 10, digits 0–9), binary (base 2, digits 0 and 1), octal (base 8, digits 0–7) and hexadecimal (base 16, digits 0–9 and letters A–F).

short.q: Self Test 2.1: If it is asked to list one application of binary number system what would your answer be?
short.a: Any one of: it is the number system of computing and digital electronics, since computers process and store everything as 0s and 1s. Others: programming (memory addresses, colour codes, IP addresses), data representation (ASCII, BCD, Unicode), digital signal processing for audio and video, and engineering — circuit design and control systems.

short.q: Self Test 2.2: Write the steps to convert binary to hexadecimal.
short.a:
1. Group the bits into sets of four, starting from the right.
2. If the leftmost group is short, pad it with zeros on the left.
3. Convert each group of four to its hexadecimal digit (0000–1111 becomes 0–F).
4. Write the digits together in the same order.

Example: 10101111 → 1010 1111 → A F → (AF)16.

short.q: Self Test 2.2: Write the steps to convert binary to decimal.
short.a:
1. Write the binary number out.
2. Number the positions from 0, starting at the rightmost bit.
3. Each position is worth 2position, so multiply each bit by its place value.
4. Add the results together.

Example: 1011 = 1×8 + 0×4 + 1×2 + 1×1 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.

long.q: Explain any five applications of the number system.
long.a:
1. Computing and digital electronics. Binary is fundamental: computers process data, perform calculations and store information using 0 and 1.

2. Programming. Binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal are used for memory addressing, colour coding in graphics, IP addresses in networking, and general data representation.

3. Mathematics. Number systems underpin arithmetic, algebra, calculus and other advanced work.

4. Data representation. ASCII represents text, BCD holds each decimal digit in four bits, and Unicode provides a universal character encoding. All are essential to compression and encoding.

5. Signal processing. Digital signal processing relies on binary to analyse and modify audio and video for transmission and storage.

6. Engineering. Used in circuit design, control systems and simulation across electrical, mechanical and civil engineering.

long.q: Why is a binary number system important for the computer?
long.a:
Because of what the hardware actually is.

1. It suits the two-state nature of the components: a transistor conducting or not, an electrical pulse present or absent, a magnetic material magnetised one way or the other.

2. It is difficult to keep a device that distinguishes ten levels reliable. Building one that is reliably either ON (1) or OFF (0) is easy.

3. Binary is much simpler — there are only two digits to deal with.

4. Operations are performed more rapidly, because the rules of binary arithmetic are the simplest possible.

The one disadvantage is that binary needs many more digits to write a given number: 255 is eight bits. That is why octal and hexadecimal exist — not for the machine, but so that people can write the same value compactly.

long.q: Explain the hexadecimal number system. Convert (ABC)<sub>16</sub> into decimal.
long.a:
Hexadecimal is the base-16 system. It uses sixteen symbols: the digits 0–9 and the letters A–F, which stand for 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15. It is subscripted 16 or H. One hexadecimal digit is exactly four bits, which is why it is the standard shorthand for binary — a byte is two hex digits.

Converting (ABC)16: A = 10, B = 11, C = 12.

(ABC)16 = 10×162 + 11×161 + 12×160

= 10×256 + 11×16 + 12×1 = 2560 + 176 + 12 = (2748)10.

long.q: Explain the octal number system. Convert the octal number (145)<sub>8</sub> into decimal.
long.a:
Octal is the base-8 system, using the digits 0 to 7, subscripted 8 or O. It was introduced because long binary strings are awkward for people to read and write; since one octal digit is exactly three bits, converting between the two is grouping rather than arithmetic.

Converting (145)8:

(145)8 = 1×82 + 4×81 + 5×80

= 1×64 + 4×8 + 5×1 = 64 + 32 + 5 = (101)10.

long.q: Write down the rules for binary addition and subtraction.
long.a:
Addition. 0 + 0 = 0; 1 + 0 = 1; 0 + 1 = 1; and 1 + 1 = 0 with a carry of 1 to the next column.

Subtraction. 0 − 0 = 0; 1 − 0 = 1; 1 − 1 = 0; and 0 − 1 = 1, borrowing 1 from the next column to the left.

The method in both cases is to align the numbers by their least significant bits and work column by column from the right, carrying or borrowing as you go.

A reliable way to check any answer is to convert to decimal, do the arithmetic there, and convert back.

practical.q: Number System Bingo — match decimal numbers to their binary, octal or hexadecimal equivalents.
practical.a:
How it works. Each card holds a grid of decimal numbers. The teacher calls out a value in another base — say 101010 in binary — and players mark the matching decimal on their card.

Conversion practice for a set of cards. Work each one out by expansion, then check by converting back:

1010102 = 32 + 8 + 2 = 42

528 = 5×8 + 2 = 42

2A16 = 2×16 + 10 = 42

All three are the same number, which is exactly the point — the value does not change, only how it is written.

Why it helps. Converting the same value into three bases is the quickest way to make the idea that these are different notations for one quantity actually stick.

practical.q: Code the Secret Message — convert a short message into binary, octal or hexadecimal and challenge another group to decode it.
practical.a:
Encoding. Take each character, look up its ASCII code, and write that code in the base you have chosen. For the word OK in binary:

O is ASCII 79 = 10011112
K is ASCII 75 = 10010112

Write the two groups with a space between them so the decoder knows where each character ends. Without that separator the message is ambiguous.

Decoding. Split on the spaces, convert each group back to decimal, and look up the character.

Why binary takes so much space. Each character needs seven bits here, so a short sentence becomes a long string — which is precisely why octal and hexadecimal exist as shorthand, and why real systems use them.

key_terms.meaning: A way of representing numbers using digits and a base (radix).
The number of different digits a system uses; shown as a subscript.
The base-10 system, using digits 0–9.
The base-2 system, using 0 and 1 — the language of the computer.
The base-8 system, using digits 0–7; one digit is three bits.
The base-16 system, using 0–9 and A–F; one digit is four bits.
A system where a digit's value depends on its position.
The bit moved to the next column when a sum exceeds what one column holds.
Taking 1 from the next column so a subtraction is possible.
American Standard Code for Information Interchange — a character encoding.
Binary-Coded Decimal — each decimal digit held in four bits.
A universal character encoding standard.

quick_revision.title: Definition
points: A number system represents numbers with digits and a base. The base is the number of digits available.

quick_revision.title: The four systems
points: Decimal (10), binary (2), octal (8), hexadecimal (16). Hex letters A–F mean 10–15.

quick_revision.title: Grouping rule
points: Three bits = one octal digit. Four bits = one hexadecimal digit.

quick_revision.title: Decimal → anything
points: Divide repeatedly by the target base; read the remainders from the bottom up.

quick_revision.title: Anything → decimal
points: Expand by place value — each digit times the base raised to its position — then add.

quick_revision.title: Between octal and hex
points: Go through binary (or decimal). There is no direct route.

quick_revision.title: Binary arithmetic
points: 1+1 = 0 carry 1. 0−1 = 1 with a borrow. Multiplication is shift and add.

quick_revision.title: Why binary
points: Two states are easy and reliable to build; ten levels are not. Operations are faster.

units.overview: Programming by assembling blocks rather than typing text — the ideas of sequence, selection and iteration, and how a visual language expresses them.

detailed.heading: Chapter 3 — Block Programming
detailed.note: Detailed teaching notes for Block Programming, written from the textbook and illustrated with the book's own figures.
learning_objectives: Define block programming and explain why it suits beginners.
Describe the concepts, advantages and applications of block programming.
Explain what Scratch is and how to obtain it.
Identify the components of the Scratch interface.
Name the block categories and give examples from each.
Describe the micro:bit and its components.

blocks.text: A visual approach to coding that uses draggable blocks instead of text-based code, so that a beginner can learn coding concepts without the frustration of syntax errors.

blocks.caption: Block programming: drag and drop instead of typing.

blocks.text: Each block represents a specific command — move a character, play a sound. Connecting blocks in sequence builds a program, rather like assembling puzzle pieces.

Platforms such as Scratch, Blockly and MIT App Inventor use this approach to teach coding interactively. The emphasis is on coding logic and computational thinking: how actions are linked, how decisions are made, and how loops are created — all without memorising syntax.

The main advantage is that block programming focuses on the logic behind coding rather than the details of a language. That makes it an excellent introduction for anyone programming for the first time.

The core idea is visual representation with modular coding: each instruction is wrapped in a graphical block, and the blocks fit together logically to form a sequence of commands that runs as a program.
The five concepts

items: Drag-and-drop interface — blocks are moved and connected without writing code by hand.
Predefined blocks — blocks represent functions such as loops, conditionals, variables and events.
Modular approach — programs are built from reusable blocks, which promotes organised coding.
Error prevention — because only valid blocks exist, syntax errors are minimised.
Logical sequencing — blocks are arranged in order to form meaningful instructions.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: "Error prevention" does not mean "no errors". You cannot make a syntax error, but you can still build a program with perfectly valid blocks that does the wrong thing — a logic error. That distinction is often what an examiner wants.
Block programming acts as a bridge before a learner moves to a text-based language such as Python or JavaScript. It is used in schools, in robot-making and in app creation.
Advantages of block programming

items: User-friendly interface — drag and drop makes it accessible to beginners, especially children, with no syntax to memorise.
Immediate feedback — the effect of a change is visible at once, which reinforces learning through experimentation.
Encourages creativity — animations, games and interactive stories can be made without the limits of traditional programming.
Promotes logical thinking — working with loops, conditionals and events develops problem-solving, and teaches learners to break problems into smaller parts.
Community and collaboration — projects can be shared and feedback received, which encourages peer learning.

blocks.text: Applications of block programming

items: Educational tool — introducing loops, conditionals and events visually.
Game development — building games, which exercises creativity and problem-solving.
Interactive storytelling — designing narratives with character interactions.
Animation creation — controlling characters and backgrounds.
STEM education — algorithms, sequencing and debugging taught engagingly.
Robotics and physical computing — integrating with hardware such as LEGO Mindstorms and Raspberry Pi.
Community and collaboration — sharing projects and peer learning.
Mobile app and web development — prototyping apps, and an easier route into HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
Modelling and simulation — visualising complex systems.
Data science and visualisation — analysing and displaying data with minimal coding knowledge.

blocks.text: Scratch is a visual programming language developed in 2003 by the MIT Media Lab's Lifelong Kindergarten Group, led by Mitchel Resnick. It was designed to make coding accessible to young learners and to non-programmers, building creativity and problem-solving through an interactive block-based approach.
Scratch has moved through versions 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0. The latest, Scratch 3.0, was launched in 2019 with enhanced features, mobile compatibility and expanded block categories.
It lets users create interactive stories, animations, games and simulations without writing traditional code.
Getting Scratch
The modern version runs directly in a browser, so nothing needs installing for ordinary use. For working without an internet connection, the offline editor can be downloaded:

items: Open a web browser and go to https://scratch.mit.edu/download.
Choose your operating system — Windows, macOS, ChromeOS or Android.
Click Download; the installer file will download.
Open the installer and follow the instructions, then launch Scratch.

blocks.text: Scratch is also available online at https://scratch.mit.edu. On a phone the editor may not work smoothly, so a computer is better for building projects.

sections.title: Components of Scratch: The Block Categories

blocks.text: In Scratch a block is the fundamental building unit used to create the scripts that control sprites and the project as a whole. Blocks are grouped into categories, each with its own colour.

blocks.caption: The Blocks Palette, colour-coded by category.
The Scripting Area — where blocks are assembled.
The Stage, where the project runs.

blocks.text: 1. Motion Blocks (18)
Control a sprite's movement. There are 18: 15 stack blocks and 3 reporter blocks. The Stage has no motion blocks, because it cannot move.

Control the flow of scripts. There are 11: 1 hat, 3 stack, 5 C-blocks and 2 cap blocks.

Hold variables. There are 5: 4 stack blocks plus one reporter block for each variable you create.

Manage lists. They live in the Variables category rather than in the left-hand bar. There are 12: 7 stack, 3 reporter and 1 boolean block.

blocks.text: My Blocks
The tenth category is My Blocks, where you define your own blocks. Once made, a custom block behaves exactly like a built-in one, and can be reused anywhere in the project.

blocks.caption: The My Blocks category for custom blocks.

blocks.text: Extensions

Extensions add functionality beyond the built-in blocks — for example Music, Pen, Video Sensing, Text to Speech and Translate, plus hardware extensions for Makey Makey, micro:bit, LEGO MINDSTORMS EV3, LEGO BOOST and LEGO Education WeDo 2.0. To add one, click the purple icon at the bottom left, open the Extensions Library and choose. An extension that is added but never used is removed automatically when the project is reloaded.
Other parts of the interface

blocks.caption: Choosing a sprite from the library.
The toolbar and the built-in tutorials.

items: Green flag and Stop — start and stop the project. A script beginning "when green flag clicked" runs when the flag is pressed.
Backdrop pane — add or change the Stage background.
Choose a Sprite — pick a different sprite from the built-in library.
Costume editor — draw or import new appearances.
Toolbar and tutorials — File, Edit, Tutorials and project settings, plus built-in tutorials to learn from.
Project information — the title, instructions and notes about the project.

blocks.text: A small programmable computer, developed by the BBC, that lets learners write code and see it act on real hardware.

The micro:bit came out of a BBC initiative to promote computer education among children in the UK. The aim was to inspire a new generation of digital creators and to meet the growing demand for computing skills. It was officially launched in 2016.
Components of the micro:bit

head: Component
What it is for
rows: A 5×5 grid of LEDs showing text, numbers and simple graphics
Two programmable buttons, A and B, for interacting with the program
Detects movement and orientation; measures acceleration in three dimensions
A digital compass detecting which way the board is facing
For programming the board and powering it
Via USB or a battery pack, so it is portable
GPIO pins for connecting sensors, motors and other components
blocks.caption: The parts of a micro:bit

blocks.text: Applications

items: Education — teaching programming, electronics and computational thinking with hands-on experience.
Robotics — acting as the brain of a robot, controlling motors and sensors.
Wearable technology — fitness trackers and interactive clothing.
Games and interactive projects.
Environmental monitoring — measuring temperature, humidity or light.
Art and creativity.
Home automation — controlling lights and fans from sensor input.
Data logging — collecting sensor data for analysis.

blocks.text: A microcontroller board used to build digital devices and interactive objects that can sense and control the physical world.

Arduino was developed in 2003 at the Interaction Design Institute Ivrea (IDII) in Italy — the name comes from a bar in Ivrea. The first official board, the Arduino Serial, was released in 2005 and was based on the ATmega8. Because both the hardware and software are open source, the platform grew through global collaboration.
Aspects of the Arduino UNO

items: Microcontroller — the ATmega328P, which executes the user's code.
Input/output pins — 14 digital I/O pins and 6 analog input pins.
Programming — via the Arduino IDE, using a simplified version of C/C++, uploaded over USB.
Power supply — USB or an external supply, with a voltage regulator.
Open source — the designs are public, which encourages collaboration.
Applications — robotics, home automation, environmental monitoring and education.
Community and resources — a large community contributing libraries, tutorials and shields.

blocks.text: Components of the Arduino UNO

head: Group
Components
rows: ATmega328P, 16 MHz, 32 KB flash, 2 KB SRAM, 1 KB EEPROM
USB Type-B port, DC jack (7–12 V), 5 V and 3.3 V regulators, Vin, GND
UART (pins 0 and 1), SPI (pins 10–13), I2C (A4 SDA, A5 SCL)
16 MHz crystal oscillator; Timer0, Timer1, Timer2
Power LED, pin 13 LED, TX/RX LEDs
blocks.caption: What is on an Arduino UNO

blocks.text: Applications

items: Robotics and automation — obstacle-avoiding robots, robotic arms, industrial automation, home automation.
Internet of Things — smart home systems, weather stations, smart agriculture.
Embedded systems — prototyping, wearables, energy management.
Education — STEM teaching, microcontroller training, circuit design.
Medical and health monitoring — heart-rate sensors, assistive devices.
Environmental monitoring — air and water quality, wildlife tracking.
Transport — obstacle detection, traffic-light control, GPS tracking.
Sound and light control — sound-activated projects, musical instruments.
Security — motion detection, RFID access control, camera systems.
