mcq.q: What is the primary advantage of block programming for beginners?
options: It simplifies coding with a drag-and-drop interface
It is only used for web development
It does not support logical sequencing
mcq.teacher_note: It simplifies coding with a drag-and-drop interface. The other three are the opposite of the truth: block programming removes the need to know syntax, is used far beyond web development, and is built around logical sequencing.

mcq.q: Block programming is widely used in:
mcq.teacher_note: Robotics and game development are both named in the chapter. The other three need the performance and libraries of text-based languages.

mcq.q: Which of the following is a popular block-based programming environment used in schools?
mcq.teacher_note: Scratch. The other three are all text-based languages.

mcq.q: Which organisation developed Scratch?
mcq.teacher_note: The MIT Media Lab — specifically its Lifelong Kindergarten Group, led by Mitchel Resnick, in 2003.

mcq.q: In Scratch, what are "sprites"?
options: Small programs used to execute Scratch code
Visual objects that can be controlled with blocks
mcq.teacher_note: Sprites are the visual objects you control with blocks. They are not programs, commands or storage.

mcq.q: Which section of the Scratch interface contains all the available programming blocks?
mcq.teacher_note: The Blocks Palette, on the left, colour-coded by category.

mcq.q: Where do users arrange and connect blocks to create scripts in Scratch?
mcq.teacher_note: The Code Area (also called the Scripting Area) — the central area where blocks are assembled.

mcq.q: What is the purpose of the Stage in Scratch?
mcq.teacher_note: The Stage is where the project runs — it displays the sprites and the action.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of the Scratch interface?
mcq.teacher_note: The Command Line Interface — Scratch has no command line. That is exactly the point of it.

mcq.q: Which category of Scratch blocks is used to control movement?
mcq.teacher_note: Motion blocks control movement. Note that the Stage has no motion blocks, because it cannot move.

mcq.q: What type of block in Scratch is used to start a script when an event occurs?
mcq.teacher_note: Events blocks — they are hat blocks, shaped to sit on top of a script, and they respond to things like the green flag or a key press. Control blocks manage the flow once a script has started.

mcq.q: What is the primary function of the micro:bit?
mcq.teacher_note: It is a microcontroller for educational programming — the whole reason it exists is to teach coding with real hardware.

mcq.q: Which programming languages can be used with the micro:bit?
mcq.teacher_note: JavaScript, Python and block-based programming are all supported — the block editor is what makes it usable in a Grade 9 classroom.

mcq.q: How many buttons are available on the front of a micro:bit?
mcq.teacher_note: Two programmable buttons, labelled A and B.

mcq.q: Which communication technology is built into the micro:bit?
mcq.teacher_note: Bluetooth — it lets the board talk to phones, tablets and other micro:bits. The micro:bit has no Wi-Fi.

mcq.q: Which organisation developed the micro:bit?
mcq.teacher_note: The BBC, as part of an initiative to promote computer education among children in the UK.

mcq.q: In which year was the micro:bit officially launched?
mcq.teacher_note: 2016. Do not confuse it with 2003 (Scratch) or 2005 (the first Arduino board).

mcq.q: Why was the micro:bit developed?
options: To teach computer programming to students
To create a new gaming console
mcq.teacher_note: To teach programming to students — it was an education initiative, not a commercial product.

mcq.q: Which sensor in the micro:bit detects movement and orientation?
mcq.teacher_note: The accelerometer measures acceleration in three dimensions, which is how it detects tilt and shake.

mcq.q: Which part of the micro:bit allows it to communicate with other devices wirelessly?
mcq.teacher_note: The Bluetooth module — the USB port is a wired connection.

mcq.q: How is the micro:bit used in education?
mcq.teacher_note: Teaching coding and electronics basics. It is far too small for any of the other three.

mcq.q: What type of device is the Arduino UNO?
mcq.teacher_note: A single-board microcontroller — a whole computer small enough to sit in a project.

mcq.q: Which programming language is primarily used for Arduino?
mcq.teacher_note: C/C++, in a simplified form, written in the Arduino IDE. SQL is a database language and has no business here.

mcq.q: Which software is used to program an Arduino UNO?
mcq.teacher_note: The Arduino IDE. The others can be made to work, but the IDE is the intended tool.

mcq.q: Who developed the first Arduino board?
mcq.teacher_note: Massimo Banzi and team, at the Interaction Design Institute Ivrea in Italy in 2003.

mcq.q: Why was Arduino developed?
options: To simplify microcontroller programming for students
mcq.teacher_note: To simplify microcontroller programming for students, making it affordable and accessible.

mcq.q: Which microcontroller is used in Arduino UNO?
mcq.teacher_note: The ATmega328P, an 8-bit AVR running at 16 MHz. The others are far more powerful parts from phones and bigger boards.

mcq.q: How many digital input/output pins does Arduino UNO have?
mcq.teacher_note: 14 digital I/O pins, plus 6 analog input pins (A0–A5).

mcq.q: Which component is used for connecting Arduino UNO to a computer for programming?
mcq.teacher_note: The USB port — a USB Type-B, which also supplies 5 V power.

mcq.q: Which of the following projects can be built using an Arduino UNO?
mcq.teacher_note: Temperature monitoring systems. The other three are pure software, and an Arduino has no way to run them.

short.q: Define block programming.
short.a: Block programming is a visual approach to coding that uses draggable blocks instead of text-based code. Each block represents one command, and connecting blocks in sequence builds a program. It lets beginners learn coding concepts without the frustration of syntax errors.

short.q: Write any one application of block programming.
short.a: It is used as an educational tool for learning programming — Scratch is widely used in schools to introduce loops, conditionals and events through a visual approach. Others include game development, interactive storytelling, animation and robotics.

short.q: Enlist any one feature of Scratch.
short.a: Scratch is free and runs in a browser, so nothing needs installing. Other features: it is block-based and drag-and-drop, it uses colour-coded blocks by category, it is event-driven, and projects can be shared with a large online community.

short.q: What is a sprite?
short.a: A sprite is an object in a Scratch project that can be controlled with blocks. Each sprite can have its own scripts, costumes and sounds. A new project starts with a cat sprite, which can be replaced using the "Choose a Sprite" option.

short.q: Define stage.
short.a: The Stage is the area where the project runs — it displays the sprites and their animations, and it carries the backdrop. It differs from a sprite in that it cannot move, which is why it has no Motion blocks.

short.q: What is Scratch?
short.a: Scratch is a visual programming language developed in 2003 by the MIT Media Lab's Lifelong Kindergarten Group, led by Mitchel Resnick. It was designed to make coding accessible to young learners and non-programmers by using a block-based, drag-and-drop approach. Scratch 3.0, the current version, was launched in 2019. Users create interactive stories, animations, games and simulations without writing traditional code.

short.q: List down the components of the Scratch interface.
short.a: The Stage (where the project runs), the Sprite Info Pane (listing and managing sprites), the Blocks Palette (all the blocks, colour-coded by category), the Scripting Area (where scripts are assembled), the Costumes and Sounds tabs, the Backdrop pane, the Choose a Sprite library, and the toolbar with File, Edit and Tutorials. There is also a green flag and a stop button to start and stop the project.

short.q: What is a micro:bit? Give any two applications of micro:bit.
short.a:
The micro:bit is a small programmable computer developed by the BBC and launched in 2016, to promote computer education. It has a 5×5 LED matrix, two programmable buttons, an accelerometer, a compass and Bluetooth.

Two applications: education — teaching programming, electronics and computational thinking; and robotics — acting as the brain of a robot, controlling motors and sensors. Others include wearable technology, environmental monitoring and data logging.

short.q: How does a micro:bit help in physical computing?
short.a: Physical computing means building programs that sense and act on the real world. The micro:bit supports this because it carries both inputs and outputs on the board: an accelerometer and compass to sense movement and direction, buttons to accept input, a 5×5 LED matrix to show a result, and GPIO pins to connect external sensors, motors and other components. You write a program and see it act on real hardware rather than only on a screen — which is what makes the idea stick.

short.q: What is ATmega328P?
short.a: The ATmega328P is the 8-bit AVR microcontroller at the heart of the Arduino UNO — the "brain" of the board. It runs at 16 MHz and has 32 KB of flash memory for programs, 2 KB of SRAM and 1 KB of EEPROM. It executes the code uploaded by the user.

short.q: List two main features of micro:bit.
short.a: Any two of: a 5×5 LED matrix for displaying text, numbers and simple graphics; two programmable buttons (A and B); an accelerometer for detecting movement and orientation; a compass; Bluetooth connectivity; a USB connector; and GPIO pins for external components.

short.q: What is the function of the LED matrix on the micro:bit?
short.a: It is the board's display: a 5×5 grid of LEDs that can show text, numbers and simple graphics. It gives a project a visual output without any extra hardware being connected.

short.q: What type of sensor is used in micro:bit to detect movement?
short.a: The accelerometer. It measures acceleration in three dimensions, which is how the board detects tilting, shaking and orientation. (The compass detects direction, which is a different thing.)

short.q: What type of USB port is used in Arduino UNO for connecting to a computer?
short.a: A USB Type-B port. It both supplies 5 V power to the board and carries the uploaded program from the computer.

short.q: Write the full forms: MIT, BBC, IDE, ICSP, PIR, GPIO, MCU, IDI, GND, PWM.
short.a: MIT — Massachusetts Institute of Technology. BBC — British Broadcasting Corporation. IDE — Integrated Development Environment. ICSP — In-Circuit Serial Programming. PIR — Passive Infra-Red. GPIO — General Purpose Input/Output. MCU — Microcontroller Unit. IDI — Interaction Design Institute Ivrea, the Italian design institute whose work on programmable bricks led to Scratch; it is sometimes printed as IDII. GND — Ground. PWM — Pulse Width Modulation.

short.q: Self Test 3.1: What is block programming?
short.a: Block programming is a visual way of coding that uses draggable blocks instead of typed code. Each block is one command, and connecting blocks in sequence builds a program, rather like assembling puzzle pieces. It lets a beginner learn coding concepts without the frustration of syntax errors.

short.q: Self Test 3.1: Name two block-based programming languages.
short.a: Scratch and Blockly. Others include MIT App Inventor and Snap.

short.q: Self Test 3.1: How does block programming help beginners in coding?
short.a: It removes syntax errors, because only blocks that fit together can be joined — so a beginner spends their effort on the logic rather than on commas and brackets. It also gives immediate visual feedback, so the effect of a change is obvious at once.

short.q: Self Test 3.1: Name one application of block programming.
short.a: Any one of: teaching programming in schools; game development; animation; interactive storytelling; robotics and physical computing with hardware such as LEGO Mindstorms; and prototyping mobile apps.

short.q: Self Test 3.2: Where can you download Scratch?
short.a: From the official Scratch website at https://scratch.mit.edu/download, where you pick your operating system. The current version also runs directly in a browser, so nothing needs installing for ordinary use.

short.q: Self Test 3.2: What is the official website for downloading Scratch?
short.a: https://scratch.mit.edu, with the offline editor at https://scratch.mit.edu/download.

short.q: Self Test 3.2: List two features of Scratch.
short.a:
1. A drag-and-drop, block-based interface with colour-coded categories, so no syntax has to be memorised.
2. Immediate feedback — you see the result of a change at once. Others: event-driven scripts, a large online community for sharing projects, built-in tutorials, and extensions for hardware such as micro:bit and LEGO.

short.q: Self Test 3.2: Name one main component of the Scratch interface.
short.a: Any one of: the Stage (where the project runs), the Blocks Palette (all the blocks, colour-coded), the Scripting Area (where scripts are assembled), or the Sprite Info Pane (listing and managing sprites).

short.q: Self Test 3.2: What is the purpose of the stage in the Scratch interface?
short.a: The Stage is where the project runs and is displayed — it shows the sprites, their animation and the backdrop. It is the area the audience sees. Note that the Stage cannot move, which is why it has no Motion blocks.

short.q: Self Test 3.3: What is the purpose of the motion block in Scratch?
short.a: Motion blocks control a sprite's movement and position: moving it forward, turning it, sending it to a particular place, gliding it there over time, and reporting where it is. There are 18 of them. The Stage has none, because it cannot move.

short.q: Self Test 3.3: What is the function of the events block in Scratch?
short.a: Events blocks control what triggers a script. Most are hat blocks that sit on top and start a script when something happens — the green flag being clicked, a key being pressed, the sprite being clicked, the backdrop changing, or a broadcast arriving. Without one, a script never runs.

short.q: Self Test 3.3: What is the function of the Looks block in Scratch?
short.a: Looks blocks control how a sprite appears: speech and thought bubbles, switching costumes and backdrops, changing size, applying graphic effects, and showing or hiding the sprite. There are 21 of them.

short.q: Self Test 3.3: Which block category in Scratch allows adding custom-defined blocks?
short.a: My Blocks. You define your own block there, and once made it behaves exactly like a built-in one and can be used anywhere in the project.

short.q: Self Test 3.3: Which block category controls loops and conditions in Scratch?
short.a: Control. It holds the loops — repeat, forever, repeat until — and the conditionals — if () then and if () then / else.

short.q: Self Test 3.4: List two main features of Micro:Bit.
short.a: Any two of: a 5×5 LED matrix; two programmable buttons (A and B); an accelerometer; a compass; Bluetooth; a USB connector; and GPIO pins.

short.q: Self Test 3.4: What is the function of the LED matrix on the Micro:Bit?
short.a: It is the board's display — a 5×5 grid of LEDs that can show text, numbers and simple graphics. It gives a project a visible output with no extra hardware attached.

short.q: Self Test 3.4: What type of sensor is used in Micro:Bit to detect movement?
short.a: The accelerometer. It measures acceleration in three dimensions, which is how the board detects tilting, shaking and orientation.

short.q: Self Test 3.4: What type of USB port is used in Arduino UNO for connecting to a computer?
short.a: A USB Type-B port. It supplies 5 V power and carries the uploaded program from the computer.

long.q: Define block programming along with its features.
long.a:
Definition. Block programming is a visual approach to coding that uses draggable blocks instead of text-based code. Each block represents one command — moving a character, playing a sound — and connecting blocks in sequence builds a program, rather like assembling puzzle pieces. Platforms include Scratch, Blockly and MIT App Inventor.

Features.

1. Drag-and-drop interface — blocks are moved and connected without writing code by hand.

2. Predefined blocks — blocks represent functions such as loops, conditionals, variables and events.

3. Modular approach — programs are built from reusable blocks, which promotes organised coding.

4. Error prevention — because only valid blocks exist, syntax errors are minimised.

5. Logical sequencing — blocks are arranged in order to form meaningful instructions.

Advantages. A user-friendly interface; immediate feedback, so the cause-and-effect is visible; it encourages creativity; it promotes logical thinking; and it has a community for sharing and collaboration.

One caution worth carrying into an exam: "error prevention" covers syntax only. A program built entirely from valid blocks can still do the wrong thing.

long.q: What are the applications of block programming? Explain in brief.
long.a:
1. Educational tool — introducing loops, conditionals and events visually, which is the main use.

2. Game development — building games, exercising creativity and problem-solving.

3. Interactive storytelling — designing narratives with character interactions.

4. Animation creation — controlling characters and backgrounds to make animated sequences.

5. STEM education — teaching algorithms, sequencing and debugging in an engaging way.

6. Robotics and physical computing — integrating with hardware such as LEGO Mindstorms and Raspberry Pi.

7. Community and collaboration — sharing projects and learning from peers.

8. Mobile app and web development — prototyping apps, and a route into HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

9. Modelling and simulation — visualising complex systems.

10. Data science and visualisation — analysing and displaying data with minimal coding knowledge.

What unites these is accessibility: block programming lets people who could not write a line of text-based code build something real.

long.q: What is an Arduino UNO? Write down its types of components.
long.a:
What it is. The Arduino UNO is an open-source single-board microcontroller used to build digital devices and interactive objects that sense and control the physical world. It was developed in 2003 at the Interaction Design Institute Ivrea in Italy, and the first official board appeared in 2005. It is built around the ATmega328P and programmed through the Arduino IDE in a simplified C/C++.

Components.

1. Microcontroller — ATmega328P, 16 MHz, 32 KB flash, 2 KB SRAM, 1 KB EEPROM.

2. Power — USB Type-B port (5 V), DC jack (7–12 V), 5 V and 3.3 V regulators, Vin and GND pins.

3. Digital I/O — 14 pins, with PWM on pins 3, 5, 6, 9, 10 and 11.

4. Analog input — pins A0–A5.

5. Communication — UART on pins 0 and 1, SPI on pins 10–13, and I2C on A4 (SDA) and A5 (SCL).

6. Clock and timing — a 16 MHz crystal oscillator and three timers.

7. Control — a reset button and an ICSP header.

8. Indicators — a power LED, the pin 13 LED and TX/RX LEDs.

long.q: What is a microcontroller? Why is it used?
long.a:
A microcontroller is a small computer on a single integrated circuit: a processor, memory and input/output peripherals all on one chip. The ATmega328P in an Arduino UNO is one; so is the chip at the heart of a micro:bit.

Why it is used.

It is cheap — a whole computer for very little money. It is small and low-power, so it can run from a battery inside a product. It has input/output pins built in, so it can read sensors and drive motors directly, with no extra hardware. It is dedicated — it runs one program reliably, over and over, which is exactly what a washing machine or a thermostat needs. And it is simple to program, which is why it is the standard way into electronics.

The contrast is with a general-purpose computer, which runs many programs for a person. A microcontroller runs one program for a machine.

long.q: You are given a program where the cat sprite rotates 90° and says "Namaste" when the sprite is clicked. List and explain the block components used in this program.
long.a:
Three blocks are needed, one from each of three categories.

1. Events — "when this sprite clicked". This is a hat block, so it sits on top and starts the script. Nothing below it runs until the cat is clicked.

2. Motion — "turn 90 degrees". This is a stack block. It rotates the sprite clockwise by 90° from the direction it was facing. Because it sits directly beneath the hat block, it runs immediately after the click.

3. Looks — "say Namaste". Also a stack block. It shows a speech bubble containing "Namaste" above the sprite. Placed last, it runs after the turn.

Why the order matters. Blocks run from top to bottom, so the cat turns and then speaks. Swap the two stack blocks and the cat speaks first and then turns — the same blocks, a different result. That is logical sequencing.

Note on the two "say" blocks. Plain say keeps the bubble until the sprite says or thinks something else; say () for () seconds removes it after a time. Either works here.

practical.q: Create a Maze Game — a character moves with the arrow keys, sensing blocks stop it passing through walls, with a goal and a timer.
practical.a:
How to build it.

1. Draw the maze as the backdrop, with walls in a colour you can test for — say black.

2. Make the player a small sprite. Under when green flag clicked, set its starting position with go to x: () y: ().

3. For movement, use four when () key pressed hat blocks, each with change x by () or change y by () and a point in direction so the sprite faces the way it moves.

4. The wall test is the important part: after each move, check if touching color () ? and, if true, undo the move by changing the coordinate back. That is what stops the sprite walking through walls.

5. Add a goal sprite; when the player touching (goal) ?, broadcast a "win" message and show a message.

6. For the timer, use reset timer at the start and read the timer reporter block to display elapsed seconds.

What a finished result looks like. The sprite starts at the maze entrance, cannot pass through the walls, and reaching the goal shows how long it took.

practical.q: Build a Virtual Pet Simulator — feed, play with and care for a pet, using variables to track hunger, happiness and energy.
practical.a:
How to build it.

1. Create three variables: hunger, happiness and energy. Show them on the stage so you can watch them change.

2. Make the hunger rise over time with a forever loop containing change hunger by 1 and a wait 5 seconds.

3. Add button sprites for Feed, Play and Rest. Each starts with when this sprite clicked and then changes the relevant variable — Feed reduces hunger, Play raises happiness but lowers energy, Rest raises energy.

4. Use costumes so the pet looks different when happy, hungry or tired, switching with if () then tests on the variables.

5. Add sounds and simple animations to make it feel alive.

What a finished result looks like. The pet's state drifts when left alone and responds to each button; ignoring it long enough leads to an unhappy pet.

practical.q: Develop a Space Shooter Game — a spaceship moves with the arrow keys and shoots with the spacebar, with clones for enemies and variables for score and health.
practical.a:
How to build it.

1. Move the ship with when () key pressed and change x by ().

2. For shooting, press space to create clone of (laser). In the laser sprite, use when I start as a clone to move it upward until it touches the edge, then delete this clone.

3. Enemies are also clones, created at random positions using pick random () to ().

4. Keep score and health variables. Add to score when a laser touches an enemy; reduce health when an enemy touches the ship or reaches the bottom.

5. End the game when health reaches zero, with stop all.

Why clones matter. Without them you would need a separate sprite for every enemy and every shot. Clones let one sprite become many.

practical.q: Make a Story Animation — an interactive story with characters, dialogue and backgrounds, using Broadcast and Wait.
practical.a:
How to build it.

1. Plan the story first as a short sequence of scenes.

2. Give each character a script beginning when I receive (). Each scene is a broadcast message.

3. Use broadcast () and wait so one character finishes speaking before the next begins — plain broadcast would let them all talk at once.

4. Switch backdrops with switch backdrop to () and wait, so the scene changes in step with the dialogue.

5. Add sound effects and music, and buttons that let the viewer choose what happens next.

What a finished result looks like. The story plays in order, each character speaking in turn, and the viewer can influence the outcome.

practical.q: Design a Musical Instrument Simulator — a virtual piano, drum set or xylophone that plays notes when keys are pressed.
practical.a:
How to build it.

1. Draw or choose one sprite for each key or drum.

2. For each key, use when this sprite clicked — or when () key pressed for real keyboard keys — followed by start sound () to play that note.

3. Use start sound rather than play sound until done, so notes can overlap instead of queuing up.

4. Add a visual effect on the key, such as a colour change, so you can see what was pressed.

5. Optionally record what was played into a list and add a playback button.

What a finished result looks like. Each key makes its note, several can sound at once, and the keys respond visually.

practical.q: Lab Activity — create a program that adds two numbers, defining your own block of code to do it.
practical.a:
This is the exercise that introduces My Blocks — defining your own block and then using it like a built-in one.

The steps.

1. Create three variables: num1, num2 and sum.

2. Under when green flag clicked, ask for the first number with ask () and wait, then set num1 to answer. The reply is stored in the answer reporter.

3. Do the same for the second number, storing it in num2.

4. Now make your own block. Go to My Blocks, choose Make a Block, name it add, and put the addition inside it: set sum to (num1 + num2).

5. Call that block from the main script, then say (sum) for () seconds to show the result.

Why define a block at all? For one addition it is more work, not less. The reason is reuse: once add exists it can be called anywhere in the project, and changing the addition means changing it in one place instead of everywhere it appears. That is the habit the exercise is teaching.

practical.q: Learning Workshop 3 activity: Block Coding Puzzle
practical.a:
Learning outcome: students understand block-based programming and use it to build small Scratch projects.

Materials needed: computers running MIT Scratch (online or the offline version), Scratch blocks printed on cards for the sorting round, flashcards with short programming-logic challenges.

How to run it

1. Print individual Scratch blocks on separate cards — an event block, a few motion blocks, a loop and a conditional — and give one shuffled set per team.

2. Set a task such as "make the sprite walk to the right and turn around when it touches the edge".

3. Teams lay the cards out in the order that solves the task. Because the blocks are on paper they cannot rely on the shapes clicking together, so they have to think about the actual sequence.

4. Each team then rebuilds its solution in Scratch and checks whether it runs.

What it teaches: sequence, and why a loop belongs around the blocks that must repeat rather than after them. Teams that put the forever block in the wrong place get a sprite that never moves — worth pointing out to the whole class.

practical.q: Learning Workshop 3 activity: Create a Mini Animation
practical.a:
How to run it

1. Ask each student to make a short animation in Scratch — a ball bouncing, or a character that speaks.

2. Require at least three of the following: two costumes or backdrops, a loop, a conditional, and a sound.

3. Students then add polish of their own: a change of colour, a size effect or a glide between two points.

4. Have everyone show their work at the end and say which block did the most work in their animation.

What it teaches: how a small number of blocks combine into something that looks like a finished program, and that animation is really just repeated change over time.

units.title: Chapter 4 — Web Technology
units.overview: How the web works: clients, servers and browsers; HTML for structure; CSS for presentation.
units.summary: Chapter 4 — Web Technology. Review the chapter summary for definitions and key points.

concepts.text: How the web works: clients, servers and browsers; HTML for structure; CSS for presentation.

detailed.heading: Chapter 4 — Web Technology
detailed.note: Detailed teaching notes for Web Technology, written from the textbook and illustrated with the book's own figures.
learning_objectives: Explain what web technology is and name its core technologies.
Distinguish a browser from a server, and HTTP from HTTPS.
Distinguish UI from UX and describe what a wireframe is for.
Explain what HTML is, where it came from and what it is used for.
Write the basic structure of an HTML document.
Use formatting tags, list tags, table tags, image tags and links.
Build a form and explain the common input types.
Explain the three types of CSS and write class and ID selectors.

blocks.text: The tools, techniques and protocols used to create, manage and interact with web applications and websites. It governs how information is shared and accessed over the internet.

blocks.caption: Web technology: browser, server and the protocols between them.

blocks.text: 1. Core technologies

items: HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) — the standard markup language for the structure of a page: headings, paragraphs, links, images.
CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) — describes the presentation: layout, colours, fonts and overall appearance.
JavaScript — a scripting language adding behaviour: dynamic content, form validation and user interaction.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: The three are often confused. A useful line to remember: HTML is the skeleton, CSS is the skin and clothes, JavaScript is the muscle. Structure, presentation, behaviour.
2. Web browsers
Applications such as Chrome, Firefox and Safari that retrieve, present and navigate pages. A browser interprets the HTML, CSS and JavaScript it is given and displays the result.
3. Web servers
Computers that store web content and serve it to users. They handle requests from browsers and deliver the right page. Common server software includes Apache and Nginx.
4. Protocols

items: HTTP — Hypertext Transfer Protocol. The rules for transferring data over the web, defining how messages are formatted and sent.
HTTPS — HTTP Secure. HTTP with encryption (SSL/TLS) added, so that data stays private and unaltered in transit.

blocks.text: 5. Responsive design
An approach that makes pages work well on any screen size, using flexible layouts, flexible images and CSS media queries.
6. Frameworks, databases, APIs and security

items: Frameworks — React, Angular and Vue.js provide ready-made components and tools, making complex applications quicker to build.
Databases — MySQL, PostgreSQL and MongoDB store and manage the data, reached through server-side languages such as PHP, Python or Node.js.
APIs — Application Programming Interfaces let different software talk to each other, so a site can use payment processing or social media services.
Web security — protection against hacking, data breaches and malware, using HTTPS, input validation, and authentication and authorisation.

blocks.text: UI and UX are two different things that are often mentioned together, and the distinction is worth getting right.
The visual elements of a product — layout, colours, typography, buttons and other interactive elements. It aims for an interface that looks good and is easy to navigate.
The overall experience of using the product. It involves understanding user needs, behaviour and pain points, and uses research, user testing and iteration to make the experience seamless.

head: UI
UX
rows: Can the user do the task without friction?
blocks.caption: UI compared with UX

blocks.text: Wireframes
A low-fidelity visual representation of an interface — a blueprint showing the layout and structure of a page without colours, images or detailed graphics.
Features of wireframes

items: Simplicity — no colour, images or detailed graphics; basic shapes and lines stand in for UI elements.
Focus on structure — where the header, footer, navigation, content areas and buttons go.
User flow — how a user moves from one screen to the next.
Collaboration tool — a shared reference that lets stakeholders, designers and developers discuss layout before anything is built.

blocks.text: The wireframe process

items: Define goals and requirements — who the product is for and what it must do.
Sketch ideas roughly, on paper or digitally, to try out layouts quickly.
Choose a tool — Balsamiq, Sketch, Figma or Adobe XD.
Create the wireframe, placing elements according to the agreed structure.
Add annotations explaining interactions and design decisions.
Review and iterate with stakeholders.
Move to high-fidelity design, adding colour, type and imagery.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Wireframes are deliberately plain. If a design has colour and finished graphics, it is no longer a wireframe — it is a mock-up.
Hypertext Markup Language — a set of markup tags that tell the browser how to display the content of a web page. It is not a programming language.

The three words in the name each carry meaning. Hypertext is ordinary text with extra features such as formatting, images, multimedia and links to other documents. Markup is the process of adding those extra features. Language means it has its own syntax and rules.

HTML is platform independent — the same file works on Windows, macOS and Linux. It is a set of markup tags, not a programming language like C, C++, Java or BASIC: it has no variables, no loops and no decisions.
History

HTML was developed by Tim Berners-Lee in 1990 at CERN, the European Particle Physics Laboratory in Geneva. The World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) was formed in September 1994 and controls the HTML standards today. Versions include HTML 4.01, which added Cascading Style Sheets and multimedia, and HTML 5.0, which added local storage and offline databases.
Uses of HTML

items: Creating the basic layout and design of a web page.
Without HTML, the World Wide Web would not exist.
Embedding text, images, multimedia (audio and video) and links.
Creating structured documents using paragraphs, character formatting, links and lists.
Embedding scripts such as CSS and JavaScript that affect behaviour and design.

blocks.text: Advantages of HTML

items: Highly flexible and user friendly.
An open technology, supported by almost every browser and platform.
Easily understood — it does not need long training.
Designed so that pages interact with one another, which makes it effective.
HTML pages load quickly.

sections.title: Structure of HTML and Types of Tags

blocks.text: Every HTML document has the same basic skeleton. The <html> element wraps everything; inside it are a <head>, holding information about the page such as its title, and a <body>, holding the content that is actually shown.

blocks.caption: The basic structure of an HTML document.

blocks.text: Singular and paired tags

head: Type
Meaning
Examples
rows: Have an opening and a closing tag, and wrap around content.
Stand alone with no closing tag; they insert something.
blocks.caption: The two kinds of tag

blocks.text: Attributes
An extra piece of information inside a tag that modifies how that element behaves or appears. Attributes are written as name="value" pairs in the opening tag.
For example <p align="center"> — align is the attribute and center its value. Attributes give you control that the bare tag does not.
Character formatting tags
These tags change the appearance of text without changing its meaning.

head: Tag
Purpose
rows: Important text — bold, and it carries meaning for screen readers
blocks.caption: Formatting tags and what they do
How the formatting tags render in a browser.

blocks.text: Nested tags
Tags can go inside other tags. When you nest them, they must close in the reverse order to the one they opened — they must never overlap.
Correct: <b><i>text</i></b>. Incorrect: <b><i>text</b></i>. The second version may still render in some browsers, but it is wrong and it will eventually break.
The font tag
The <font> tag sets the size, colour and typeface of text. It is a paired tag with three attributes.

head: Attribute
Explanation
Example
rows: Font size from 1 (smallest) to 7 (largest); the default is 3.
Colour by name or as a hexadecimal code #RRGGBB.
blocks.caption: Attributes of the font tag

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: If a named font is not installed on the computer, the browser falls back to its own default. Not every browser understands every colour name, but all understand the six digit hexadecimal form — where the first two digits are red, the next two green and the last two blue, each from 00 to FF. For example #00FFFF is cyan.

head: Colour
Hex
Colour
Hex
blocks.caption: Common colours and their hexadecimal values

blocks.text: Lists
HTML supports three kinds of list.
1. Ordered list

An ordered list uses a numbering scheme — Arabic numerals, letters or Roman numbers. It starts with <ol> and ends with </ol>, with each item in an <li> tag. The browser numbers the items automatically.

head: Attribute
Values
Explanation
rows: Capital letters, small letters, capital Roman, small Roman, Arabic numerals (default is 1)
The value the list starts from
Asks the browser to compact the list; ignored by most browsers
blocks.caption: Attributes of the ordered list

blocks.text: 2. Unordered list
An unordered list is for items whose order does not matter. It starts with <ul> and ends with </ul>, and items carry a bullet marker.

blocks.caption: Ordered and unordered lists as a browser renders them.

blocks.text: 3. Definition list
A definition list pairs a term with an indented description. Three tags are used: <dl> for the list, <dt> for the term and <dd> for the description.
Nested lists
Lists can be placed inside one another to show hierarchy.

blocks.caption: A nested list — sub-items inside a list item.
A definition list: terms with indented descriptions.

blocks.text: Character entities

A browser collapses multiple spaces into one, so typing a hundred spaces still shows only a single gap. To force extra spaces, or to show a character that HTML would otherwise treat as markup, you use a character entity.
An entity has three parts: an ampersand (&), then an entity name or a hash and an entity number, then a semicolon (;). Entity numbers are more reliable than names.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Entities are case sensitive — write them exactly as shown.
Tables
A table is a two-dimensional structure of rows and columns. It makes data easier to interpret, and each cell can hold text, graphics or links.

head: Tag
Description
rows: The main tag; everything else goes inside it
Table Row — adds a horizontal row
Table Header — a header cell, shown in bold
A title for the table, centred at the top by default
blocks.caption: The five table tags

head: Attribute
Explanation
rows: Alignment of the table: LEFT, CENTER or RIGHT
Border thickness; BORDER="0" means no border
Space between a cell's content and its edge
Minimum width, in pixels or as a percentage
blocks.caption: Attributes of the table tag

blocks.text: Two further attributes belong only to <td> and <th>: COLSPAN, the number of columns a cell spans, and ROWSPAN, the number of rows it spans. These are how cells are merged.

blocks.caption: A simple table as the browser renders it.
Merging cells into one column using COLSPAN.
Merging cells down rows using ROWSPAN.

blocks.text: Images
Images make a page more attractive. The widely used formats are JPEG and GIF. Images are inserted with the singular <img> tag.

head: Attribute
Explanation
rows: The location and name of the image
Positioning: LEFT, RIGHT, TOP, BOTTOM or MIDDLE
Border width around the image, in pixels
Height, in pixels or as a percentage
Width, in pixels or as a percentage
Text shown if the image cannot be displayed
Horizontal space to the left and right
blocks.caption: Attributes of the image tag
An image inserted into a page.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Keep the image in the same folder as the page unless you give a full path. Setting HEIGHT and WIDTH lets the browser reserve the space before the image loads, so the page does not jump about.
Hyperlinks
The anchor tag <a> creates a hyperlink to a page, a file, an email address or a location. The text between the opening and closing tags is what the user clicks.

blocks.caption: Links as they appear in a browser.

blocks.text: Link colours are set on the <body> tag:

head: Attribute
Meaning
Standard colour
rows: An active link, while the mouse is on it
blocks.caption: Link colour attributes

blocks.text: By default a link opens in the current window. The target attribute changes that — _blank opens a new window, and _self (the default) uses the current one.
Comments
A comment is a note in the source that the browser does not display. It is written <!-- This is a comment --> and is used to explain the code to whoever reads it next.
A collection of fields for gathering information from visitors — text boxes, radio buttons, checkboxes and drop-down menus — which is then submitted and processed.
A form is created with <form> </form>, and every form element goes between those two tags. The form element itself has no formatting attributes.
Attributes of the form tag

head: Attribute
Purpose
rows: The URL of the program on the server that will process the data
How the data is sent to the server
How the form contents are encoded; leave it alone unless uploading a file
The form's name, used by scripts
The frame or window where the response appears
blocks.caption: Attributes of the form tag

blocks.text: Form elements
The elements are specified as attributes of the <input> tag. Common attributes are TYPE, NAME, VALUE, CHECKED, SIZE and MAXLENGTH.

head: Type
Description
Syntax
rows: A field where each keystroke shows as an asterisk
A general button, used with a script
Lets the user pick more than one option
Lets the user pick exactly one from a group
Sends the data to the address in ACTION
blocks.caption: The main input types

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Checkboxes and radio buttons look similar but behave differently: checkboxes are independent, radio buttons in a group are mutually exclusive. Choosing between them is a regular exam question.
The div tag

The <div> tag groups elements together so they can be styled or moved as one block. It is a container with no visual effect of its own, which is exactly why it is useful — it gives CSS something to attach to.
Cascading Style Sheets — a set of styles defining how HTML elements are displayed, added to HTML 4.0 because tags alone could not make a site look good.
Advantages of CSS

items: Pages load faster.
Design is consistent across every page of the site.
More control over font, size and colour, which helps users with disabilities.
Future redesigns are more efficient — change one file, not every page.
The same markup can be presented differently on a desktop and a phone.
Pages work in almost every browser.

blocks.text: The three types of CSS
"Embedding CSS in HTML" just means adding style instructions to a page. There are three ways to do it.
1. Inline CSS
Used when a unique style applies to a single occurrence of one element. The style goes in a style attribute on the tag itself.
<p style="color: red; margin-left: 20px">This is a paragraph.</p>
2. Internal CSS
Used when a single document has its own style. The rules are defined in the head section inside a <style> tag.
<head><style type="text/css">body {background-color: red} p {margin-left: 20px}</style></head>
3. External CSS
Used when the same style applies to many pages — the right choice for a whole website, because one file controls the look of everything. Each page links to it with a <link> tag in the head.
<head><link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="mystyle.css"></head>

head: Type
Where it lives
Best for
rows: In a style attribute on one tag
One-off changes to a single element
In a <style> tag in the head
One page with its own style
A whole site; change one file, update all
blocks.caption: Choosing a type of CSS

blocks.text: A CSS rule has three parts: a selector, a property and a value.
selector {property: value}

The selector is the element you want to define; the property is the attribute you want to change; the value is what you want to change it to. Property and value are separated by a colon and the pair is wrapped in curly brackets. Put quotes around a value of more than one word, as in p {font-family: "sans serif"}. Separate several declarations with semicolons.
Class selector
A class lets you define different styles for the same element — for example one right-aligned paragraph and one centre-aligned one.
p.right {text-align: right}   p.center {text-align: center}
Apply it in the HTML with <p class="right">. You can also drop the tag name and write .center {text-align: center}, which then applies to every element carrying that class.
ID selector
An ID applies to exactly one element, and must be unique within the document. That is the difference from a class, which may be shared.
p#para1 {text-align: center; color: red}

blocks.caption: CSS border styles applied to paragraphs.

blocks.text: The box model

Every element is drawn as a box: the content, then padding (space between content and border), then the border, then the margin (space outside the border). The space inside the border is filled with the background colour and is controlled by the padding properties.
Measurement units

items: em — the current font size.
px — one screen pixel.
mm — a millimetre; centimetres and inches are also available.
