mcq.q: What is the primary purpose of web technology?
options: Connect and share information over the internet
mcq.teacher_note: To connect and share information over the internet. Web technology is about the web; standalone applications and system software are not what it is for.

mcq.q: Which protocol is used for secure web communication?
mcq.teacher_note: HTTPS — the S is what adds the encryption. HTTP on its own sends data in the clear.

mcq.q: Which of the following is a client-side technology?
mcq.teacher_note: HTML runs in the browser, which is the client. PHP and Node.js run on the server, and MySQL is a database.

mcq.q: What is the main benefit of using a web framework?
options: Faster development and better code organisation
mcq.teacher_note: Faster development and better code organisation. A framework gives you ready-made components. It does not remove HTML, and it certainly does not remove the need to debug.

mcq.q: What does UI stand for?
mcq.teacher_note: User Interface. UX, its partner, is User Experience.

mcq.q: Wireframes in web design are used for:
mcq.teacher_note: Planning structure and layout — they are blueprints made before any code is written.

mcq.q: What does HTML stand for?
mcq.teacher_note: Hypertext Markup Language. "Hypertext" is the key word — text with links.

mcq.q: Which of the following is a correct structure of an HTML document?
mcq.teacher_note: The correct nesting is <html> wrapping <head> and <body>: <html><head>...</head><body>...</body></html>.

mcq.q: The <title> tag is used for:
options: Setting the title of the webpage
mcq.teacher_note: Setting the title — it appears in the browser tab. Bold text is <b>, images are <img>.

mcq.q: Which HTML tag is used to create a hyperlink?
mcq.teacher_note: The anchor tag, <a>. Note that href is an attribute inside it, not a tag, and <link> is for linking a stylesheet.

mcq.q: Which tag is used for inserting an image in HTML?
mcq.teacher_note: <img>. Again, src is an attribute of it, not a tag.

mcq.q: Which HTML tag is used for creating a paragraph?
mcq.teacher_note: <p> — one of the shortest tags in the language.

mcq.q: Which HTML tag is used for the largest heading?
mcq.teacher_note: <h1>. The numbers run the "wrong" way: h1 is the biggest, h6 the smallest. There is no <heading> tag.

mcq.q: What is the correct syntax for a comment in HTML?
mcq.teacher_note: <!-- ... -->. The // and /* */ forms belong to JavaScript and other languages, not to HTML.

mcq.q: What type of list uses bullet points?
mcq.teacher_note: The unordered list, <ul>. There is no <tl> tag at all.

mcq.q: What type of list uses numbering?
mcq.teacher_note: The ordered list, <ol> — "ordered" means the order matters, so it is numbered.

mcq.q: How do you create a table row in HTML?
mcq.teacher_note: <tr> — table row. <td> is a cell, <th> a header cell, and <table> the whole table.

mcq.q: Which tag is used to create a form in HTML?
mcq.teacher_note: <form>. The <input> tags for the fields go inside it.

mcq.q: What is the purpose of the <marquee> tag?
options: To create a scrolling text effect
mcq.teacher_note: It makes text scroll across the page. Worth knowing that it is deprecated in modern HTML — CSS animation is the current way.

mcq.q: Which tag is used to group elements together in HTML?
mcq.teacher_note: <div> is the general-purpose grouping container. <section> and <article> are more specific HTML5 elements, and <span> groups inline text rather than blocks.

mcq.q: How do you create an email input field in an HTML form?
mcq.teacher_note: <input type="email">. It behaves like a text field but the browser checks that what was typed looks like an email address.

mcq.q: What does CSS stand for?
mcq.teacher_note: Cascading Style Sheets. "Cascading" because several style definitions can combine, with rules for which one wins.

mcq.q: What is the main purpose of CSS?
options: To create the structure of a webpage
To program logic in web applications
mcq.teacher_note: To style HTML. Structure is HTML's job; logic is JavaScript's; storage is the database's.

mcq.q: Where is CSS mainly used?
mcq.teacher_note: For designing and formatting webpages. It does nothing on the back end.

mcq.q: Which HTML tag is used to link an external CSS file?
mcq.teacher_note: <link>. <style> is for internal CSS, <script> is for JavaScript, and there is no <css> tag.

mcq.q: How do you apply CSS to an HTML document?
options: Using inline, internal, or external styles
mcq.teacher_note: Through inline, internal or external styles — the three types.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of CSS?
options: Allows consistent styling across multiple pages
mcq.teacher_note: Increases webpage loading time — CSS makes pages load faster, so that is a disadvantage, not an advantage. The other three are genuine benefits.

mcq.q: What is an advantage of using External CSS?
options: It allows applying styles to multiple pages
It only works on one page
It must be written inside HTML tags
mcq.teacher_note: It lets one file style many pages — change the file, and the whole site updates.

mcq.q: Which type of CSS is defined inside the <head> section of an HTML page?
mcq.teacher_note: Internal CSS, written in a <style> tag in the head. Inline goes on the element itself; external lives in its own file.

mcq.q: Which type of CSS is best for styling a single element?
mcq.teacher_note: Inline CSS — it is meant for a unique style on one occurrence of one element.

mcq.q: How is Internal CSS applied?
options: By using the <style> tag inside the <head> section
By writing CSS in an external file
By embedding CSS in a SQL database
mcq.teacher_note: With a <style> tag in the head. An external file is external CSS, not internal.

mcq.q: Where is Inline CSS applied?
options: Inside an HTML element using the style attribute
mcq.teacher_note: On the element itself, using the style attribute.

mcq.q: Which of the following is the correct syntax for Inline CSS?
mcq.teacher_note: The attribute is style. There is no css attribute, and link and id do something else entirely.

mcq.q: Which type of CSS is best for applying styles to multiple pages?
mcq.teacher_note: External CSS. Internal covers one page; inline covers one element.

mcq.q: How is External CSS linked to an HTML page?
mcq.teacher_note: <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">. The rel="stylesheet" is what tells the browser what is being linked.

mcq.q: What is the main disadvantage of using Inline CSS?
options: It makes HTML code longer and harder to manage
It does not work in all browsers
It is required for JavaScript to work
mcq.teacher_note: It makes the HTML longer and harder to manage, because the styles are scattered through the markup instead of being in one place. It can certainly change colours.

mcq.q: Where should an External CSS file be stored?
mcq.teacher_note: In a separate .css file, which the HTML then links to.

mcq.q: Which CSS property is used to change the text color?
mcq.teacher_note: Just color. font-color and text-color do not exist, which is a common beginner mistake.

mcq.q: Which CSS property controls the text size?
mcq.teacher_note: font-size. font-style controls italic, not size.

mcq.q: Which CSS selector applies styles to a single, unique element?
mcq.teacher_note: The ID selector, because an ID must be unique in the document. A class can repeat; the universal selector hits everything.

mcq.q: Which CSS selector applies styles to multiple elements of the same type?
mcq.teacher_note: The class selector — that is exactly what classes are for, marking several elements as sharing a style.

mcq.q: Which type of CSS selector is most specific?
mcq.teacher_note: The ID selector. Specificity runs: ID, then class, then element, with the universal selector lowest of all.

short.q: What is Web Technology?
short.a: Web technology is the set of tools, techniques and protocols used to create, manage and interact with web applications and websites. It governs how information is shared and accessed over the internet, and it includes the core technologies (HTML, CSS, JavaScript), browsers, servers, protocols such as HTTP and HTTPS, and approaches such as responsive design.

short.q: List two common web server software.
short.a: Apache and Nginx. Both are widely used, free and open-source, and between them they serve a large share of the web.

short.q: List two primary goals of UI design.
short.a: To create an interface that is aesthetically pleasing, and one that is intuitive to navigate — so that a user can find what they need without being taught how.

short.q: What is hypertext markup language?
short.a: HTML is the standard markup language used to create web pages. It is a set of tags that tell the browser how to display content — headings, paragraphs, links, images and more. It is not a programming language: it has no variables, loops or decisions, and it is platform independent.

short.q: Define attribute.
short.a: An attribute is an extra piece of information placed inside a tag, in the opening tag, that modifies how that element behaves or appears. It is written as a name="value" pair — for example <p align="center">, where align is the attribute and center is its value.

short.q: What is a character formatting tag?
short.a: A tag that changes the appearance of text without changing its meaning — for example <b> for bold, <i> for italic, <u> for underline, <sub> for subscript and <sup> for superscript.

short.q: What is a nested tag?
short.a: A tag placed inside another tag. When nesting, the tags must close in the reverse order to the one they opened in — they must never overlap. Correct: <b><i>text</i></b>. Incorrect: <b><i>text</b></i>.

short.q: What are the properties of the font tag?
short.a: Three: SIZE (1 to 7, default 3), COLOR (a colour name or a hexadecimal code such as #RRGGBB) and FACE (the typeface). For example <font size="5" color="green" face="arial">text</font>.

short.q: List out the different types of lists that can be created in HTML.
short.a: Three: the ordered list (<ol>), numbered automatically; the unordered list (<ul>), bulleted; and the definition list (<dl>), pairing a term (<dt>) with a description (<dd>).

short.q: Write a tag to insert an image in an HTML document.
short.a: <img src="mypic.jpg" width="200" height="150" alt="A photo">. The src attribute gives the location, and alt supplies text shown if the image cannot be displayed.

short.q: What do UI and UX stand for, and what is their role in digital product design?
short.a:
UI is User Interface and UX is User Experience. UI design deals with the visual elements — layout, colour, typography, buttons — aiming for something attractive and easy to navigate. UX design covers the whole experience of using the product: understanding what users need, researching and testing, and iterating until the product is genuinely usable.

They are complementary. A product can look superb and still be frustrating, which is a UI success and a UX failure. Good design needs both.

short.q: Define HTTP and HTTPS. What is the main difference between them?
short.a:
HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) is the set of rules for transferring data over the web — it defines how messages are formatted and transmitted.

HTTPS (HTTP Secure) is HTTP with encryption added, using SSL/TLS.

The difference is encryption. With HTTP, data crosses the network in plain text and anyone intercepting it can read it. With HTTPS it is encrypted, so the data stays private and cannot be quietly altered. That is why HTTPS is now the standard for any site handling passwords or payments.

short.q: Compare and contrast a web server and a web browser.
short.a:
A browser runs on the user's device. It requests pages, then receives and displays them — interpreting the HTML, CSS and JavaScript it is given. Chrome, Firefox and Safari are browsers.

A server runs remotely. It stores the pages and files, waits for requests, and sends the right ones back. Apache and Nginx are server software.

They are the two ends of the same conversation: the browser asks, the server answers. One is client software for a person; the other is host software for a site.

short.q: What are APIs, and why are they important in web applications?
short.a:
An API (Application Programming Interface) is a defined way for two pieces of software to communicate. In web work it lets an application use someone else's service — payment processing, social media sign-in, maps, weather data — without building that service itself.

They matter because they save enormous effort and let applications combine. A small site can accept card payments through a payments API without ever handling card numbers itself, which is both quicker and safer.

short.q: Write any two differences between the ordered and unordered list.
short.a:
1. An ordered list (<ol>) numbers its items, so the sequence matters. An unordered list (<ul>) uses bullet markers, and the order does not matter.

2. Their attributes differ: <ol> takes TYPE (1, a, A, i, I) and START, while <ul> takes TYPE (disc, circle, square).

short.q: How to insert an image in HTML?
short.a:
Use the singular <img> tag with a src attribute naming the file. For example:

<img src="mypic.jpg" alt="A photo" width="300" height="200" border="2">

Two practical points: keep the image in the same folder as the page unless you give a full path, and set WIDTH and HEIGHT so the browser can reserve the space before the image loads.

short.q: What is a link in HTML? Explain.
short.a:
A link (hyperlink) is clickable text or an image that takes you to another location — another page, a file, an email address, or a place within the same page. Links are what make the web a web rather than a pile of separate documents.

It is created with the anchor tag: <a href="page.html">Click here</a>. The href attribute gives the destination; the text between the tags is what the user clicks. Add target="_blank" to open the destination in a new window.

short.q: List out any two elements of form in HTML.
short.a: Any two of: a text field (<input type="text">), a password field (<input type="password">), a checkbox (<input type="checkbox">), a radio button (<input type="radio">), a submit button (<input type="submit">) and a reset button (<input type="reset">).

short.q: Define singular tag and paired tag with four examples.
short.a:
A paired tag has an opening and a closing tag and wraps around content. Examples: <html>...</html>, <p>...</p>, <b>...</b> and <title>...</title>.

A singular tag (also called an empty tag) stands alone and has no closing tag; it inserts something. Examples: <br>, <hr>, <img> and <input>.

short.q: Write the basic structure of HTML.
short.a:
Every HTML document has the same skeleton:

<html>
<head>
  <title>Page Title</title>
</head>
<body>
  content that is displayed
</body>
</html>

The <html> tag wraps everything. The head holds information about the page, such as its title; the body holds what the user actually sees.

short.q: Define CSS.
short.a: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is a set of style rules that define how HTML elements are displayed. It controls layout, colour, fonts and spacing, so that the presentation of a page is separate from its structure. It was added in HTML 4.0 because HTML tags alone could not make a site look good.

short.q: What are the advantages of using CSS?
short.a: Pages load faster; the design is consistent across every page of the site; there is more control over font, size and colour, which helps users with disabilities; future redesigns are more efficient because one file can be changed; the same markup can be presented differently on different devices; and pages work in almost every browser.

short.q: What is body in CSS?
short.a: body is the selector that targets the <body> element — that is, the whole visible page. Because it contains everything else, rules set on it tend to apply throughout: body {background-color: yellow} colours the entire background. Properties such as colour and font set on the body are inherited by the elements inside it.

short.q: What are the different types of selectors in CSS?
short.a: The main ones are the element selector (targets a tag, such as p), the class selector (.name, which can apply to many elements), the ID selector (#name, which must apply to exactly one), and the universal selector (*, which targets everything).

short.q: Define class selector.
short.a: A class selector applies a style to every element carrying that class, using a full stop before the name. Write .center {text-align: center} and then <p class="center"> to use it. Unlike an ID, a class may be reused on as many elements as you like, which is what makes it the workhorse of CSS.

short.q: Write the CSS syntax for a property and value.
short.a: selector {property: value} — for example p {color: red}. The property and value are separated by a colon, the pair is wrapped in curly brackets, and several declarations are separated by semicolons: p {text-align: center; color: red}.

short.q: Define two types of selectors used in CSS.
short.a:
Class selector. Written with a full stop, as in .note. It can be applied to many elements, and is used when several things should share a style.

ID selector. Written with a hash, as in #header. It must be unique within the document, so it is used when one specific element needs its own style.

short.q: List out any two common measuring units in CSS.
short.a: px — one screen pixel, a fixed size. em — relative to the current font size, so it scales when the user changes their text size. Others include mm, cm and percentages.

short.q: What are inline styles? Write its syntax.
short.a:
An inline style is CSS applied directly to a single element through its style attribute. It is used when a unique style applies to one occurrence of one element.

Syntax: <p style="color: red; margin-left: 20px">This is a paragraph.</p>

short.q: Define any two advantages of CSS.
short.a:
Consistency. One stylesheet gives every page of a site the same look, which would be almost impossible to maintain by hand.

Efficient maintenance. Changing the stylesheet changes the whole site at once, so a redesign is a change to one file rather than to hundreds.

Other advantages: faster loading, better accessibility, and the same content presented differently for different devices.

short.q: Self Test 4.1: What is Web Technology?
short.a: Web technology is the set of tools, techniques and protocols used to create, manage and interact with web applications and websites — the core technologies (HTML, CSS, JavaScript), browsers, servers, protocols such as HTTP and HTTPS, and approaches such as responsive design. It governs how information is shared over the internet.

short.q: Self Test 4.1: Define a wireframe in web design.
short.a: A wireframe is a low-fidelity visual representation of a user interface — a blueprint showing the layout and structure of a page without colours, images or finished graphics. It uses simple shapes and lines to show where elements go.

short.q: Self Test 4.2: What is one disadvantage of HTML?
short.a: Any one of: HTML alone can only produce static pages — anything dynamic needs CSS, JavaScript or a server-side language. Others: it gives limited control over layout and appearance on its own; it has no logic, so it cannot process data; and older markup can render differently between browsers.

short.q: Self Test 4.2: Which tag is used to define the title of a webpage in HTML?
short.a: <title>, placed inside the <head> section. The text appears in the browser tab and is used as the bookmark name — it is not shown on the page itself.

short.q: Self Test 4.2: Which tag is used to create a paragraph in HTML?
short.a: <p>, closed with </p>.

short.q: Self Test 4.3: What is the purpose of the <b> tag in HTML?
short.a: It displays the enclosed text in bold. Note that <strong> also bolds text but additionally marks it as important, which screen readers can announce — so <strong> is usually the better choice.

short.q: Self Test 4.3: Which HTML tag is used to create a hyperlink?
short.a: The anchor tag, <a>, with the destination in its href attribute: <a href="page.html">Click here</a>.

short.q: Self Test 4.3: What is the function of the <ul> tag in HTML?
short.a: It creates an unordered list — a bulleted list for items whose order does not matter. Each item goes in an <li> tag. The bullet style can be changed with the type attribute (disc, circle, square).

short.q: Self Test 4.3: What is the purpose of the <td> tag in an HTML table?
short.a: <td> — table data — defines a single cell in a table row. It holds the actual content: text, an image or a link. Use <th> instead for a header cell, which the browser bolds.

short.q: Self Test 4.4: What is the purpose of the <form> tag in HTML?
short.a: It creates a form — a collection of fields for gathering information from visitors, such as text boxes, checkboxes and radio buttons. All the form elements go between <form> and </form>, and the completed data is submitted to the address given in the action attribute.

short.q: Self Test 4.4: What does the method attribute in the <form> tag specify?
short.a: It specifies how the data is sent to the server. With get, the data is appended to the URL, so it is visible and limited in length — fine for a search. With post, the data is sent in the request body, so it is not visible in the address bar and has no length limit — the right choice for passwords and anything sensitive.

short.q: Self Test 4.4: Name one difference between a radio button and a checkbox in an HTML form.
short.a: A checkbox lets the user select several options independently; a radio button allows only one choice within a group. So checkboxes for "which sports do you play", radio buttons for "male / female".

short.q: Self Test 4.4: What is the purpose of the <div> tag in HTML?
short.a: It groups elements together so they can be styled or moved as one block. It has no appearance of its own, which is exactly why it is useful — it gives CSS something to attach to, and lets a page be divided into sections.

short.q: Self Test 4.5: What is the purpose of the comment tag in HTML?
short.a: A comment is a note in the source that the browser does not display. It is used to explain the code to whoever reads it next — labelling a section, or saying why something was done a particular way.

short.q: Self Test 4.5: Write the syntax for adding a comment in HTML.
short.a: <!-- This is a comment --> — it can span several lines, and everything between the opening <!-- and the closing --> is ignored.

short.q: Self Test 4.5: Name two attributes of the <marquee> tag.
short.a: Any two of: direction (left, right, up, down), behavior (scroll, slide, alternate), scrollamount (the speed), bgcolor (the background colour), and width / height.

short.q: Self Test 4.5: List two types of links in HTML.
short.a: Any two of: an external link (to another site), an internal link (to another page of the same site), an email link (using mailto:), an anchor link (to a section of the same page, using #), and an image link (an image inside an anchor).

short.q: Self Test 4.5: Which attribute is used to define the color of a link in HTML?
short.a: Three, set on the <body> tag: LINK for an unvisited link (blue by default), VLINK for a visited one (purple) and ALINK for an active one while the mouse is on it (red).

short.q: Self Test 4.6: What is embedded CSS in HTML?
short.a: It means adding CSS styling to an HTML document. There are three ways: inline, in a style attribute on one tag; internal, in a <style> tag in the head; and external, in a separate .css file linked with <link>.

short.q: Self Test 4.6: Name the three types of CSS.
short.a: Inline CSS, internal CSS and external CSS.

short.q: Self Test 4.6: Which CSS selector is used to style a specific element by its ID?
short.a: The ID selector, written with a hash: p#para1 or just #para1. An ID must be unique in the document, so it targets exactly one element.

short.q: Self Test 4.6: Name two common measurement units used in CsS.
short.a: Any two of: px (one screen pixel), em (relative to the current font size) and mm (a millimetre). Percentages are also common.

long.q: Explain the importance of web security. Why is it crucial to validate user input in web applications?
long.a:
Why web security matters. A web application is reachable by anyone, from anywhere, at any hour — and it usually holds data worth stealing. Without security, a site is open to hacking, data breaches and malware. The consequences fall on real people: stolen passwords, leaked personal details, financial loss, and a reputation that does not recover. HTTPS, authentication, authorisation and input validation are the standard defences.

Why input validation matters. Anything a user types is untrusted, because you cannot control what arrives. If an application accepts it unchecked, several attacks become possible. In SQL injection, a user types database commands into a text box and the application runs them, exposing or destroying data. In cross-site scripting, a user submits a script that the site then shows to other visitors, and it runs in their browsers. Malformed input can also simply crash the application.

Validating means checking input against what is actually expected — the right type, length and format — before doing anything with it. It is a small amount of code that prevents a large amount of damage, which is why it is treated as a fundamental rule rather than an optional extra.

long.q: Write any four advantages and disadvantages of using HTML.
long.a:
Advantages.

1. It is flexible and user friendly, and simple enough to learn quickly.

2. It is an open technology, supported by almost every browser and platform.

3. It is easily understood and needs no long training.

4. HTML pages load quickly, being plain text.

Disadvantages.

1. HTML alone can only make static pages — anything dynamic needs CSS, JavaScript or a server-side language.

2. It gives limited control over layout and appearance on its own, which is precisely why CSS exists.

3. It has no logic — no variables, loops or decisions, so it cannot process data.

4. Older code can render differently between browsers, which makes testing necessary.

long.q: What is a formatting tag? Write any four formatting tags with their descriptions.
long.a:
A formatting tag changes how text appears without changing what it means. Four examples:

1. <b> </b> — displays the enclosed text in bold.

2. <i> </i> — displays it in italic.

3. <u> </u> — underlines it.

4. <sub> </sub> — lowers the text as a subscript, as in H2SO4.

Others worth knowing are <sup> for superscript, <big> and <small> for size, <em> for emphasis, <strong> for importance, and <code> for computer code.

long.q: Create an HTML page using ordered and unordered lists.
long.a:
A page demonstrating both kinds of list:

<html>
<head><title>Lists</title></head>
<body>
<h3>Types of Computer</h3>
<ol>
  <li>Supercomputer</li>
  <li>Mainframe</li>
  <li>Minicomputer</li>
  <li>Microcomputer</li>
</ol>
<h3>Input Devices</h3>
<ul type="square">
  <li>Keyboard</li>
  <li>Mouse</li>
  <li>Scanner</li>
</ul>
</body>
</html>

The ordered list is numbered automatically, because the order — by speed and size — is meaningful. The unordered list is bulleted, because the order of input devices is arbitrary.

long.q: What is a hyperlink? How many types of hyperlinks are used in HTML, and write the tags for them.
long.a:
A hyperlink is clickable text or an image that takes the user to another location. It is created with the anchor tag, <a>, whose href attribute gives the destination.

Types, with their tags.

1. External link — to another site: <a href="https://www.example.com">Example</a>

2. Internal link — to another page of the same site: <a href="about.html">About us</a>

3. Email link — opens the mail program: <a href="mailto:info@example.com">Email us</a>

4. Anchor link — jumps to a section of the same page: <a href="#top">Back to top</a>

5. Image link — an image that is clickable: <a href="page.html"><img src="pic.jpg"></a>

Adding target="_blank" opens any of these in a new window.

long.q: What are the uses of a table in a webpage? Write any three attributes of the table using an HTML page.
long.a:
Uses. A table presents data in rows and columns, which makes it easier to interpret than the same information in a paragraph, and each cell can hold text, graphics or links. Tables are the natural way to show anything grid-shaped: timetables, bills, mark sheets, price lists.

Example using three attributes — BORDER, CELLPADDING and CELLSPACING:

<table border="1" cellpadding="8" cellspacing="2">
  <tr><th>SN</th><th>Particulars</th><th>Rate</th></tr>
  <tr><td>1</td><td>Pen</td><td>20</td></tr>
  <tr><td>2</td><td>Book</td><td>150</td></tr>
</table>

BORDER sets the border thickness, CELLPADDING the space between a cell's content and its edge, and CELLSPACING the space between the cells themselves.

long.q: Write the full forms: HTML, HTTPS, UI, APL, APIs.
long.a: HTML — Hypertext Markup Language. HTTPS — Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure. UI — User Interface. APL — A Programming Language — an array-programming language named after the book of that title; it is the odd one out in this list, which otherwise covers web technology. APIs — Application Programming Interfaces.

long.q: Write the purpose and syntax of: <a>, <ol>, <ul>, <hr>, BGCOLOR, <u>, <img>, <sup>, <sub>, <table>.
long.a:
<a> — creates a hyperlink. <a href="page.html">text</a>

<ol> — starts a numbered, ordered list. <ol type="a"><li>item</li></ol>

<ul> — starts a bulleted, unordered list. <ul type="square"><li>item</li></ul>

<hr> — a horizontal rule, a singular tag drawing a dividing line. <hr>

BGCOLOR — an attribute setting the background colour. <body bgcolor="yellow">

<u> — underlines text. <u>text</u>

<img> — inserts an image, singular tag. <img src="pic.jpg" alt="photo">

<sup> — superscript. (a+b)<sup>2</sup>

<sub> — subscript. H<sub>2</sub>O

<table> — starts a table. <table border="1"><tr><td>cell</td></tr></table>

long.q: Write a short note on: structure of HTML; types of tags; formatting tags of HTML; ordered/unordered list; HTML links and their types.
long.a:
Structure of HTML. Every document has the same skeleton: <html> wrapping a <head> (information about the page, including <title>) and a <body> (the visible content). Tags nest and must close in reverse order.

Types of tags. Paired tags have an opening and a closing form and wrap content — <p>, <b>. Singular tags stand alone and insert something — <br>, <hr>, <img>, <input>. Nested tags sit inside one another and must not overlap.

Formatting tags. <b> bold, <i> italic, <u> underline, <em> emphasis, <strong> importance, <big> and <small> for size, <sub> and <sup> for scripts, and <code>, <kbd>, <tt>, <samp> and <var> for technical text.

Ordered and unordered lists. An ordered list (<ol>) numbers its items, with TYPE (1, a, A, i, I) and START attributes; use it when the sequence matters. An unordered list (<ul>) bullets its items, with TYPE (disc, circle, square); use it when the order is arbitrary. Both use <li> for each item, and both can be nested inside one another.

Links and their types. A link is created with <a href="...">. The types are external (another site), internal (another page of the same site), email (mailto:), anchor (a section of the same page, using #), and image links (an <img> inside the anchor). Link colours are set on the body with LINK, VLINK and ALINK.

long.q: What are the types of CSS? Explain.
long.a:
There are three ways to add CSS to a page.

1. Inline CSS. The style goes in a style attribute on the element itself. Use it when a unique style applies to a single occurrence of one element.

<p style="color: red; margin-left: 20px">This is a paragraph.</p>

2. Internal CSS. The rules sit in a <style> tag in the head, and apply to that one document. Use it when a single page has its own style.

<head><style type="text/css">body {background-color: red} p {margin-left: 20px}</style></head>

3. External CSS. The rules live in a separate .css file, and each page links to it. Use it when the style applies to many pages.

<head><link rel="stylesheet" type="text/css" href="mystyle.css"></head>

Which to choose. External is the right answer for a real website: one file controls the look of everything, so a redesign means editing a single file. Internal suits a one-off page. Inline suits a single element, but used widely it makes the HTML long and hard to maintain — that is its main disadvantage.

long.q: Write the full forms of mm and px.
long.a: mm — millimetre. px — pixel (picture element), one dot on the screen. Both are measurement units in CSS; em, which is relative to the current font size, is the third common one.

long.q: Write the purpose and syntax of: <style>, <body>, <title>, <h1>.
long.a:
<style> — holds internal CSS rules, placed in the head. <style type="text/css">p {color: red}</style>

<body> — contains the visible content of the page. <body>...content...</body>

<title> — sets the page title shown in the browser tab; it goes in the head. <title>My Page</title>

<h1> — the largest heading, with h2 to h6 progressively smaller. <h1>Heading</h1>

long.q: List any five CSS properties with their use.
long.a:
PropertyWhat it doesExample
colorSets the colour of textcolor: crimson;
background-colorSets the colour behind the contentbackground-color: #f0f8ff;
font-sizeSets how large the text isfont-size: 18px;
text-alignAligns text left, right, centre or justifiedtext-align: center;
borderPuts a border around an elementborder: 2px solid navy;

Five more that are just as common: font-family (typeface), margin (space outside the element), padding (space inside it), width and height (size), and list-style-type (the bullet or number style of a list).

The property name and its value are separated by a colon, and each pair ends with a semicolon.

long.q: Write the CSS for a webpage to demonstrate setting the style of the four borders.
long.a:
Each of the four borders can be styled on its own, so all four can look different.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <title>Four different borders</title>
  <style>
    p {
      border-top:    4px solid   crimson;   /* solid line        */
      border-right:  8px dashed  seagreen;  /* dashed line       */
      border-bottom: 4px dotted  royalblue; /* dotted line       */
      border-left:   8px double  darkorange;/* two parallel lines*/
      padding: 14px;
      width: 320px;
    }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <p>This paragraph has four different borders.</p>
</body>
</html>

How the shorthand works. Each border-* value is three things in one: thickness, style and colour — 4px solid crimson. The style is the only part you must give; if you leave it out the border will not appear, because the default style is none.

The shorthand for all four at once is border: 2px solid navy;, which sets all four sides to the same thing. Use the individual properties when the sides should differ.

The available styles worth knowing are solid, dashed, dotted, double, groove, ridge, inset and outset.

long.q: Write the CSS for a webpage to demonstrate the different list-item styles.
long.a:
The list-style-type property changes the bullet or number that appears beside each item.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <title>List item styles</title>
  <style>
    ul.disc   { list-style-type: disc;    }  /* filled circle - default */
    ul.circle { list-style-type: circle;  }  /* hollow circle           */
    ul.square { list-style-type: square;  }  /* filled square           */
    ul.none   { list-style-type: none;    }  /* no marker at all        */

    ol.decimal  { list-style-type: decimal;        }  /* 1, 2, 3        */
    ol.roman    { list-style-type: upper-roman;    }  /* I, II, III     */
    ol.alpha    { list-style-type: lower-alpha;    }  /* a, b, c        */
    ol.zero     { list-style-type: decimal-leading-zero; } /* 01, 02, 03 */
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <ul class="disc">
    <li>Disc bullet</li><li>Second item</li>
  </ul>
  <ul class="circle">
    <li>Circle bullet</li><li>Second item</li>
  </ul>
  <ol class="roman">
    <li>Roman one</li><li>Roman two</li>
  </ol>
  <ol class="alpha">
    <li>Alpha a</li><li>Alpha b</li>
  </ol>
</body>
</html>

Points worth making in class

The markers are attached to the list element, not to each <li>, so the property goes on ul or ol and is inherited by the items.

list-style-type: none is what turns a list into a plain navigation menu — it removes the bullets so the items can be styled as buttons.

You can also supply your own bullet image with list-style-image: url("dot.png");, or set the marker position with list-style-position: inside;.

long.q: Write the CSS for a webpage to demonstrate adding different colors to a hyperlink.
long.a:
A link has several states, and each can be given its own colour. The pseudo-classes are :link, :visited, :hover and :active.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
  <title>Coloured hyperlinks</title>
  <style>
    a:link    { color: royalblue;   }  /* never visited            */
    a:visited { color: purple;      }  /* already visited          */
    a:hover   { color: crimson;     }  /* mouse is over the link   */
    a:active  { color: darkorange;  }  /* being clicked right now  */

    /* extra touches */
    a            { text-decoration: none;      }  /* remove underline */
    a:hover      { text-decoration: underline;  }  /* underline on hover */
    a:focus      { outline: 2px solid crimson;  }  /* keyboard users  */
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <p>
    Visit <a href="https://www.example.com">Example</a>
    for a demonstration.
  </p>
</body>
</html>

The order matters. These four rules must be written in the order link, visited, hover, active — often remembered as LoVe HAte. If :visited is placed after :hover, a visited link keeps its visited colour and the hover colour never appears, because the later rule wins.

Keep it accessible. Do not rely on colour alone to mark a link, because a person who cannot distinguish the colours will not see the difference. Keep the underline, or add it on hover. Also style :focus so someone using the keyboard can see where they are.

practical.q: Create a single webpage document using image, audio and video.
practical.a:
Use one <img> tag for the picture, and the HTML5 <audio> and <video> elements with the controls attribute so the visitor can play them:

<img src="pic.jpg" alt="A photo" width="300">
<audio src="song.mp3" controls></audio>
<video src="clip.mp4" controls width="400"></video>

Keep all the media files in the same folder as the page, or the browser will not find them. Always include alt on an image — it is shown if the image cannot load.

practical.q: Create a table using TABLE tags with table rows, columns and attributes.
practical.a:
<table border="1" cellpadding="8" cellspacing="2" width="60%">
  <caption>Class 9 Marks</caption>
  <tr><th>Name</th><th>Marks</th></tr>
  <tr><td>Ram</td><td>85</td></tr>
</table>

Use <th> for headers — the browser bolds them — and <caption> for the title.

practical.q: Create a webpage which has scrolling text.
practical.a:
<marquee behavior="scroll" direction="left">Welcome to our school website</marquee>

Worth knowing: <marquee> is deprecated in modern HTML, so the current way to do this is with a CSS animation. It still works in every browser though, which is why it appears in the textbook.

practical.q: Create a simple webpage with a title, two headings, and three paragraphs.
practical.a:
<html>
<head><title>My School</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Welcome</h1>
  <p>First paragraph.</p>
  <h2>About us</h2>
  <p>Second paragraph.</p>
  <p>Third paragraph.</p>
</body></html>

Use <h1> for the main heading and <h2> for the section heading — headings run from h1 (largest) to h6 (smallest).

practical.q: Create a webpage with hyperlinks to different sections of the same page and links to two external websites.
practical.a:
Internal links jump using # and an id; external links use a full address:

<a href="#contact">Jump to contact</a>
<h2 id="contact">Contact us</h2>

<a href="https://www.example.com" target="_blank">Example</a>

target="_blank" opens the external site in a new tab so the visitor does not lose your page.

practical.q: Create a webpage that uses four ordered items, three unordered, and definition lists.
practical.a:
Use <ol> where order matters, <ul> where it does not, and <dl> for terms and their meanings:

<ol><li>Step one</li>…</ol>
<ul><li>Item</li>…</ul>
<dl><dt>HTML</dt><dd>Hypertext Markup Language</dd></dl>

Pick content where the distinction is real: steps in a recipe are ordered; a shopping list is not.

practical.q: Design a structured table containing rows, columns, headers and merged cells of a commercial bill, using SN, particulars, rate, quantity, amount and total amount.
practical.a:
Use colspan to merge across columns for the total row, and rowspan if any cell spans rows:

<tr><td colspan="5"><strong>Total Amount: Rs. 2,450</strong></td></tr>

Build the header row with <th> for SN, Particulars, Rate, Quantity and Amount, put each purchase in its own <tr>, and finish with the merged total row.

practical.q: Create a form with a submit button.
practical.a:
<form action="thanks.html" method="post">
  Name: <input type="text" name="name"><br>
  Email: <input type="email" name="email"><br>
  <input type="submit" value="Send">
</form>

Every input needs a name, because that is how the server identifies each value when the form is submitted.

practical.q: Create a webpage with images that are clickable and lead to different URLs.
practical.a:
Wrap the image in an anchor tag:

<a href="https://www.example.com">
  <img src="logo.jpg" alt="Example logo">
</a>

The image itself becomes the link. Adding border="0" removes the default border some browsers draw around linked images.

practical.q: Use the <div> tag to create sections of a webpage and apply basic CSS styles.
practical.a:
<div style="background:#eef; padding:12px; margin:8px 0;">
  <h2>Section One</h2>
  <p>Content here.</p>
</div>

<div> has no appearance of its own — it exists to group elements so a style can be applied to them all at once. In real work the styles would go in a stylesheet rather than inline.

practical.q: Marquee effect — design a webpage where text scrolls using the <marquee> tag.
practical.a:
<marquee direction="right" scrollamount="5">Announcements</marquee>

scrollamount controls the speed and direction which way it travels. You can also use behavior="alternate" to bounce the text back and forth.

practical.q: Design a wireframe and create an HTML structure for a simple homepage layout.
practical.a:
Sketch the layout first — header, navigation, main content, sidebar, footer — before writing any code. Then build it with <div> containers:

<div id="header">…</div>
<div id="nav">…</div>
<div id="main">…</div>
<div id="footer">…</div>

Keep the wireframe plain — no colour, no finished graphics. If it has colour, it has stopped being a wireframe.

practical.q: Develop a simple portfolio webpage with headings, images, tables and a contact form.
practical.a:
Combine the pieces: an <h1> with your name, a photo, a table of your skills or grades, and a contact form at the bottom.

Use one external stylesheet so the whole page shares a consistent look, and keep the structure in the HTML and the appearance in the CSS.

practical.q: Learning Workshop 4 activity: Web Tech Scavenger Hunt
practical.a:
Learning outcome: students reinforce what they know about web technology, HTML, CSS and user experience through hands-on activities.

Materials needed: computers with a text editor, printed handouts covering HTML and CSS basics, flashcards with web terms on them.

How to run it

1. Give each team a pack of term cards — HTML, CSS, UI, UX, hyperlink, web browser, web server, URL, domain name.

2. Write the definitions on sticky notes on the board, in a different order.

3. Teams match each term to its definition. Score one point per correct pair, and ask for a one-sentence justification on any pair you suspect was guessed.

What it teaches: the vocabulary has to be exact before any coding starts. The pairs students get wrong are nearly always UI versus UX and web browser versus web server, so be ready to draw the distinction on the board: a browser is the program you use, a server is the computer that sends you the page.

practical.q: Learning Workshop 4 activity: HTML and CSS Speed Challenge
practical.a:
How to run it

1. Prepare a broken web page for each team — the same one for everyone, with an unclosed <p>, a missing </html>, an <img> with no alt and a heading that should be a list.

2. Teams race to repair the markup so the page validates and displays correctly.

3. Once it displays, they add CSS: a background colour, a different font, and centred headings.

4. Teams compare results and vote on the best-looking page, but require them to say what specifically made it better.

What it teaches: paired tags must be closed in the right order, and HTML carries the structure while CSS carries the appearance. Insist they do not move styling into HTML attributes — that is the habit this activity is meant to break.

practical.q: Learning Workshop 4 activity: UI/UX Design Challenge
practical.a:
How to run it

1. Give each student a sheet of paper and ask for a sketch of a home page — a school site or a hobby site works well.

2. Every element has to be labelled with the HTML tag that would produce it: header, navigation list, main heading, paragraphs, image, form, footer.

3. Students then annotate two decisions they made to help the visitor — for example putting the navigation where people expect it, or keeping the form short.

4. Volunteers present, and the class says which sketch would be easiest to use and why.

What it teaches: designing on paper first is faster than coding first, because changing a sketch costs seconds while changing a page costs much longer. It also separates the two questions "is it attractive?" (UI) and "is it easy to use?" (UX), which students tend to collapse into one.

key_terms.meaning: Tools, techniques and protocols for creating and using websites.

sections.title: WWW, Browsers, Search Engines and URLs

blocks.text: A collection of linked documents and pages stored on millions of computers around the world — a system for accessing information over the internet through interconnected web pages. Also called the web, WWW or W3, it refers to all the public websites users can reach.

blocks.caption: How a browser reaches a page on the web.

blocks.text: The sites hold text, images, audio and video, and can be reached from anywhere using a computer, laptop or phone. The pages are joined together by hyperlinks, which users click to move between them.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: The internet and the web are not the same thing. The internet is the physical network of connected computers; the web is one of the services that runs on top of it, alongside email and file transfer. This is a classic exam question.
Uses of the WWW

items: Information access — finding facts of any kind.
Communication — email, messaging, forums.
Entertainment — video, music, games.
Research — gathering material for study and work.
E-commerce — buying and selling online.
Collaboration — working with others at a distance.

blocks.text: Web browsers

Software for retrieving and presenting information on the web. It lets the user display and interact with the text, images and video on a page, and acts as the interface between the user and what is available on the web.
Popular browsers include Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, Safari and Opera. Older users may remember Netscape Navigator.
Key features of a browser

items: Bookmarks — save and organise sites you visit often.
Tabs — open several pages in one window and switch between them.
Extensions — add-ons that expand what the browser does, such as blocking adverts.
Private browsing — does not save history, cookies or cached data for the session.
Synchronisation — keeps bookmarks, history and settings the same across your devices through an account.

blocks.text: Search engines
A tool or website that helps you find information on the internet efficiently, using powerful computers and algorithms to reach the content you want.
A search engine collects and organises content from across the internet. You type a query describing what you are after, and it returns links to matching content along with the URLs of those pages.
Well-known search engines include Google, Bing and Yahoo; older ones include WebCrawler, AltaVista and Excite.

blocks.caption: Entering a query into a search engine.

blocks.text: How to use a search engine

items: Open the search engine in your browser.
Type keywords, or a question, into the search bar.
Press Enter, or click the Search button.

blocks.text: How Google works

items: You enter a search query.
Google's web servers receive the request, using large numbers of linked computers to handle queries and produce results.
The request goes to index servers, which hold data about which pages contain the keywords and where those pages are.
PageRank software measures how important or popular each page is, by solving an equation with millions of variables — the pages most likely to be what you want.
Short text summaries are prepared for each result.
Results are delivered to you, ten to a page.

blocks.text: URL
The unique address of a specific web page or resource on the internet. It says which server to go to and what path to follow there to find the information.
A URL carries three pieces of information:

items: the protocol — the type of service, such as HTTP or FTP;
the domain name of the site, such as abc.com.np;
the location and name of the resource in the server's directory structure, such as /start/main.html.

blocks.text: Taking http://www.abc.com.np/start/main.html as an example: http is the protocol, www.abc.com.np is the address of the site, and start/main.html is the path to the particular page.
The ability to reach data stored on a computer from a different location — opening, editing and saving files on your own device from anywhere in the world.
It means accessing a network from a remote place without being at the actual workplace. It is useful for people working off-site, travelling, or working out of the office.
An internet utility that lets you log on to a remote computer system.
Advantages

items: Flexibility — work from anywhere, at any time, on any device with a connection.

Shared resources, greater efficiency and collaboration — exchanging and transferring information becomes easy, so cooperation flows more freely. Many people report higher productivity working from home on their own devices.
Cost savings — businesses can resolve technical problems at lower cost, without sending anyone anywhere.

blocks.text: Disadvantages

items: Security risks — every device connecting to the network must be protected and kept up to date with firewalls and anti-virus software.
Hardware issues — if your office computer develops a fault, you may have no way to reach it remotely.
Complex software and hardware — enterprise setups can be difficult to install and maintain.

blocks.text: Remote desktop software
AnyDesk

To use it: download from www.anydesk.com; install it; activate it by applying your licence key; adjust the security settings to enable unattended access; then connect by entering the remote computer's AnyDesk-ID or alias. If the connection request is valid, an Accept window appears on the remote device, and once accepted you can use that device from inside AnyDesk.
TeamViewer

TeamViewer is remote access and remote control software, first released in 2005. It is proprietary, requires registration, and is free for non-commercial use. It uses secure data channels and end-to-end encryption. Each device is given a unique 9- or 10-digit ID, rather like a phone number, which stays the same even if the software is reinstalled.
To create a remote session: open TeamViewer Remote, go to the Remote Support tab, click Create a session, enter a session name, share the session with the participant, and click Save.
A standardised set of rules determining how data is transmitted between devices on a network. Protocols are what enable computers to communicate with one another.
HTTP

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol is the foundation of the World Wide Web. It enables the transfer of data between a client and a server, and provides the standard by which a browser and a web server establish communication.

head: Advantages of HTTP
Disadvantages of HTTP
rows: Platform independence — works on any operating system
Lack of security — vulnerable to attacks such as man-in-the-middle
Compatibility — works with various protocols and technologies
Performance issues — can be slow for large transfers
Statelessness — needs extra mechanisms to keep track of state
Can support encryption when used as HTTPS
blocks.caption: HTTP: advantages and disadvantages

blocks.text: HTTPS
HTTP Secure is the encrypted version of HTTP, used to protect sensitive data — for instance when logging in to a bank account.
How HTTPS works

HTTPS encrypts communication using Transport Layer Security (TLS), formerly known as Secure Sockets Layer (SSL). It secures communication through an asymmetric public key infrastructure, which uses two different keys:

items: the public key, which is available to anyone and is used to encrypt the message;
the private key, controlled by the website owner and kept secret, which decrypts it.

blocks.text: Only the holder of the private key can read what was encrypted with the public key, which is what keeps the data safe in transit.

head: Advantages of HTTPS
Disadvantages of HTTPS
rows: Initial drawbacks — possible errors or a drop in traffic at first
Trust — builds confidence with visitors and customers
SSL certificate — you need to obtain one
Performance — HTTPS sites may load faster
Mixed mode issues — mixing secure and insecure content causes warnings
Search results — can help a site rank higher
Compliance — meets Payments Card Industry requirements
Large sites need to weigh the change more carefully
blocks.caption: HTTPS: advantages and disadvantages

blocks.text: Email protocols

items: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) — used for sending email.
POP (Post Office Protocol) — used for receiving email.
IMAP (Internet Mail Access Protocol) — used for receiving email, keeping messages on the server.

blocks.text: TCP

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) breaks data into packets, sends them, and reassembles them at the other end, checking for errors on the way. It is the reason data arrives complete and in order rather than in pieces.
An electronic message sent from one computer to another — a fast, easy and cheap way to communicate with people anywhere in the world.

Text, pictures and sound can be sent across the globe, and the whole exchange takes minutes. The same message can go to many people at once. Every user has a unique email address, rather like a postal address — for example asmitapublication@gmail.com.
Email works together with POP or IMAP for receiving mail, and SMTP for sending it.
Uses of email

items: Communicating within an organisation, or personally.
Flexibility in communication — messages wait until you read them.
Acting as a newsletter, sending advertisements, promotions and other content.
Easy to use and easy to access, from almost any device.
Sharing information quickly, with attachments.
Sending messages at any time, without disturbing anyone.

blocks.text: Creating a Gmail account

items: Go to the Gmail sign-up page.

Fill in your first and last name, choose a username (this becomes your address — if the name is taken, Gmail will suggest alternatives), and set a strong password mixing letters, numbers and special characters.
Click Next.
Enter a phone number and a recovery email address, both optional but recommended for getting back into the account.
Confirm your details and accept the terms.

blocks.text: CC and BCC

items: CC — Carbon Copy. Everyone can see who else received the message.
BCC — Blind Carbon Copy. Recipients cannot see who else was sent it, which protects their privacy.

blocks.text: Interactive technologies that let people create, share and gather content — ideas, interests and other forms of expression — within virtual communities and networks.

Social media is used to document memories, to learn and to form friendships. It is used to promote people, companies, products and ideas, and to consume, publish or share news. Mobile social media means using it on a phone or tablet, which changes things because users no longer have to sit at a desk to take part, and services can make use of where the user actually is.
Appropriate use of social media

items: Brand monitoring — learning what customers say about you.
Influencer marketing — working with people who have an audience.
Social listening — understanding what is being said about your brand, products, people and industry.
Performance analysis — using analytics to track engagement and whether a campaign worked.
Contests and giveaways — to increase engagement and awareness.
Localising content — adapting what you share to the culture and language of your audience.

blocks.text: Social media in education

items: Class updates, group projects and shared educational resources.
Polls and quizzes in real time.
Showcasing student work on school accounts.
Bulletin boards and discussion forums.
Video conferencing with teachers anywhere in the world.
Digital storytelling, livestreaming lectures, and collaborative learning.
Developing critical thinking.

blocks.text: How to access websites safely

A secure site's URL begins with https rather than http. The "s" stands for secure and means the connection uses SSL, so your information is encrypted before it is sent. Safe Browsing, a service run by Google, keeps a catalogue of fraudulent and malicious sites and is built into Brave, Chrome, Safari and Firefox, so they can warn you before you visit one.

blocks.caption: The warning a browser shows for an unsafe site.

items: Keep your browser and any plugins updated.
Use a browser with good privacy and security features.
Block pop-ups.
Pay attention to the URL and the security icons.
Use an ad blocker.
Enable "do not track" in your browser.
Clear your browser cache and cookies.
Turn on private browsing.
Use a VPN.
Use a password manager.
Keep antivirus and firewall protection up to date.
Review your privacy settings and read privacy policies.
Be careful of suspicious links and where you click.
Be careful what you download.

blocks.text: A communication tool that lets people meet in real time using video and audio — a live meeting between two or more people in different locations. It transmits audio, video, text and presentations as they happen.
It is used for business meetings, events, seminars and courses, as well as for personal calls. Common features include screen sharing, virtual backgrounds and real-time file sharing.
Advantages

items: It suits all kinds of meetings, from presentations about major events to remote and international ones.
It helps remove the risk of misunderstanding, because people can see each other.
It is easy to see who is taking part in a discussion.

blocks.text: Zoom
Zoom is a cloud-based communications platform letting users connect with video, audio, phone and chat. It needs an internet connection and a supported device.

items: One-on-one meetings — unlimited, even on the free plan.
Group video conferences — the free plan allows up to 100 participants for 40 minutes; the Enterprise plan goes much higher.
Screen sharing — show participants what is on your screen.
Recording — record meetings and events.

blocks.text: To join: open join.zoom.us in a browser, enter the meeting ID and click Join, or open the Zoom app, enter the meeting ID and your display name, and choose whether to connect audio and video. You can also click a join link from an email or calendar invitation, or join as a guest.
To create a meeting: sign in, click Meetings, click Schedule a Meeting, enter the topic, date and time, choose your settings and click Save.
Google Meet
Google Meet is a video conferencing app for voice and video calls and screen sharing.

items: Share your screen with other participants.
Record meetings and save them to play back later.
Mute or unmute participants.
Chat with other participants during the meeting.

blocks.text: To join, open the app, enter the meeting code or nickname, and tap Join. To create one, go to Google Meet, click New Meeting, select "Create a meeting for later", then copy the link and share it. You can also schedule a meeting through Google Calendar.
Microsoft Teams

Teams is a collaboration app that lets users communicate, share files and meet in one place. Users can chat by text, audio and video, share files, and use the calendar to connect before, during and after a meeting. Private chats let ideas develop before being shared more widely, and documents can be worked on together using Word, PowerPoint and Excel.

items: Communication — instant messaging, audio and video calling, screen sharing.
File sharing — upload, share and edit files in real time.
Collaboration — work together regardless of location or device.
Security — enterprise-grade protection, including multi-factor authentication and encryption.

blocks.text: To join, go to your Teams calendar, find the meeting, select Join, set your camera and audio on the pre-join screen, and select Join now. To create one, go to Calendar, select New meeting, give it a title, date and time, add attendees and select Send.

Short for "weblog" — a frequently updated web page used for personal commentary or business content. It is an online journal displaying information in reverse chronological order, with the newest posts at the top.
Blogs are usually interactive, with a section at the bottom of each post where readers can leave comments. A blog is where a writer, or a group of writers, share their views on a subject.
Blog hosts

head: Free
Paid
blocks.caption: Where you can host a blog

blocks.text: Features of a successful blog

items: A blog must always be dynamic — it needs regular new content.
Clear and helpful taxonomy, so readers can find things.
Most blogs share the same basic structure.
Easy navigation.
The blog's leading star is its content.
Headlines should grab attention.
Blogs and links go hand in hand — a blog points outwards.
All blogs are about communication.
Relevancy to the audience.
Author profiles, so readers know who is writing.
Multimedia integration — images and video.

blocks.text: Types of blog

items: Personal blogs — individuals sharing thoughts, experiences and interests.
Business or corporate blogs — companies communicating with their audience and promoting their products.
Fashion blogs — trends, styles and tips.
Blog newsletters — content delivered straight to subscribers' inboxes.
Travel blogs — stories, destination guides and planning advice.
Food blogs — recipes, cooking tips and restaurant reviews.
News blogs — current events, analysis and commentary.

blocks.text: Creating a blog with Blogger

items: Sign in to Blogger.
On the left, click the down arrow.
Click New blog.
Enter a name for your blog and click Next.
Choose a blog address or URL and click Save.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: The order of posts is worth remembering: reverse chronological, newest first. That is the feature that distinguishes a blog from an ordinary website.
