mcq.q: A word of a web page which on clicking opens another document is called:
mcq.teacher_note: A hyperlink. The anchor is the tag that creates it, and the URL is the address it points to — the clickable word itself is the hyperlink.

mcq.q: Which is not a search engine?
mcq.teacher_note: Gmail is an email service, not a search engine. Google, Bing and WebCrawler all search the web.

mcq.q: Which of the following is used for a secure website?
mcq.teacher_note: HTTPS — the "s" means secure. HTTP is unencrypted, FTP transfers files and SMTP sends email.

mcq.q: What is the full form of CC in email?
mcq.teacher_note: Carbon copy — a term carried over from typing, where a sheet of carbon paper made a duplicate. In email it means a copy everyone can see.

mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT a social media platform?
mcq.teacher_note: Amazon is a shopping site. The other three are social networks.

mcq.q: The internet and the World Wide Web are:
options: The web is a service running on the internet
The internet is a service running on the web
mcq.teacher_note: The web is a service that runs on the internet. The internet is the network itself, which also carries email and file transfer.

mcq.q: Which part of the URL http://www.abc.com.np/start/main.html is the domain name?
mcq.teacher_note: www.abc.com.np — http is the protocol and start/main.html is the path to the page.

mcq.q: Which protocol is used to send email?
mcq.teacher_note: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) sends. POP and IMAP receive.

mcq.q: In email, what does BCC do?
options: Sends a copy that other recipients cannot see
mcq.teacher_note: BCC hides the other recipients, which protects their privacy — the whole point of using it.

mcq.q: Which of these is a remote access tool?
mcq.teacher_note: TeamViewer. AnyDesk is another. Firefox is a browser, Gmail is email and PageRank is Google's ranking method.

mcq.q: HTTPS secures data using:
mcq.teacher_note: TLS — Transport Layer Security, previously called SSL. A VPN encrypts your whole connection, which is a different thing.

mcq.q: A blog displays its posts:
mcq.teacher_note: In reverse chronological order — newest first, at the top.

mcq.q: Which of the following indicates a website may be unsafe?
options: A padlock icon in the address bar
A browser warning saying "Deceptive site ahead"
mcq.teacher_note: The warning. A padlock and an https address are good signs, not bad ones.

mcq.q: Which feature lets you open several pages in one browser window?
mcq.teacher_note: Tabs. Bookmarks save addresses, extensions add features, and synchronisation syncs data across devices.

mcq.q: What does a search engine use to decide which results are most important?
options: An algorithm measuring importance, such as PageRank
mcq.teacher_note: A ranking algorithm — Google's is called PageRank, and it measures how important or popular each page is.

short.q: Define WWW.
short.a: The World Wide Web (WWW, or W3) is a collection of linked documents and pages stored on millions of computers around the world — a system for accessing information over the internet through interconnected web pages. It refers to all the public websites users can reach with their devices. It is one of the services the internet provides, and its pages are joined together by hyperlinks.

short.q: What is HTTP?
short.a: The Hypertext Transfer Protocol is the foundation of the World Wide Web. It enables the transfer of data between a client and a server, providing the standard by which a browser and a web server communicate. Its weakness is that it sends data unencrypted.

short.q: Define email.
short.a: Email (electronic mail) is an electronic message sent from one computer to another. It is a fast, easy and cheap way to communicate with people anywhere in the world, and it can carry text, pictures and sound. Every user has a unique address, and mail is sent using SMTP and received using POP or IMAP.

short.q: What is video conferencing?
short.a: Video conferencing is a communication tool that lets people meet in real time using video and audio — a live meeting between two or more people in different locations. It transmits audio, video, text and presentations as they happen, and typically offers screen sharing and recording. Zoom, Google Meet and Microsoft Teams are the common tools.

short.q: Define blog.
short.a: A blog, short for "weblog", is a frequently updated web page used for personal commentary or business content. It is an online journal displaying information in reverse chronological order, with the newest posts first. Blogs are usually interactive, letting readers leave comments.

short.q: Write any two advantages of HTTPS over HTTP.
short.a:
1. Security — HTTPS encrypts data using SSL/TLS, so anything intercepted on the way cannot be read. HTTP sends data in the clear.

2. Trust — visitors and customers can see the connection is secure, which builds confidence. HTTPS can also help a site rank higher in search results and load faster.

short.q: Write any two uses of a search engine.
short.a:
1. Finding information — typing a query and getting links to pages that match, with their URLs.

2. Research — gathering material for study or work from across the internet, quickly.

Others: finding images and video, checking facts, and locating a specific site whose address you do not know.

short.q: List any two uses of email.
short.a:
1. Communication, within an organisation or personally — flexible, because messages wait until you read them.

2. Sharing information, including attachments such as documents and photos.

Others: acting as a newsletter for promotions and announcements, and sending messages at any hour without disturbing anyone.

short.q: What is social media?
short.a: Social media is a set of interactive technologies that let people create, share and gather content — ideas, interests and other forms of expression — within virtual communities and networks. It is used to document memories, to learn, to form friendships, to promote people and products, and to consume, publish or share news. On mobile devices it can also make use of where the user is.

short.q: Write any two advantages of remote login.
short.a:
1. Flexibility — you can work from anywhere, at any time, on any device with a connection.

2. Cost savings — a business can fix technical problems without sending anyone anywhere.

Also: sharing resources and collaborating becomes easier, which raises productivity.

short.q: What is a protocol?
short.a: A protocol is a standardised set of rules that determine how data is transmitted between devices on a network. Protocols are what make it possible for computers from different makers to communicate. Examples include HTTP and HTTPS for the web, SMTP, POP and IMAP for email, and TCP for moving packets reliably.

short.q: Define SMTP.
short.a: SMTP — Simple Mail Transfer Protocol — is the protocol used for sending email. It carries the message from the sender to the mail server, and between servers. Receiving is a different job, handled by POP or IMAP.

short.q: What is telnet?
short.a: Telnet is an internet utility that lets you log on to a remote computer system — an early form of remote login. It sends data, including passwords, without encryption, which is why it has largely been replaced by secure alternatives.

short.q: List any three video conferencing tools.
short.a: Zoom, Google Meet and Microsoft Teams. Zoom is known for screen sharing and recording; Google Meet integrates with Google accounts and Calendar; Teams combines meetings with chat and Microsoft Office file collaboration.

short.q: Write the full forms: WWW, HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, TLS, SSL, TCP, CC, BCC, Email.
short.a: WWW — World Wide Web. HTTP — Hypertext Transfer Protocol. HTTPS — Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure. SMTP — Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. TLS — Transport Layer Security. SSL — Secure Sockets Layer. TCP — Transmission Control Protocol. CC — Carbon Copy. BCC — Blind Carbon Copy. Email — Electronic mail.

short.q: Self Test 5.1: What is URL?
short.a: A URL — Uniform Resource Locator — is the unique address of a page or resource on the internet. It carries three things: the protocol (such as http), the domain name (such as abc.com.np), and the path to the particular resource (such as /start/main.html).

short.q: Self Test 5.1: List out any two popular web browser.
short.a: Any two of: Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, Safari and Opera.

short.q: Self Test 5.1: What is search engine?
short.a: A search engine is a tool that helps you find information on the internet. It collects and organises content from across the web; you type a query, and it returns links to matching pages. Google, Bing and Yahoo are examples.

short.q: Self Test 5.2: What is telnet?
short.a: Telnet is an internet utility that lets you log on to a remote computer system — an early form of remote login. It sends data, including passwords, without encryption, which is why it has largely been replaced by secure alternatives.

short.q: Self Test 5.2: What is remote login?
short.a: Remote login is the ability to reach data stored on a computer from a different location — opening, editing and saving files on your own device from anywhere. It means using a network from a remote place without being at the actual workplace.

short.q: Self Test 5.2: Write the uses of AnyDesk.
short.a: AnyDesk is remote desktop software, used to reach and control another computer over the internet. It is used for remote support, working from home, accessing office files while travelling, administering servers, and collaboration. You connect by entering the remote machine's AnyDesk-ID or alias.

short.q: Self Test 5.3: Define protocol.
short.a: A protocol is a standardised set of rules that determine how data is transmitted between devices on a network. Protocols are what let computers from different makers communicate. Examples include HTTP, HTTPS, SMTP, POP, IMAP and TCP.

short.q: Self Test 5.3: Enlist any two differences between HTTP and HTTPs.
short.a:
1. HTTP sends data unencrypted; HTTPS encrypts it using SSL/TLS, so it cannot be read in transit.
2. HTTP gives no guarantee about who you are talking to; HTTPS authenticates the site through a certificate, so you know it is genuine.
Also, HTTPS sites show a padlock, may load faster, and rank better in search results.

short.q: Self Test 5.3: Define SMTP.
short.a: SMTP — Simple Mail Transfer Protocol — is the protocol used for sending email. It carries the message from the sender to the mail server and between servers. Receiving is a separate job, handled by POP or IMAP.

short.q: Self Test 5.3: Write any two advantages of email.
short.a:
1. It is fast and cheap — a message reaches anywhere in the world in minutes for no extra cost.
2. It is flexible — the message waits until the recipient is ready, and the same message can go to many people at once.
Others: attachments can carry documents and photos, and it provides a written record.

short.q: Self Test 5.4: Define social media.
short.a: Social media is a set of interactive technologies that let people create, share and gather content — ideas, interests and other forms of expression — within virtual communities and networks. It is used to document memories, learn, form friendships, and consume, publish or share news.

short.q: Self Test 5.4: Write any two uses of social media.
short.a:
1. Communication — keeping in touch with friends, family and colleagues.
2. Education — sharing resources, group projects, polls and discussions.
Others: news, marketing and promotion, entertainment, and networking.

short.q: Self Test 5.4: List out any three video conferencing tool.
short.a: Zoom, Google Meet and Microsoft Teams. Others include Skype and Webex.

long.q: How can you access sites safely? Explain.
long.a:
Safe browsing comes down to a handful of habits, and the first is knowing what to look for.

1. Check the address. A secure site's URL begins with https, not http. The "s" means the connection uses SSL/TLS, so your information is encrypted before it is sent. Look for the padlock icon too. Browsers such as Brave, Chrome, Safari and Firefox use Google's Safe Browsing service, which warns you — "Deceptive site ahead" — if you are about to visit a known fraudulent or malicious site. Take that warning seriously and go back.

2. Keep software current. Update the browser and its plugins, and keep antivirus and firewall protection up to date. Most attacks exploit faults that have already been fixed in a newer version.

3. Reduce what leaks. Block pop-ups, use an ad blocker, enable "do not track", clear cache and cookies, turn on private browsing, use a VPN, and review privacy settings and policies.

4. Be careful what you click and download. Suspicious links and unexpected attachments are how most infections begin. Hover over a link before clicking to see where it really goes.

5. Use a password manager. It lets you have a different, strong password for every site, so one breach does not unlock everything else.

The habits matter more than any single tool. A browser warning is a last line of defence, not a substitute for care.

long.q: Explain the features of a blog.
long.a:
The features that make a blog work:

1. It must be dynamic. A blog needs regular new content; a page that is never updated stops being a blog.

2. Reverse chronological order. The newest post appears first, at the top — the defining structural feature.

3. Clear and helpful taxonomy. Categories and tags let readers find what they want.

4. Easy navigation. Readers should never have to hunt.

5. Content is the leading star. Everything else supports the writing.

6. Attention-grabbing headlines. The headline decides whether anyone reads further.

7. Blogs and links go hand in hand. A blog points outwards to other material.

8. All blogs are about communication. Comments sections make them conversations rather than broadcasts.

9. Relevancy. Content should matter to the audience it is written for.

10. Author profiles. Readers want to know who is writing.

11. Multimedia integration. Images and video bring posts to life.

Types of blog include personal, business or corporate, fashion, newsletter, travel, food and news blogs. Free hosts include Blogger, WordPress.com, Tumblr, SimpleSite and Wix; paid ones include GoDaddy, Bluehost, HostGator and Hostmonster.

long.q: Explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web.
long.a:
The two are often used as if they meant the same thing, and they do not.

The internet is the global network of connected computers — the physical and logical infrastructure: cables, routers, servers and the protocols that join them. It is the roads.

The World Wide Web is one of the services that runs on top of that network: a collection of linked documents and pages, reached through a browser. It is one kind of traffic on the roads.

Email, file transfer and video conferencing are other services on the same internet, and none of them is "the web". That is the practical test: you can use the internet without using the web at all — sending an email does not involve a web page.

long.q: Explain how HTTPS works, and why it matters.
long.a:
HTTPS is HTTP with encryption added. It matters because, without it, everything you send crosses the network in plain text — passwords, card numbers, messages — readable by anyone who intercepts it.

How it works. HTTPS uses Transport Layer Security (TLS), formerly called Secure Sockets Layer (SSL). It secures communication using an asymmetric public key infrastructure, which relies on two different keys:

The public key is available to anyone and is used to encrypt the message. Once encrypted with it, the message cannot be undone with that same key.

The private key is held by the website owner and kept secret. It is the only thing that can decrypt what the public key encrypted.

So you can safely encrypt a message for a site using a key everyone can see, confident that only that site can read it.

Why it matters. Beyond the encryption itself, HTTPS builds trust with visitors, can make pages load faster, can help a site rank higher in search results, and is required for compliance with payment card standards. The costs are real but small: you need a certificate, and there can be mixed-content and caching problems to sort out.

long.q: Compare Zoom, Google Meet and Microsoft Teams.
long.a:
All three let people meet in real time with video and audio, and all three offer screen sharing. They differ in where they sit.

Zoom is a dedicated cloud conferencing platform. Its free plan offers unlimited one-on-one meetings and group calls of up to 100 participants for 40 minutes; paid plans go much further. It is known for screen sharing and recording, and for being easy to join — by meeting ID, a join link, or straight from a browser at join.zoom.us.

Google Meet is tied to Google accounts. You can share your screen, record meetings, mute participants and chat during a call. Its strength is the integration with Google Calendar and Workspace — a meeting scheduled in Calendar simply has a Meet link attached.

Microsoft Teams is a broader collaboration app rather than a pure meeting tool. Alongside messaging, audio and video calling, it offers file sharing and real-time collaboration on Word, Excel and PowerPoint documents, plus enterprise security features such as multi-factor authentication.

Which to use. For a quick call with people outside your organisation, Zoom is simplest. If your school or workplace already runs on Google accounts, Meet is already there. If it runs on Microsoft 365 and people need to work on documents together, Teams fits best.

practical.q: Demonstrate the mechanism of searching for different learning materials from the internet.
practical.a:
How to go about it.

1. Choose the topic you want material on, then pick out the key words.

2. Type those words into the search engine. Start broad, then narrow down: adding words usually helps more than removing them.

3. Use the search tools to filter by type — images, video, or a date range — when the first results are not what you need.

4. Judge what you find. Check who published it and when, and look for the same fact in a second source before relying on it.

5. Keep a note of the useful addresses in bookmarks so you can return to them.

The skill being tested is not typing a query — it is narrowing and checking what comes back.

practical.q: Create a profile using social media such as Facebook, YouTube or X, if your age allows.
practical.a:
Before you start. Most platforms require users to be at least 13, and some more. Check the age requirement first, and involve a parent or teacher.

Settings to get right.

Set the profile to private so only people you approve can see your posts. Use a real name only if you are comfortable doing so, and avoid a screen name that reveals your school or address.

Do not put your date of birth, phone number, home address or school in a public profile. Do not accept friend requests from people you do not know.

Worth remembering. Anything you post becomes part of your digital footprint and can be found later. Post on the assumption that a future employer may see it.

practical.q: Create a virtual meeting using any application such as Zoom, Meet or Teams.
practical.a:
Using Google Meet as the example.

1. Go to Google Meet and click New Meeting, then choose "Create a meeting for later".

2. Copy the meeting link and share it with the participants.

3. At the meeting time, open the link, check your camera and microphone, and join. Mute yourself when you are not speaking.

4. Use screen sharing to show your work, and the chat for links.

5. End the meeting for everyone when you are done, so the room does not stay open.

Test your audio and video beforehand — that is what causes most problems at the start of a real meeting.

practical.q: Create a personal web blog using suitable tools such as BlogSpot, GitHub or similar.
practical.a:
Using Blogger as the example.

1. Sign in to Blogger and click the down arrow on the left, then New blog.

2. Give the blog a name and click Next.

3. Choose a blog address and click Save.

4. Write your first post and publish it.

Making it worth reading. Posts appear newest first, so the most recent one is what visitors see. Use clear categories so people can find things, write headlines that say what the post is about, and add images where they help.

Be careful what personal information goes into a public blog — it becomes part of your digital footprint.

practical.q: Learning Workshop 5 activity: Internet Treasure Hunt
practical.a:
Learning outcome: students explore how the internet works, how a search engine finds things, and how to behave safely on social media.

Materials needed: printed quiz sheets, computers with internet access.

How to run it

1. Write ten questions that can only be answered by searching — for example "what does the https in a web address tell you?", "who registers domain names in Nepal?", "what is the difference between a web browser and a search engine?".

2. Teams race to answer them, and each answer must name the site it came from.

3. Award a bonus to any team that used a search operator such as quotes around a phrase, or site: to limit results to one domain.

4. Finish by comparing which sources teams trusted. Ask why a government or educational domain is usually safer to cite than an anonymous blog.

What it teaches: searching is a skill, not a single box you type into, and the reliability of a result depends on where it came from.

practical.q: Learning Workshop 5 activity: Social Media Debate
practical.a:
How to run it

1. Split the class in two and give them the motion: social media does more good than harm. Assign sides rather than letting students choose, so both cases get argued properly.

2. Give ten minutes to prepare. Require each side to bring at least one real example — a campaign that raised money, a rumour that caused damage, a group that found support they could not find locally.

3. Run short opening statements, then open debate, then a closing summary from each side.

4. Take a class vote at the end and see whether anyone changed their mind.

What it teaches: the effects of social media depend on how it is used, so the honest answer to "is it beneficial or harmful?" is "both, depending". Students also learn to separate a claim from the evidence offered for it, which is the same skill they need to judge anything they read online.

units.title: Chapter 6 — Cybersecurity and Digital Citizenship
units.overview: Staying safe online: threats, cybercrime, and what it means to be a responsible digital citizen.
units.summary: Chapter 6 — Cybersecurity and Digital Citizenship. Review the chapter summary for definitions and key points.

concepts.text: Staying safe online: threats, cybercrime, and what it means to be a responsible digital citizen.

detailed.heading: Chapter 6 — Cybersecurity and Digital Citizenship
detailed.note: Detailed teaching notes for Cybersecurity and Digital Citizenship, written from the textbook and illustrated with the book's own figures.
learning_objectives: Define cybersecurity and explain why it matters.
Describe the types of cybersecurity and Nepal's legal provisions.
Define cybercrime and name its types and effects.
Explain the methods used to prevent cybercrime.
Explain what a digital citizen is and what digital citizenship involves.
Describe netiquette and give examples of its rules.
Explain what a digital footprint is and how to protect it.

blocks.caption: Cybersecurity: protecting systems, networks and data.

blocks.text: The application of technologies, processes and controls to protect systems, internet-connected devices, services, networks, programs and data from malicious attacks by hackers, spammers and cybercriminals.

It covers how to defend devices and services from electronic attacks, and it includes the specialised tools used to detect and remove harmful software. Practising good cybersecurity habits keeps our data private and makes our time online safe. Companies use it to guard against phishing, ransomware, identity theft, data breaches and financial loss.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) defines it as "the art of protecting networks, devices and data from unauthorized access or criminal use and the practice of ensuring confidentiality, integrity and availability of information".
Cybersecurity laws in Nepal

head: Law or policy
Year
What it does
rows: Defines computer systems, networks and databases; sets out cybercrime offences and penalties
Introduced to address global challenges in cyberspace
Protects personal data; sets penalties for violation
Protects digital content such as text, music, video and software
blocks.caption: Key cybersecurity provisions in Nepal

blocks.text: Why cybersecurity matters

items: Protecting personal data
Safeguarding business information
Ensuring online transaction security
Preventing unauthorized access
Mitigating the risk of cyber attacks
Enhancing customer trust
Protecting national security
Legal compliance
Intellectual property protection

blocks.text: Advantages of cybersecurity

items: Protection of sensitive data — using access control, firewalls and web servers to keep data from hackers.
Compliance with regulations — a risk management system with defined security measures, ensuring devices, systems and networks meet legal requirements.
Enhanced customer trust — strong measures build confidence among customers, partners and stakeholders.
Early detection and response — monitoring networks, applications, user activity and data to spot threats before they do much damage.
Intellectual property protection — guarding patents, trade secrets and copyrighted material.
Remote work security — strong protocols for remote access, plus training so staff can recognise risks.

blocks.text: Types of cybersecurity

head: Type
Concerned with
Example
rows: Securing a computer network from unauthorized access
blocks.caption: Types of cybersecurity

blocks.text: Illegal activities carried out using computers, network devices or the internet — using a computer as an instrument to commit fraud, traffic in illegal material, steal identities or violate privacy.

A cybercriminal is someone who uses their technical skills to do illegal things. Cybercrime can target individuals, businesses or society as a whole. Examples include stealing and selling corporate data, demanding payment to prevent an attack, installing viruses on a targeted computer, and hacking into government or corporate systems.
Effects of cybercrime

head: On individuals
On businesses
On society
rows: Impact on healthcare and public safety
blocks.caption: Who cybercrime hurts, and how

blocks.text: Types of cybercrime

head: Type
Forms
rows: Phishing — fraudulent messages tricking people into revealing sensitive information. Online fraud — fake websites or schemes stealing money or personal details.
Hacking — unauthorized access to steal or manipulate data. Data theft — stealing personal or corporate information.
Cyberbullying — online harassment, threats or abuse. Revenge porn — sharing explicit images without consent.
Viruses and Trojans — malicious software that damages or steals data. Ransomware — files are encrypted and payment demanded to release them.
Dark web crimes — drug, weapons and human trafficking. Piracy — unauthorized distribution of films, music or software.
blocks.caption: The five types of cybercrime

blocks.text: How to prevent cybercrime

items: Use strong passwords — complex, mixing letters, numbers and symbols, with two-factor authentication switched on.
Stay aware of phishing — do not click suspicious links or attachments.
Keep software and systems updated — update the operating system, browser and antivirus, and install security patches.
Secure your network and devices — use a firewall and a VPN, and avoid public Wi-Fi for anything sensitive.
Be cautious on social media — limit what you share and tighten your privacy settings.
Back up your data regularly — external drives or cloud storage, so an attack cannot take everything.

blocks.text: Individuals, businesses and governments all have to take active measures to keep cybercrime out. The main methods are set out below.
Multifactor authentication (MFA)
A security process requiring more than one form of identification to log in. Usually seen as two-factor authentication (2FA), it asks for a password and then a second piece of evidence.

MFA prevents data breaches, hacks and direct cyber-attacks, because stealing the password alone is no longer enough. Examples are an SMS verification code, biometric authentication, and a mobile app push notification.
Virtual Private Network (VPN)

A service that creates an encrypted point-to-point tunnel between your computer and a remote server owned by the VPN provider. It encrypts data, masks your IP address and leaves your browsing history and location untraceable.

A VPN acts as an intermediary between your device and the site you are visiting, adding its own encryption and routing traffic through its own servers. That makes it far harder for an attacker to intercept your data, and it is particularly effective against email frauds such as phishing, because your address and location are hidden.

items: Get a VPN subscription.
Download and install the VPN app.
Sign in to the app.
Select a VPN server.
Enable the VPN.

blocks.text: Email security solutions
These protect email communications and accounts from unauthorized access, data breaches and threats such as phishing, malware and spam, keeping messages confidential, intact and available.

head: Component
What it does
rows: Detect and block malicious emails that try to trick people into revealing information or installing harmful software
Scans attachments and links to stop viruses and ransomware spreading
Encodes messages in transit so the content stays confidential
Requires two forms of verification to reach the account
blocks.caption: Components of email security

blocks.text: Their importance comes down to three things: maintaining confidentiality, meeting regulatory requirements, and preserving an organisation's reputation.
Password managers
Software that securely stores, generates and manages passwords for your various online accounts, encrypting them in a database locked behind one master password.

Cybercriminals attack passwords constantly. A password manager lets you have a strong, unique password for every account without having to remember any of them, and fills them in for you. You remember one master password instead of fifty weak ones.
Firewalls

A network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing traffic against a set of rules, forming a barrier between a trusted internal network and an untrusted one such as the internet.

Setting rules generally means: going to the firewall's Rules tab; adding a new rule; naming it so you can identify it later; choosing Allow or Deny; and specifying the traffic, covering both inbound and outbound where possible.
Antivirus software
A program that detects, blocks and removes malicious software — viruses, worms, Trojans and ransomware — and is an essential part of any system or network setup.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Students often confuse a firewall and antivirus. A firewall controls what traffic comes and goes; antivirus deals with malicious software that has reached the machine. You need both.

A person who has the knowledge and skills to use digital technologies effectively, to communicate with others, to take part in society, and to create and consume digital content — using technology ethically and recognising their rights and responsibilities online.
Using technology safely, responsibly and ethically. It begins the moment someone signs up for an email address, posts a picture, or buys something online.
What education in digital citizenship covers

head: Concept
What it means
rows: The knowledge and skills to navigate, evaluate and create information using digital technologies
Understanding the impact of your behaviour online and following ethical guidelines — respecting others' opinions, avoiding harassment, not spreading misinformation
Protecting personal data and recognising the risks of online activity, such as identity theft and phishing
Managing privacy settings and protecting sensitive information
Knowing the laws governing digital spaces: copyright, intellectual property, anti-cyberbullying laws
Keeping a good reputation online through what you create, share and how you interact
blocks.caption: The six concepts of digital citizenship

blocks.text: Responsibilities of a digital citizen

items: Communicate respectfully, even when you disagree.
Decline to share false information.
Respect the intellectual property rights of others.
Do not reveal other people's personal or private information.
Do not break into computer systems without permission.

blocks.text: A word built from "net" and "etiquette" — the rules of conduct for respectful and appropriate communication on the internet. Not legally binding, but recommended rules of behaviour.

Netiquette is the acceptable way of using the internet and behaving online. It applies to email, forums, social media and video chats. Practising it is like practising ordinary etiquette — both are about treating people respectfully — except that the rules are specific to online communication.
Rules of netiquette

items: Be respectful — treat others with respect.
Be considerate — consider gender and cultural differences, and avoid jokes that could offend.
Respect the privacy of others — do not forward something sent to you without the sender's permission.
Be careful what you share — nothing embarrassing, illegal or inappropriate.
Be mindful of your language — avoid offensive or derogatory terms.
Be clear — use proper grammar and spelling so your message is taken seriously.
Forgive the mistakes of others — everyone was a beginner once.
Do not abuse your power — having more authority, as a moderator or administrator, does not give you the right to exploit it.
Use a neutral nickname — so that others do not feel insulted.
Be a good listener — read earlier posts before replying.
Be helpful — share your knowledge and experience.
Be prepared — before a video meeting, check audio and video and tidy the background.
Be professional — choose a professional screen name.

blocks.caption: What makes up a digital footprint.

blocks.text: The trail of traces a person leaves behind online — a record of all online activity. It is your online identity; what makes you unique.

Your footprint includes what you post on social media, comments on news articles and records of online purchases. It also includes what others post about you, and what websites collect about you through cookies.
What your footprint may include

items: Websites visited
Search history
Posts on social media
Records of online purchases
Comments on news articles
Messages sent

blocks.text: How to protect your digital footprint

items: Delete old email accounts.
Limit the number of social media accounts you have.
Skip surveys.
Keep your personal email address private.
Unsubscribe from unwanted newsletters.
Create a separate spam email address for sign-ups.
Remove yourself from people-search sites.
Use stealth or private mode when searching.

blocks.text: Advantages and disadvantages

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Fraud or legal issues can be detected more easily
Personal data can be used to generate revenue without your knowledge
Personalisation — suggested products and relevant advertising add value
Purchase behaviour may be used to reduce credit limits or raise interest rates
Companies can offer incentives matched to your interests, sometimes cutting costs
blocks.caption: A digital footprint cuts both ways

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: The point about a digital footprint is that it is largely permanent and not entirely under your control — other people and cookies add to it. Assume anything you post can be found later.

mcq.q: Which of these refers to the exploration of apt, ethical behaviours related to digital media platforms and the online environment?
mcq.teacher_note: Cyber ethics — it is about what is right, not what is safe (security), what is cautious (safety) or what is legal (law). The question asks about ethical behaviour, so the answer is cyber ethics.

mcq.q: Which of the following is not a cybercrime?
mcq.teacher_note: Installing antivirus software is the opposite — it is a defensive act. The other three are offences.

mcq.q: Downloading a copy, or extracting data from an open system, done fraudulently is treated as:
mcq.teacher_note: Cybercrime. The word "fraudulently" is what settles it — the act is criminal. Cyber-warfare is a state-level attack; a data backup is legitimate.

mcq.q: What is cybersecurity?
options: It protects a system from cyber attacks
mcq.teacher_note: All of the mentioned — each of the first three is a true but partial description. Cybersecurity covers malware, cyber-terrorists and attacks generally.

mcq.q: Which of the following is considered unsolicited commercial email?
mcq.teacher_note: Spam. "Unsolicited commercial email" is the standard definition of spam. A virus and malware are types of harmful software, which is a different thing — spam need not contain either.

mcq.q: What does a firewall do?
options: Controls incoming and outgoing network traffic
mcq.teacher_note: A firewall controls traffic according to rules. Removing viruses is antivirus work; encryption and password generation are different tools again.

mcq.q: What does VPN stand for?
mcq.teacher_note: Virtual Private Network. It creates an encrypted tunnel, hiding your IP address and location.

mcq.q: Which of these is the strongest password?
mcq.teacher_note: K7$mQp2!xL9 — it is long and mixes upper and lower case, numbers and symbols. The others are common words or sequences that appear in every attacker's list.

mcq.q: Ransomware is software that:
options: Encrypts your files and demands payment
mcq.teacher_note: It encrypts files and demands payment to release them. That demand is the defining feature.

mcq.q: What is phishing?
options: Fraudulent messages tricking people into revealing information
mcq.teacher_note: It is deception — a fraudulent message designed to make you hand over passwords or card details.

mcq.q: Two-factor authentication means:
options: Two people must approve each login
You need two different forms of identification
mcq.teacher_note: Two different kinds of proof — something you know (a password) and something you have (a code sent to your phone), or something you are (a fingerprint).

mcq.q: Which is the best defence against losing everything to ransomware?
mcq.teacher_note: Regular backups. If you have a clean copy elsewhere, the encryption stops being a catastrophe — you restore and move on.

mcq.q: Netiquette is:
options: Recommended rules for respectful online behaviour
mcq.teacher_note: Recommended rules of conduct for communicating online — good manners, not legislation.

mcq.q: Your digital footprint includes:
options: What you post, what others post about you, and what sites collect
mcq.teacher_note: All three. Other people's posts about you and the data sites gather through cookies are part of it, which is why you cannot control it entirely.

mcq.q: A digital citizen is someone who:
options: Uses technology ethically and takes responsibility online
mcq.teacher_note: It is about how you behave, not what you own or how many accounts you have.

short.q: List any two advantages of cybersecurity.
short.a:
1. Protection of sensitive data from unauthorized access, using access control, firewalls and secure servers.

2. Enhanced customer trust — strong measures build confidence among customers, partners and stakeholders.

Others include regulatory compliance, early detection of threats, protection of intellectual property, and making remote work safe.

short.q: What is cybercrime?
short.a: Cybercrime is illegal activity carried out using a computer, a network device or the internet. It means using a computer as an instrument to commit fraud, steal identities, spread malware, violate privacy or traffic illegal material. It can target individuals, businesses or society.

short.q: What is a digital citizen?
short.a: A digital citizen is someone who has the knowledge and skills to use digital technologies effectively — to communicate, take part in society, and create and consume digital content — and who uses technology ethically, recognising their rights and responsibilities online.

short.q: What is a digital footprint?
short.a: A digital footprint is the trail of traces you leave behind online: a record of everything you do. It includes social media posts, comments on news articles, online purchases, websites visited, search history and messages sent — plus what others post about you and what sites collect through cookies.

short.q: Define netiquette.
short.a: Netiquette, from "net" and "etiquette", is the set of rules for respectful and appropriate communication on the internet. These are recommended rules of conduct rather than laws, applying to email, forums, social media and video chats.

short.q: Write any two importances of cybersecurity.
short.a:
1. It protects data from theft and loss — personal data, business information and intellectual property all depend on it.

2. It keeps online transactions safe, which is what makes banking and shopping online possible at all.

Beyond that it prevents unauthorized access, maintains customer trust, protects national security and keeps organisations on the right side of the law.

short.q: List any two disadvantages of cybercrime.
short.a:
1. Financial loss — for individuals and businesses alike, whether through theft, fraud or the cost of putting things right.

2. Damage to reputation — once trust is lost, it is very hard to win back.

Other effects include identity theft, loss of intellectual property, and wider harm to society through economic damage and increased harassment.

short.q: List any two methods to minimise your digital footprint.
short.a:
1. Delete old accounts you no longer use, including email accounts.

2. Keep your personal email address private and use a separate address for sign-ups, so the personal one does not spread.

Others: limit the number of social media accounts, unsubscribe from unwanted newsletters, remove yourself from people-search sites, and use private browsing.

short.q: List any two methods for preventing cybercrime.
short.a:
1. Use strong passwords — complex, unique to each account, with two-factor authentication enabled.

2. Keep software updated, including the operating system, browser and antivirus, and install security patches promptly.

Others: use a firewall and a VPN, avoid phishing links, avoid public Wi-Fi for sensitive work, and back up data regularly.

short.q: Define digital citizenship.
short.a: Digital citizenship is using technology safely, responsibly and ethically. It begins as soon as someone signs up for an email address, posts a picture or buys something online. It covers digital literacy, responsible use, cybersecurity awareness, privacy protection, legal awareness and maintaining a positive digital footprint.

short.q: What is a firewall?
short.a: A firewall is a network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic against a set of rules. It stands as a barrier between a trusted internal network and an untrusted one such as the internet, allowing wanted traffic through and blocking the rest.

short.q: Define 2FA.
short.a: 2FA — two-factor authentication — is a security process requiring two different forms of identification to log in, such as a password together with a code sent to your phone. It is the most common form of multifactor authentication, and it means a stolen password on its own is not enough to get in.

short.q: Define antivirus.
short.a: Antivirus is software that detects, blocks and removes malicious software — viruses, worms, Trojans and ransomware. It is an essential part of any system or network setup, and needs keeping up to date to recognise new threats.

short.q: Why is netiquette used?
short.a: Netiquette exists so that online communication stays respectful and pleasant. Because people online cannot see each other's faces or hear tone of voice, misunderstandings happen easily; shared rules reduce that. It also protects privacy, keeps discussion useful, and makes online spaces places people actually want to be.

short.q: Write the full forms: VPN, 2FA, MFA, IT.
short.a: VPN — Virtual Private Network. 2FA — Two-Factor Authentication. MFA — Multifactor Authentication. IT — Information Technology.

short.q: Self Test 6.1: What is cybersecurity?
short.a: Cybersecurity is the application of technologies, processes and controls to protect systems, devices, networks, programs and data from malicious attack. CISA defines it as "the art of protecting networks, devices and data from unauthorized access or criminal use and the practice of ensuring confidentiality, integrity and availability of information".

short.q: Self Test 6.1: Define cybercrime.
short.a: Cybercrime is illegal activity carried out using a computer, a network device or the internet — using technology as the instrument for fraud, theft, harassment or privacy violation. It can target individuals, businesses or society.

short.q: Self Test 6.1: List any three forms of cybercrime.
short.a: Any three of: phishing (fraudulent messages tricking people into revealing information); hacking (unauthorized access to systems); identity theft; ransomware (encrypting files and demanding payment); cyberbullying; data theft; piracy; and online fraud.

short.q: Self Test 6.2: What is VPN?
short.a: A VPN — Virtual Private Network — creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and a remote server run by the VPN provider. It encrypts your data, masks your IP address, and leaves your browsing and location untraceable. It is especially important on public Wi-Fi.

short.q: Self Test 6.2: What is multifactor authentication?
short.a: MFA is a security process that requires more than one form of identification to log in — usually seen as two-factor authentication (2FA). As well as a password, you supply something else: a code sent by SMS, a fingerprint, or an app notification. A stolen password alone is then not enough.

short.q: Self Test 6.2: What is the use of data backup and recovery solutions?
short.a: They keep a copy of your data somewhere separate, so it can be restored if the original is lost, corrupted, stolen or encrypted by ransomware. Backup is the single most effective protection against ransomware: with a clean copy elsewhere, the attack becomes an inconvenience rather than a disaster. Back up often, and to a place that is not the same machine.

short.q: Self Test 6.3: What is a firewall?
short.a: A firewall is a network security system that monitors and controls incoming and outgoing traffic according to rules. It stands between a trusted internal network and an untrusted one such as the internet, allowing wanted traffic through and blocking the rest.

short.q: Self Test 6.3: Define 2FA.
short.a: 2FA — two-factor authentication — requires two different forms of identification to log in, such as a password and a code sent to your phone. It is the most common form of multifactor authentication.

short.q: Self Test 6.3: Define antivirus.
short.a: Antivirus is software that detects, blocks and removes malicious software — viruses, worms, Trojans and ransomware. It needs to be kept up to date so it recognises new threats.

short.q: Self Test 6.4: Why is netiquette used?
short.a: Netiquette exists so online communication stays respectful and pleasant. Online, people cannot see faces or hear tone, so misunderstandings happen easily; shared rules reduce that. It also protects privacy, keeps discussion useful, and makes online spaces somewhere people want to be.

short.q: Self Test 6.4: List the types of information in a digital footprint.
short.a: Websites visited; search history; social media posts; records of online purchases; comments on news articles; and messages sent. It also includes what other people post about you, and what websites collect about you through cookies.

short.q: Self Test 6.4: Write any two advantages of a digital footprint.
short.a:
1. Fraud and legal issues can be detected more easily — the trail helps investigate wrongdoing.
2. Personalisation — suggested products and relevant advertising add value, and companies can offer incentives matched to your interests, sometimes cutting costs.

long.q: Explain digital footprint and privacy in online.
long.a:
What a digital footprint is. It is the trail of traces you leave behind online — a record of everything you do. It is, in effect, your online identity: what makes you recognisable.

Your footprint includes websites visited, search history, social media posts, records of online purchases, comments on news articles and messages sent. Crucially, it is not only what you do yourself. It also includes what other people post about you, and what websites collect about you through cookies.

Why privacy matters. A footprint is largely permanent and only partly under your control. Once something is online it can be copied, screenshotted and found later — by a future employer, for instance. And the data collected about you has commercial value: it can be used to generate revenue without your knowledge, and purchase behaviour has been used to reduce credit limits or raise interest rates.

That said, a footprint is not all bad. It lets fraud and legal issues be detected more easily, allows personalisation that genuinely helps, and lets companies offer incentives matched to what you want.

How to protect it. Delete old email accounts; limit how many social media accounts you have; skip surveys; keep your personal email address private and use a separate one for sign-ups; unsubscribe from newsletters you do not read; remove yourself from people-search sites; and use private or stealth mode when searching.

The rule of thumb: assume anything you post can be found later, and post on that basis.

long.q: Explain different techniques for browsing the web safely.
long.a:
1. Check the connection. A secure site's address begins with https — the "s" means the traffic is encrypted using SSL/TLS, so it cannot be read in transit. Look for the padlock, and never ignore a browser warning that a site is deceptive.

2. Keep everything updated. Update the browser, its plugins, the operating system and your antivirus. Most successful attacks use faults that were fixed months earlier.

3. Use a VPN. It encrypts your connection and masks your IP address and location, which matters particularly on public Wi-Fi, where anyone nearby could otherwise watch your traffic. Avoid public Wi-Fi for anything sensitive.

4. Guard your accounts. Use strong, unique passwords — best managed with a password manager — and turn on two-factor authentication wherever it is offered.

5. Be suspicious of links and attachments. Phishing is still the most common way in. Hover over a link before clicking to see where it really goes, and do not open attachments you were not expecting.

6. Reduce what leaks. Block pop-ups, use an ad blocker, enable "do not track", clear cache and cookies, use private browsing, and review your privacy settings.

7. Run a firewall and antivirus. The firewall controls what traffic reaches you; the antivirus deals with anything malicious that gets through. They do different jobs and you need both.

8. Back up. Keep copies of important files on an external drive or in the cloud, so that ransomware or a hardware failure is an inconvenience rather than a disaster.

long.q: Explain the types of cybersecurity and how they differ.
long.a:
1. Network security is about securing a computer network from unauthorized access — stopping attackers getting onto the network in the first place. Firewalls and VPNs are the tools here.

2. Application security is about securing software itself, so that weaknesses in a program cannot be exploited.

3. Information security is about protecting the information, wherever it sits. Encryption is the main tool: even if data is taken, it cannot be read.

4. IoT security covers internet-connected devices — wearables, industrial sensors, smart appliances. These often have weak security and are easy targets.

The distinction is what is being protected: the network, the software, the information itself, or the devices. A real defence needs all four, because an attacker only has to find the one gap you left.

long.q: What is cybercrime? Explain its types and how to prevent it.
long.a:
Definition. Cybercrime is illegal activity carried out using a computer, network device or the internet — using technology as the instrument for fraud, theft, harassment or privacy violation. It can be aimed at individuals, businesses or society.

Types.

1. Financial cybercrime — phishing, where fraudulent messages trick people into revealing information, and online fraud using fake websites.

2. Identity theft — hacking to gain unauthorized access, and data theft of personal or corporate information.

3. Cyber harassment — cyberbullying, and sharing explicit images without consent.

4. Malware and ransomware — viruses and Trojans that damage or steal, and ransomware that encrypts files and demands payment.

5. Illegal online activity — dark web crimes such as trafficking, and piracy of films, music and software.

Prevention. Use strong passwords with two-factor authentication; stay alert to phishing; keep software and systems updated with security patches; secure your network with a firewall and a VPN and avoid public Wi-Fi for sensitive work; be careful what you share on social media; and back up your data regularly.

Prevention is mostly unglamorous — updates, backups and strong passwords stop far more attacks than any clever tool.

long.q: Describe netiquette and the responsibilities of a digital citizen.
long.a:
Netiquette — from "net" and "etiquette" — is the set of rules for respectful and appropriate communication online. They are recommended rules of conduct, not laws, and they apply to email, forums, social media and video calls. The main ones: be respectful; be considerate of gender and cultural differences; respect others' privacy by not forwarding what was sent to you without permission; be careful what you share; mind your language; write clearly; forgive beginners' mistakes; do not abuse any power you have; use a neutral nickname; read before replying; be helpful; be prepared before a video call; and choose a professional screen name.

The responsibilities of a digital citizen go further than manners. A digital citizen communicates respectfully even when they disagree; declines to share false information; respects the intellectual property rights of others; does not reveal other people's personal information; and does not break into computer systems without permission.

The two overlap but are not the same. Netiquette is about how you treat people in conversation. Digital citizenship covers that and adds your legal and ethical duties — to truth, to others' property, and to the security of systems. You can be perfectly polite online and still be a poor digital citizen, if you spread misinformation or share someone else's work as your own.

practical.q: Demonstrate the use of antivirus software.
practical.a:
What to demonstrate.

1. Open the antivirus program and show what protection is active: real-time scanning, web protection, and whatever else it offers.

2. Check that the virus definitions are up to date, and run an update if they are not. An antivirus with old definitions misses new threats.

3. Run a scan — a quick scan first, then explain when a full scan is worth the time.

4. Show how a detected threat is quarantined or removed.

5. Set a scheduled scan so it happens without anyone remembering to start it.

The point to make. Antivirus deals with malicious software that has reached the machine. Controlling what reaches it in the first place is the firewall's job — you need both.

practical.q: Demonstrate the use of a firewall, hardware and software.
practical.a:
Software firewall. Open the operating system's firewall settings and show that it is switched on. Show the list of rules, and explain that each rule either allows or denies particular traffic. Add a simple rule: name it, choose Allow or Deny, and specify the traffic.

Hardware firewall. Point out the firewall built into the router — a separate device standing between the local network and the internet. It protects every device on the network at once, including ones that cannot run their own firewall.

The contrast. A software firewall protects one machine; a hardware firewall protects the whole network. Both control traffic according to rules; neither removes viruses.

practical.q: Apply safe browsing techniques and list your techniques.
practical.a:
A checklist worth writing out and keeping:

1. Check that the address begins with https before entering anything personal.

2. Keep the browser, its plugins and the operating system updated.

3. Never ignore a browser warning that a site is deceptive — go back.

4. Hover over a link before clicking, to see where it really goes.

5. Do not open attachments you were not expecting.

6. Use a password manager so every account has its own strong password, and turn on two-factor authentication.

7. Avoid public Wi-Fi for anything sensitive; use a VPN if you must.

8. Clear cookies and cache, and review privacy settings.

9. Keep antivirus and the firewall switched on.

10. Back up important files, so ransomware is an inconvenience rather than a disaster.

practical.q: Demonstrate the use and implementation of a strong password in an online system or school application.
practical.a:
What makes a password strong. Length matters more than substitution. A passphrase of four or five random words beats P@ssw0rd, which appears in every attacker's list.

To demonstrate. Create two passwords — one weak, one strong — and compare them against the rules: at least 12 characters, mixing upper and lower case, numbers and symbols, with no dictionary word and no personal detail such as a name or birthday.

Then show the practice that matters more than the password.

Use a different password for every account, so one breach does not unlock everything. Store them in a password manager, so you only have to remember one master password. Turn on two-factor authentication, so a stolen password alone is not enough.

Never reuse a password, and never write one down where it can be found.

practical.q: Learning Workshop 6 activity: Cybercrime Role-Playing
practical.a:
Learning outcome: students recognise the common types of cybercrime and know how to prevent them.

Materials needed: flashcards with cybersecurity terms on them, printed example passwords for the ranking game.

How to run it

1. Give each group a scenario card describing an attack without naming it — an email from a bank asking the reader to confirm a password, a USB stick found in the car park, a pop-up claiming the computer is infected and offering a fix, a message from a friend asking urgently for money.

2. The group acts the scenario out for the class.

3. The rest of the class names the threat — phishing, baiting, scareware, account takeover — and proposes what the victim should have done.

4. Debrief on the pattern every scenario shares: urgency, an unfamiliar sender, and a request for credentials or money.

What it teaches: attacks are recognised by their shape, not by memorising a list of names. Once students can spot urgency plus a request for credentials, they can handle a scam that has not been invented yet.

practical.q: Learning Workshop 6 activity: Safe Password Challenge
practical.a:
How to run it

1. Give each student the same list of candidate passwords: password, nepal123, their own name, a birthday, and two long passphrases made of unrelated words.

2. Students write a stronger replacement for each one, following the rules they have been taught — at least twelve characters, no single dictionary word, and a different password for every account.

3. Collect them and rank the results from weakest to strongest as a class, discussing each judgement.

4. Ask what makes a password hard to guess, then what makes it hard to remember. Longer usually beats more symbols: a passphrase of four unrelated words is both stronger and easier to recall than eight characters of punctuation.

What it teaches: length counts more than complexity, reusing one password everywhere means one breach exposes every account, and a password manager removes the need to memorise any of it.

blocks.caption: Python — the language this chapter is about.

blocks.text: A set of instructions that command the computer to perform a particular operation or a specific task.

A program is written using a programming language, and a language processor then translates it into machine code so the computer can carry out the task. The statements written by the programmer are the source program or source code. Compiling the source code produces object code — values in terms of 0s and 1s — which is then linked with library code to make the finished program.
A program is a list of instructions for one job, and each instruction is also called a statement. Generally a statement does only one task; a group of statements together forms the program.

head: Program
Software
rows: A set of instructions telling the computer to carry out certain operations
A collection of programs with a series of instructions that tell the computer how to solve a problem
Needs a collection of programs to build
Created by a team of programmers
Categorised by use — application, system or utility software
Example: a C program to check whether a number is even or odd
blocks.caption: Program compared with software

blocks.text: Programming and the programmer
The process of writing a program following the grammar — the syntax — of the programming language.
Why programming matters

items: Communication with computers — it turns human ideas into instructions a computer can execute.
Automation — repetitive tasks get done efficiently.
Problem solving — it supports building solutions to complex problems through logical thinking.

blocks.text: Common programming languages include C, C++, Java and Python.
Languages are grouped by generation, from the bare machine code of the first to the natural languages still being developed.

head: Generation
Type
Examples
rows: Mnemonics such as ADD, SUB, DIV
blocks.caption: The five generations

blocks.text: Low level languages
Machine level language (1GL)
The first generation, and a low level language. Programs are written as combinations of binary numbers — 0s and 1s. It is the only language the computer understands directly.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: The only language the computer understands directly
Tedious, difficult and time consuming to write and debug
Operation codes and memory addresses must be remembered
Machine dependent — a program will not run elsewhere without change
The programmer needs detailed knowledge of the hardware
blocks.caption: Machine level language

blocks.text: Assembly level language (2GL)
Also a low level language, but it uses mnemonics — ADD, SUB, DIV — in place of 0s and 1s. An assembler converts the program into machine code.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Easier to write and debug than machine language, thanks to mnemonics
Cannot be executed directly — an assembler is needed
Simpler: the programmer need not know exact storage locations
Faster execution than high level languages
blocks.caption: Assembly language

blocks.text: High level languages
Procedure oriented language (3GL)

A high level, user-oriented language using simple English and mathematical statements. It is machine independent. It is called procedure oriented because the programmer has to specify the working procedure in detail.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Easier to write and debug than low level languages
Cannot be executed directly — a compiler or interpreter is needed
More advanced, user friendly software can be built
Machine independent, so it runs on similar hardware elsewhere
blocks.caption: Procedure oriented language

blocks.text: Problem oriented language (4GL)
A non-procedural, problem-oriented language: you say what output you want without describing how to produce it.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Even easier to write and debug than 3GL
Cannot be executed directly — needs translation
blocks.caption: Problem oriented language

blocks.text: Natural language (5GL)
Uses ordinary sentences and graphical tools, so that instructions look like normal communication. It is still in development.

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Even easier to develop and debug
Still needs translation to object code
blocks.caption: Natural language

blocks.text: High level languages you may meet: JavaScript, C++, PHP, Java, Visual Basic, BASIC, VB.Net and Python.
Program design tools are used to design a program before it is written. They define how the program takes input, processes it, and produces the output needed.

blocks.caption: The two program design tools: algorithm and flowchart.

blocks.text: Algorithm
A step-by-step description of a program — a stepwise list of statements explaining how a program can be developed or a problem solved, written in simple English and mathematical statements.
Properties of an algorithm

items: It should have an input.
The steps must be executable by a computer.
Every instruction should be in simple language.
The number of steps should be finite.
It should not depend on a particular language or computer.
It should give an output after a finite number of steps.

blocks.text: Worked examples

head: Problem
Algorithm
rows: 1. START. 2. Go to the counter and wait. 3. If a ticket is available, buy it, else go to step 2. 4. Watch the movie. 5. END.
1. START. 2. Read the two numbers A and B. 3. Add A and B, storing the result in D. 4. Display D. 5. END.
1. START. 2. Read principal, rate and time. 3. Multiply principal, rate and time. 4. Divide the product by 100 and store it in SI. 5. Print SI. 6. END.
