blocks.text: Advantages and disadvantages

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Easier to explain the logic of a program
Bugs are easier to detect, locate and remove
Turning one into a program is hard for a beginner
blocks.caption: Algorithms

blocks.text: Flowchart
A pictorial representation of a program — the sequence of steps drawn with predefined graphical symbols.
After designing an algorithm, the next stage is a flowchart, to check that the logic flows properly.

head: Symbol
Function
Meaning
rows: Marks the start and end of a program
Marks an input or output operation
Movement, editing or calculation of data
A branch point; one entry, two exits, for true and false
Links the flow from one page to another
Shows which way the logic runs
blocks.caption: Flowchart symbols
Flowcharts: area of a circle, and odd or even.

blocks.text: Advantages and disadvantages

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: Easier to understand and more attractive
Difficult to draw for complex problems
Communicates the logic of a problem clearly
Makes coding more effective and faster
Not a standard tool, and there is no way to test one for correctness
blocks.caption: Flowcharts

head: Flowchart
Algorithm
rows: A diagrammatic representation of a program
A finite set of step-by-step instructions
Takes time, because the symbols must be drawn
You must know what the symbols mean to follow it
Written in human language, so easier to understand
blocks.caption: Flowchart compared with algorithm

blocks.text: Coding
Coding is the act of writing the program itself — turning the design into instructions a computer can carry out.
Testing

Testing means running the code to check that it works as expected, confirming it meets the requirements and behaves correctly. It is like double-checking a recipe to see whether the result tastes right. If something is wrong, testing makes it easier to spot before anyone else uses the program.
Debugging

Debugging is the process of finding and correcting the errors that stop a program running smoothly — going through the code to identify what is causing an unexpected result. Fixing those errors makes the program reliable.
Language translators

A program is written in an assembly or high level language for the programmer's convenience, but the computer does not understand it. A language translator converts it into machine code. There are three kinds.

head: Compiler
Interpreter
rows: Translates the whole program into object code at once
Translates one line or statement at a time
Reports errors after compiling the whole program
Reports errors after translating each line
A larger program needing more memory
A smaller program needing less memory
Saves the object code for reuse
blocks.caption: Compiler compared with interpreter

blocks.text: Python was created by Guido van Rossum in 1991. It is a high-level, interpreted language known for its readability and versatility, letting you express an idea in fewer lines than C++ or Java would need. It reads a little like English, with an influence from mathematics, and it is used in web development, game development, software development, data analysis and artificial intelligence.
Features of Python

items: Easy to read and write — a simple, clear way of writing code, easy to learn even for beginners.
Interpreted — it reads and runs each line one at a time, so errors are quick to spot and fix.
Flexible with variables — you do not have to state the type of data when you create a variable.
A large collection of tools — a wide variety of libraries, from maths to games, so you rarely start from nothing.
Works on many platforms — the same program runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.
Great for beginners and experts — simple enough to start with, powerful enough to keep using.

sections.title: Python Basics: Indentation, Comments and I/O

blocks.text: Indentation
Indentation is the space at the start of a line. In Python it is not decoration — it is how you show which block a line belongs to. Other languages use braces; Python uses the layout.

blocks.code:
age = 15
if age > 18:
    print("You are an adult.")   # indented: part of the if
print("Done.")                      # not indented: runs either way

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Getting indentation wrong is the most common beginner error in Python. Lines in the same block must line up exactly, and a block must be indented further than the statement that opens it.
Case sensitivity
Python is case sensitive: Name and name are two different things.
Comments
Comments are notes explaining what the code does. Python skips over them. A single-line comment starts with #, and can follow code on the same line.

blocks.code:
# This is a single-line comment explaining the next line
age = 15  # a comment can come after code too
print(age)

blocks.text: For a longer explanation, use triple quotes — this is how multi-line comments are written.

blocks.code:
"""
This program checks the age of the user.
If the age is above 18 it prints "You are an adult."
Otherwise it says "You are a minor."
"""
print("Program starting")

blocks.text: Naming variables

items: Start with a letter or an underscore.
After the first character, use letters, numbers or underscores.
Avoid reserved words — print, if and for are Python commands and cannot be variable names.
Names are case sensitive, so Name and name differ.

blocks.code:
age = 15
user_name = "Sabitra"
score_1 = 75
print(age, user_name, score_1)

blocks.text: Input and output
input() asks the user for information. print() shows information on the screen.

blocks.code:
name = input("Enter your name: ")
print("Hello," + name + "!")

blocks.text: String formatting
Formatting makes messages easier to read. Two simple ways:

items: Concatenation — joining strings with +.
f-strings — put f before the quotes and the variable in { }.

blocks.code:
name = "hari"
age = 16
address = "bhaktapur"

print("My name is " + name + ". I am " + str(age) + " years old.")
print("My name is {}. I am {} years old. I live in {}.".format(name, age, address))
print(f"My name is {name}. I am {age} years old. I live in {address}.")

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Concatenating needs str() around numbers — "I am " + 16 is an error. An f-string converts them for you, which is why it is usually the better choice.
Data types
A data type classifies data, telling the computer how to use it.

head: Type
What it holds
Examples
rows: Whole numbers, positive, negative or zero
Letters, numbers or symbols inside quotes
One of two values: True or False
blocks.caption: The four basic data types

blocks.code:
number = 10
pi = 3.14
message = "Hello"
is_student = True

print(type(number))
print(type(pi))
print(type(message))
print(type(is_student))

blocks.text: Variables
A container for storing a data value. It holds a piece of data — a number, a string — which can be reused and changed easily.

blocks.code:
x = 5
x = x + 2
print(x)

blocks.text: The rules for naming them: a name cannot start with a number, cannot contain spaces, cannot contain special characters other than the underscore, and no two variables can share a name.
Constants
A special kind of variable whose value should not change once it is set. In Python, constants are written in capital letters to show they are not meant to change.

blocks.code:
import math
PI = math.pi
GRAVITY = 9.8
print(PI)
print(GRAVITY)

blocks.text: Type casting
Changing data from one type to another — for example turning a number stored as text into a real number so that it can be calculated with.

items: Implicit casting — done by Python itself, changing an integer to a float when it is needed.
Explicit casting — done by you, using int(), float() or str().

blocks.code:
# Implicit casting
num_int = 5
num_float = 5.0
num_combined = num_int + num_float
print(num_combined)

# Explicit casting
num_str = "10"
num_int = int(num_str)
print(num_int * num_int)

blocks.text: Note that num_combined is a float even though num_int was an integer, and that int(num_str) turns text into a number.

blocks.code:
num_str = "123"
num_int = int(num_str)
result = num_int + 10
print(result)

blocks.text: A symbol that performs an operation on variables and values — used to manipulate data, do calculations, compare values and control the flow of a program.

head: Group
Operators
rows: + addition, − subtraction, * multiplication, / division, % modulus, ** exponent, // floor division
= assign, += add and assign, −= subtract and assign, *= multiply and assign, /= divide and assign, %= modulus and assign, //= floor divide and assign
== equal, != not equal, > greater than, < less than, >= greater or equal, <= less or equal
blocks.caption: The four groups of operator

blocks.code:
a = 10
b = 3
print("sum      =", a + b)
print("diff     =", a - b)
print("product  =", a * b)
print("division =", a / b)
print("modulus  =", a % b)
print("power    =", a ** b)
print("floor div=", a // b)

x = 5
x += 3      # adds 3 to x, so x becomes 8
print(x)
x *= 2      # doubles it
print(x)

blocks.text: Expressions
A combination of values, variables and operators that produces a new value — for example a + b.

A conditional statement tells the program what to do depending on whether a condition is met. It is how a program makes decisions. Every conditional statement starts with if, which asks a true/false question and runs a block based on the answer. elif adds a further condition, and else covers everything the earlier conditions did not.
if
if – else
if – elif – else
More examples

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Conditions are checked in order, and Python stops at the first one that is true. In the grading example, a score of 95 never reaches the "B" branch, because "A" was already matched.
A block of code that runs over and over until a condition is met. It saves writing the same code again and again.

blocks.code:
# Without a loop
print("Nepal")
print("Nepal")
print("Nepal")
print("Nepal")
print("Nepal")

# With a loop
for i in range(0, 5):
    print("Nepal")

blocks.text: Python has two kinds of loop.
for loop
A for loop repeats a series of commands over a sequence of data — a list, a tuple, a dictionary, a set or a string.
while loop
A while loop repeats as long as a condition is true.

blocks.code:
count = 0
while count < 5:
    print(count)
    count += 1

total = 0
number = 1
while number <= 100:
    total += number
    number += 1
print(f"The sum is {total}.")

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Use for when you know how many times to repeat — over a list, or a range(). Use while when the loop should keep going until something happens, and you do not know in advance how long that will take.
List
An ordered collection of data, defined with square brackets [ ] and items separated by commas. Lists are mutable — the values can change.
Each value inside a list is called an item, and items are reached by their index, which starts at 0.

blocks.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "mango"]
print(fruits)
print(fruits[0])   # first item
print(fruits[2])   # third item

blocks.text: append() adds an item to the end of a list.

blocks.code:
colors = ["red", "green", "blue"]
print(colors[0])
colors.append("yellow")
print(colors)

blocks.text: Dictionary
A collection where each item is a unique key paired with a value. Defined with curly braces { }, each pair separated by a comma and written key: value.
Dictionaries are mutable, so items can be added, changed or removed after they are created.

blocks.code:
student = {
    "name": "Ramesh",
    "age": 15,
    "class": "IX"
}
print(student["name"])
print(student)

blocks.text: A block of code that performs an action when it is called. Arguments go inside the parentheses to pass data in, and it can return a result.

Functions let programmers avoid repeating the same logic. Programs are usually divided into many functions that each do one job. A library function is one that is already defined in Python and can be used straight away; a user-defined function is one you write yourself.
String functions

head: Function
What it does
rows: Centres the string within the given width
Gives the length of the string
blocks.caption: String functions

blocks.code:
text = "Hello"
print(text.upper())
print(text.lower())
print(len(text))
print(text.center(10, "*"))

blocks.text: Numerical and mathematical functions

head: Function
What it does
rows: Adds all the elements in a list
x raised to the power y
Finds the square root (needs the math module)
blocks.caption: Numerical functions

blocks.code:
import math

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print("sum      =", sum(numbers))
print("pow(2,3) =", pow(2, 3))
print("round    =", round(3.14159, 2))
print("abs(-7)  =", abs(-7))
print("sqrt(16) =", math.sqrt(16))
print("int      =", int("123"))

blocks.text: The import keyword brings in extra tools from modules such as math. Without it, math.sqrt() is not available.

figures_index.caption: Python — the language this chapter is about.
The two program design tools: algorithm and flowchart.
Flowcharts: area of a circle, and odd or even.

mcq.q: What is a computer program?
options: A set of instructions that perform a specific task
A collection of data stored in memory
mcq.teacher_note: A set of instructions performing a specific task. Hardware is the machine, data is what the program works on, and networking is something else again.

mcq.q: Which programming language consists of binary numbers (0s and 1s) and is directly understood by the computer?
mcq.teacher_note: Machine level language. Assembly uses mnemonics, and high level languages need translating — only machine code is understood directly.

mcq.q: What is the main difference between a compiler and an interpreter?
options: A compiler translates code line by line, while an interpreter translates all code at once
A compiler translates all code at once, while an interpreter translates code line by line
A compiler is used only for assembly level language, while an interpreter is used for high-level languages
A compiler is a type of debugger, while an interpreter is a type of assembler
mcq.teacher_note: The compiler takes the whole program at once; the interpreter takes one line at a time. Option (a) has them the wrong way round.

mcq.q: What is the purpose of an algorithm in programming?
options: To provide a step-by-step description of how a program should be developed
To compile the code into machine language
mcq.teacher_note: It is a step-by-step description — a plan written before any code is typed. It neither executes nor compiles anything.

mcq.q: Which programming language generation allows programmers to write statements in normal sentence form?
mcq.teacher_note: 5GL, the natural language generation, where instructions look like ordinary sentences. Fourth generation is problem-oriented but still uses structured statements.

mcq.q: Who created Python, and when was it introduced?
mcq.teacher_note: Guido van Rossum, 1991. The other pairings are real but belong to other languages: Gosling to Java, Ritchie to C, Stroustrup to C++.

mcq.q: What is the purpose of indentation in Python?
options: It is optional and does not affect the program
mcq.teacher_note: It organises code into blocks. Far from optional, it is how Python knows which lines belong to a loop or a condition.

mcq.q: Which function is used in Python to take input from the user?
mcq.teacher_note: input(). print() does the opposite — it shows output. There is no read() or get() for this.

mcq.q: What is the correct way to format a string using an f-string in Python?
mcq.teacher_note: print(f"Hello, {name}!") — the f before the quotes is what makes it an f-string. Without it the braces are printed literally.

mcq.q: What is the purpose of a conditional statement in Python?
options: To store multiple values in a list
To execute different code based on whether a condition is met or not
mcq.teacher_note: To run different code depending on a condition — that is what makes a program able to make decisions.

mcq.q: Which keyword checks an additional condition after an if statement?
mcq.teacher_note: elif. else catches everything remaining but does not test anything, and switch is not a Python keyword.

mcq.q: What is the purpose of an iteration (loop) in Python?
options: To execute a block of code repeatedly until a condition is met
To store multiple values in a variable
To assign a value to a variable
mcq.teacher_note: To repeat a block until a condition is met — that is what a loop is for.

mcq.q: What is the main difference between a for loop and a while loop in Python?
options: A for loop runs indefinitely, while a while loop runs a fixed number of times
A for loop is used with sequences, while a while loop runs as long as a condition is true
A while loop can only iterate over lists, while a for loop cannot
A for loop is used only for numerical calculations, while a while loop is not
mcq.teacher_note: A for loop works through a sequence; a while loop keeps going while a condition holds. Option (a) has it backwards.

mcq.q: What is a key characteristic of a list in Python?
options: It is an unordered collection of data
It is immutable and cannot be changed
It is an ordered collection of data that can be modified
It can only store numerical values
mcq.teacher_note: A list is ordered and mutable — the order is kept, and the contents can be changed.

mcq.q: What is a library function in Python?
options: A function created by the user to perform specific tasks
A function that is pre-defined in Python and can be used directly
A function that stores a collection of data
A function that only works with numerical data
mcq.teacher_note: A pre-defined function you can use straight away. One you write yourself is a user-defined function.

mcq.q: Which function is used to convert a string to an integer in Python?
mcq.teacher_note: int(). str() goes the other way, turning a number into text.

mcq.q: What will len("Python") return?
mcq.teacher_note: 6 — P-y-t-h-o-n is six characters. len() counts every character, including spaces.

mcq.q: Which operator gives the remainder after division?
mcq.teacher_note: % is the modulus. / is division, // is floor division and ** is exponentiation.

mcq.q: What does my_list[0] give in Python?
mcq.teacher_note: The first item — indexing starts at 0, not 1. This catches out almost everyone at first.

mcq.q: Which of these is a valid Python variable name?
mcq.teacher_note: my_name. A name cannot start with a digit, cannot contain a space, and cannot contain a hyphen — only letters, digits and underscores, after a leading letter or underscore.

short.q: What is a program?
short.a: A program is a set of instructions that command the computer to perform a particular operation or task. It is written in a programming language, and a language processor translates it into machine code so the computer can execute it. A program is made up of statements, each generally doing one task.

short.q: Who is a programmer?
short.a: A programmer is the person who writes programs — someone who creates the instructions that tell a computer what to do, following the syntax rules of a programming language.

short.q: Define coding.
short.a: Coding is the act of writing the program — turning the design, worked out as an algorithm or a flowchart, into instructions in a programming language that the computer can carry out.

short.q: What is an interpreter?
short.a: An interpreter is a language translator that converts a high level program into machine code one statement at a time, reporting an error as soon as it meets one. Translation is slower than with a compiler, but debugging is easier and faster. It does not save object code, and it needs less memory. Python, BASIC and C# use interpreters.

short.q: Define compiler.
short.a: A compiler is a language translator that converts a whole high level program into machine code in one go, provided the program is free of syntax errors. It reports errors only after compiling the entire program. Translation is fast and the object code is saved for reuse, but debugging is harder. C, C++ and Java use compilers.

short.q: List the types of programming languages.
short.a:
By generation: 1GL machine level language, 2GL assembly level language, 3GL procedure oriented (BASIC, FORTRAN, PASCAL, C, C++), 4GL problem oriented (Visual Basic, C#, PHP) and 5GL natural language.

Grouped more broadly, they are low level — machine and assembly — and high level — 3GL, 4GL and 5GL.

short.q: What is a language processor?
short.a: A language processor is the software that translates a program written in an assembly or high level language into machine code the computer can execute. The three types are the assembler, the compiler and the interpreter.

short.q: List an advantage of a flowchart.
short.a: It is easier to understand and more attractive than a written description, because the logic is shown as a picture. It also communicates the logic of a problem clearly to others, and makes the coding that follows more effective and faster.

short.q: What is Python?
short.a: Python is a high-level, interpreted programming language created by Guido van Rossum in 1991. It is known for its readability and versatility: programs can be written in fewer lines than in C++ or Java, and the code reads a little like English. It is used in web development, game development, software development, data analysis and artificial intelligence.

short.q: Who developed the Python programming language?
short.a: Guido van Rossum, who created it in 1991.

short.q: What is Python programming used for?
short.a: Web development, game development, software development, data analysis, artificial intelligence and automation. Its large collection of libraries means there is a toolkit for almost any task.

short.q: Name one feature of Python.
short.a: It is easy to read and write — the syntax is simple and clear, so it can be learned quickly. Other features: it is interpreted, variables do not need a type declared, it has a large library collection, and it runs on many platforms.

short.q: What is a variable in Python?
short.a: A variable is a container for storing a data value — a number, a string, or anything else. It can be reused and changed easily, and is assigned with the equals sign. In Python you do not have to declare its type; the language works that out from the value you give it.

short.q: Define an algorithm with an example.
short.a:
An algorithm is a step-by-step description of how to develop a program or solve a problem — a stepwise list of statements in simple English and mathematical notation.

Example — finding the sum of two numbers:

1. START. 2. Read the two numbers A and B. 3. Add A and B, storing the result in D. 4. Display D. 5. END.

short.q: What is a flowchart? Illustrate with an example.
short.a:
A flowchart is a pictorial representation of a program — the sequence of steps drawn with predefined graphical symbols such as the terminal box, the input/output box, the processing box and the decision box.

Example — checking whether a number is odd or even: START → input a number n → decision "is n mod 2 = 0?" → if yes, display "n is even"; if no, display "n is odd" → STOP.

short.q: Write the symbols used in a flowchart.
short.a: Seven: the terminal box (start/stop), the input/output box, the processing box, the decision box (one entry, two exits, for true and false), the connector (linking across pages), flow lines (showing direction) and the comment box.

short.q: Write any two differences between low-level and high-level language.
short.a:
1. A low level language is close to the machine — machine code is understood directly, with no translator needed. A high level language is user oriented and must be translated by a compiler or interpreter.

2. Low level languages are machine dependent, so a program will not run on different hardware without changes. High level languages are machine independent, so the same program runs on similar systems.

Also: low level languages need detailed hardware knowledge; high level languages do not.

short.q: Write any two advantages of a high level language.
short.a:
1. It is easier to develop and debug than a low level language, because it uses English-like and mathematical statements.

2. It is machine independent, so a program written for one system runs on others with similar hardware.

Also: no detailed hardware knowledge is needed, and more advanced, user friendly software can be built.

short.q: List the examples of high level languages.
short.a: JavaScript, C++, PHP, Java, Visual Basic, BASIC, VB.Net and Python. Older 3GL examples include FORTRAN, PASCAL and C.

short.q: What is indentation, and why is it important in Python?
short.a:
Indentation is the space at the start of a line. In Python it is not a matter of style — it is how the language knows which block a statement belongs to. Lines at the same level of indentation are in the same block; a block is indented further than the statement that opens it.

That is why indentation matters so much: other languages use braces to mark blocks, but Python uses the layout. Get the indentation wrong and the program either does the wrong thing or refuses to run.

short.q: Explain the purpose of comments in Python code.
short.a: Comments are notes that explain what the code is doing, and Python ignores them when it runs. Their purpose is to make the code understandable — to whoever reads it next, which is often the person who wrote it, months later. A single-line comment starts with #; a longer one is written between triple quotes.

short.q: How do you convert the string "123" to an integer?
short.a:
With int():

num_str = "123"
num_int = int(num_str)
print(num_int + 10)   # 133

short.q: Name two logical operators in Python.
short.a: and, or and not — any two. and is true only if both conditions are true; or is true if either is; not reverses the result.

short.q: Write down a basic if statement that checks if a number is positive.
short.a:
num = 4
if num > 0:
    print("The number is positive")

short.q: What is the purpose of the else keyword?
short.a: else catches everything the earlier conditions did not — it runs when the if (and any elif) conditions were all false. Unlike elif, it does not test anything itself, and it is always last.

short.q: What are the two types of loops in Python?
short.a: The for loop, which repeats over a sequence such as a list, a string or a range(); and the while loop, which repeats as long as a condition remains true.

short.q: What is a list, and how is it different from a dictionary?
short.a:
A list is an ordered collection written with square brackets, where items are reached by their index, starting at 0. A dictionary is a collection written with curly braces, where each item is a key–value pair and items are reached by their key.

So fruits[0] gives the first fruit, while student["name"] gives the name. Both are mutable, but a list is for a sequence of similar items, and a dictionary for related facts about one thing.

short.q: How would you access the value of a key in a dictionary?
short.a:
By putting the key in square brackets after the dictionary name:

me = {"name": "Rabita", "age": 15, "hobby": "Reading"}
print(me["name"])   # Rabita

You can also use me.get("name"), which returns None rather than raising an error if the key is missing.

short.q: Name three common data types in Python.
short.a: Integer (int) — whole numbers such as 5, −52, 0. Float — decimals such as 3.14, −45.68. String (str) — text inside quotes, such as "Hello". A fourth is Boolean (bool), which is either True or False.

short.q: What is type casting, and why is it useful?
short.a:
Type casting is converting data from one type to another — for example turning a number held as text into a real number so it can be used in a calculation.

It matters because input() always gives you a string. If you want to do arithmetic on what the user typed, you must cast it first:

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))   # without int() this would be text

Implicit casting is done for you — Python turns an integer into a float when the two are mixed. Explicit casting is you calling int(), float() or str().

short.q: Which function is used to get input from a user in Python?
short.a:
input(), with the prompt inside the brackets. It always returns a string, so cast it if you need a number:

name = input("Enter your name: ")
age = int(input("Enter your age: "))

short.q: What is string formatting? Give an example of an f-string.
short.a:
String formatting is the process of combining text and variables to make messages clearer and more readable. Two simple ways are concatenation with +, and f-strings.

An f-string has f before the quotes and the variable in braces:

name = "Arjun"
print(f"Hello, {name}! Welcome!")

This is usually the better choice, because it converts numbers for you — with concatenation you would have to wrap them in str().

short.q: What is the purpose of an arithmetic operator? Give an example.
short.a:
Arithmetic operators do mathematical calculations on numbers: + addition, − subtraction, * multiplication, / division, % modulus (the remainder), ** exponent and // floor division.

a = 10
b = 3
print(a + b)   # 13
print(a % b)   # 1, the remainder

short.q: What does the upper() string function do? What is the purpose of sqrt() and which module do you need?
short.a:
upper() converts a string to uppercase: "Hello".upper() gives "HELLO".

sqrt() finds the square root of a number. It lives in the math module, so you must import that first:

import math
print(math.sqrt(16))   # 4.0

Without the import, Python does not know what math is.

short.q: Self Test 7.1: What are the two main types of programming languages?
short.a: Low level languages — machine level (1GL) and assembly level (2GL) — and high level languages — procedure oriented (3GL), problem oriented (4GL) and natural language (5GL).

short.q: Self Test 7.1: What is one advantage of machine-level language?
short.a: Any one of: it is the only language the computer understands directly, so no translator is needed. Others: execution is fast, and it uses memory and the processor efficiently.

short.q: Self Test 7.1: What is one disadvantage of assembly language?
short.a: Any one of: it cannot be executed directly — an assembler is needed to translate it. Others: it is machine dependent, so it will not run on different hardware without change; and it requires detailed knowledge of the hardware.

short.q: Self Test 7.1: Name one advantage of third generation programming language (3GL).
short.a: Any one of: it is easier to develop and debug than a low level language, because it uses English-like and mathematical statements. Others: it is machine independent, it needs no detailed hardware knowledge, and it suits general-purpose programming.

short.q: Self Test 7.1: What is the purpose of fifth generation programming language (5GL)?
short.a: To let programs be written in something close to ordinary human language, using normal sentences and graphical tools rather than formal code. The aim is to make programming easier still and to solve problems by describing them rather than by spelling out the procedure. It is still in development and is used mainly in AI and logic programming.

short.q: Self Test 7.2: What is an algorithm?
short.a: An algorithm is a step-by-step description of how a program can be developed or a problem solved — a finite list of instructions in simple English and mathematical notation. It must have an input, produce an output, and finish after a finite number of steps.

short.q: Self Test 7.2: What is a flowchart?
short.a: A flowchart is a pictorial representation of a program — the sequence of steps drawn with predefined graphical symbols such as the terminal box, the input/output box, the processing box and the decision box. It is drawn after the algorithm, to check that the logic flows correctly.

short.q: Self Test 7.2: List two symbols used in a program flowchart.
short.a: Any two of: the terminal box (start/stop), the input/output box, the processing box, the decision box (one entry, two exits for true and false), the connector, flow lines and the comment box.

short.q: Self Test 7.2: Define debugging in programming.
short.a: Debugging is the process of finding and correcting the errors — bugs — that stop a program running properly. It means going through the code to identify what is causing an unexpected result, then fixing it so the program is reliable.

short.q: Self Test 7.2: What is the purpose of testing in programming?
short.a: Testing means running the code to check that it works as expected — confirming it meets the requirements and behaves correctly. Its purpose is to find problems before anyone else uses the program, rather than after.

short.q: Self Test 7.3: What is a language translator in programming?
short.a: Language translator is the general name for system software that converts a program written in an assembly or high level language into machine code the computer can execute.

short.q: Self Test 7.3: Name the three types of language translators.
short.a: The assembler (assembly language to machine code), the compiler (the whole high-level program at once) and the interpreter (one statement at a time).

short.q: Self Test 7.3: What is the purpose of an assembler?
short.a: An assembler converts a program written in assembly language — using mnemonics such as ADD and SUB — into the machine code the computer can execute. Without it, assembly code cannot run.

short.q: Self Test 7.3: Define a compiler in programming.
short.a: A compiler is a translator that converts a whole high level program into machine code in one go, provided there are no syntax errors. It reports errors only after compiling the entire program, translation is fast, and the object code is saved for reuse — but debugging is harder. C, C++ and Java use compilers.

short.q: Self Test 7.3: What is an interpreter used for in programming?
short.a: An interpreter converts a high level program into machine code one statement at a time, reporting an error as soon as it meets one. It is used to run programs directly, and it makes debugging easier because you see where execution stopped. Translation is slower and nothing is saved for reuse. Python, BASIC and C# use interpreters.

short.q: Self Test 7.4: What is python?
short.a: Python is a high-level, interpreted programming language created by Guido van Rossum in 1991. It is known for readability and versatility, letting you express an idea in fewer lines than C++ or Java. It is used in web development, game development, data analysis, artificial intelligence and automation.

short.q: Self Test 7.4: Name one feature of Python.
short.a: Any one of: it is easy to read and write; it is interpreted; variables need no type declared; it has a large collection of libraries; and it runs on many platforms.

short.q: Self Test 7.4: What is the file extension for a Python script?
short.a: .py — for example hello.py.

short.q: Self Test 7.4: Name one operating system that supports Python.
short.a: Any one of Windows, macOS and Linux. Python is platform independent, so the same program runs on all three.

short.q: Self Test 7.4: Which command is used to check the installed Python version?
short.a: python --version — or python -V. On some systems, where python still points to Python 2, use python3 --version.

short.q: Self Test 7.5: What is indentation in Python?
short.a: Indentation is the space at the start of a line, and in Python it is how you show which block a statement belongs to. Other languages use braces; Python uses the layout. Lines in the same block must line up exactly.

short.q: Self Test 7.5: Which symbol is used for writing a single-line comment in Python?
short.a: The hash, #. Everything after it on that line is ignored by Python. For a longer comment, use triple quotes.

short.q: Self Test 7.5: Name one rule for naming a variable in Python.
short.a: Any one of: it must start with a letter or an underscore; after that it may contain letters, numbers and underscores; it cannot contain spaces or special characters other than the underscore; it cannot start with a digit; and it cannot be a reserved word such as print, if or for.

short.q: Self Test 7.5: What does the f in an f-string stand for in Python?
short.a: Formatted. An f-string is a formatted string literal: you write f before the quotes and put expressions in braces, and Python inserts their values. For example f"Hello, {name}!".

short.q: Self Test 7.6: What is a variable in Python?
short.a: A variable is a named container holding a data value — a number, a string, anything. It is created by assigning with =, and the value can be changed later. Python works out the type from the value, so no declaration is needed.

short.q: Self Test 7.6: What is a constant in Python?
short.a: A constant is a variable whose value is not meant to change once set. Python has no enforcement, so the convention is to write the name in capital letters — PI = 3.14 — as a signal to other programmers not to change it.

short.q: Self Test 7.6: Name two types of type casting in Python.
short.a: Implicit casting, which Python does for you — turning an integer into a float when the two are mixed — and explicit casting, which you do yourself with int(), float() or str().

short.q: Self Test 7.7: What are the basic arithmetic operators in Python?
short.a: + addition, - subtraction, * multiplication, / division, % modulus (the remainder), ** exponentiation and // floor division.

short.q: Self Test 7.7: Define what an assignment operator is in Python and provide an example.
short.a:
An assignment operator gives a value to a variable. The basic one is =, and the compound ones combine an operation with the assignment — +=, -=, *=, /=, %=, //=.

x = 5 sets x to 5, then x += 3 adds 3 to it, leaving 8. That is shorthand for x = x + 3.

short.q: Self Test 7.7: What are logical operators in Python? List the three main logical operators.
short.a: Logical operators combine or invert conditions. The three are and (true only if both are true), or (true if either is true) and not (reverses the result).

short.q: Self Test 7.7: What is the syntax of a simple conditional statement using 'if' in Python?
short.a:
Write if, then the condition, then a colon, and indent the code to run on the following lines:

if condition:
    # code to run if the condition is True

For example if num > 0: print("positive") on the indented line.

short.q: Self Test 7.8: What is the syntax of a while loop in Python?
short.a:
Write while, then the condition, then a colon, and indent the code to repeat:

while condition:
    # code to repeat

The loop runs as long as the condition stays true, so something inside must eventually make it false — otherwise it never ends.

short.q: Self Test 7.8: Define what a list is in Python.
short.a: A list is an ordered collection of items, written in square brackets and separated by commas. It is mutable, so items can be changed, added or removed. Items are reached by their index, which starts at 0. For example ["apple", "banana", "mango"].

short.q: Self Test 7.8: What is a dictionary in Python?
short.a: A dictionary is a collection of key–value pairs, written in curly braces. Each key is unique and is used to look up its value, rather than using a numeric index. It is mutable. For example {"name": "Ramesh", "age": 15}, where d["name"] gives "Ramesh".

short.q: Write the full forms: 1GL, 2GL, 3GL, 5GL, PHP.
short.a: 1GL — First Generation Language — machine code, written directly in binary. 2GL — Second Generation Language — assembly language, which uses short mnemonics instead of binary. 3GL — Third Generation Language — high-level languages such as C, Java and Python, which must be compiled or interpreted. 5GL — Fifth Generation Language — based on constraints and logic rather than step-by-step instructions, as in Prolog. PHP — PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor — originally Personal Home Page Tools, a language that runs on the web server.

long.q: Differentiate between algorithm and flowchart.
long.a:
An algorithm is a step-by-step description of a program in simple English and mathematical statements — a finite list of instructions. A flowchart is the same logic drawn as a picture, using predefined symbols.

The differences:

1. An algorithm is written in human language; a flowchart is a diagram.

2. A flowchart takes longer, because the symbols have to be drawn; an algorithm is quicker to write.

3. Following a flowchart means knowing what the symbols mean; an algorithm can be read by anyone.

4. Drawing a flowchart needs some special knowledge; writing an algorithm needs none.

5. A flowchart is harder to maintain — changing the logic means redrawing it. An algorithm is easier to revise.

In practice they are used together: write the algorithm first to get the logic clear, then draw the flowchart to check the flow, then code.

long.q: What is a machine level language? Explain any two advantages and disadvantages.
long.a:
Machine level language is the first generation language, in which programs are written as combinations of binary numbers — 0s and 1s. It is the only language the computer understands directly, needing no translator.

Two advantages.

1. It is understood directly by the computer, so no language translator is needed.

2. Execution is fast, and it uses memory and the processor efficiently, because there is nothing between the program and the hardware.

Two disadvantages.

1. It is tedious, difficult and time consuming to write and debug, because every operation code and memory address has to be remembered.

2. It is machine dependent, so a program written for one system will not run on another without modification — and the programmer needs detailed knowledge of the hardware.

long.q: Differentiate between assembly language and high level language.
long.a:
1. Assembly language is a low level language using mnemonics such as ADD, SUB and DIV. A high level language is user oriented, using English-like and mathematical statements.

2. Assembly is machine dependent; high level languages are machine independent.

3. Assembly is translated by an assembler; high level languages by a compiler or an interpreter.

4. Assembly needs detailed knowledge of the hardware; high level languages do not.

5. Assembly executes faster, but is much harder to write and debug. High level languages are easier and quicker to develop, though slower to run.

6. Examples: assembly is 2GL; high level languages include C and Python.

long.q: Differentiate between compiler and interpreter with an example.
long.a:
A compiler translates the whole program into object code at once, if the program is free of syntax errors. It reports errors only after compiling the entire program. Translation is fast, the object code is saved for reuse, but debugging is harder and it needs more memory. C, C++ and Java use compilers.

An interpreter translates one statement at a time, reporting an error as soon as it meets one. Translation is slower, nothing is saved for reuse, but debugging is easier and it needs less memory. BASIC, Visual Basic, C# and Python use interpreters.

An example of the difference. Suppose line 3 of your program has an error. An interpreter runs lines 1 and 2, then stops at line 3 and tells you. A compiler checks the whole file first and reports line 3 without having run anything — so you see the error sooner, but you do not see the output of lines 1 and 2.

long.q: Write a flowchart to read three numbers and find the smallest.
long.a:
The logic: START → input three numbers x, y and z → ask "is x < y AND x < z?" → if yes, display x as smallest → if no, ask "is y < z?" → if yes, display y → if no, display z → END.

The decision box for the first question has one entry and two exits, for true and false, and the false branch leads to the second decision box.

The same logic written as a program:

x = int(input("Enter first number: "))
y = int(input("Enter second number: "))
z = int(input("Enter third number: "))

if x < y and x < z:
    print("The smallest is", x)
elif y < z:
    print("The smallest is", y)
else:
    print("The smallest is", z)

long.q: Write an algorithm to calculate the area of a circle.
long.a:
1. START. 2. Read the radius r. 3. Calculate the area as (22 × r × r) / 7. 4. Display the area. 5. END.

Written as a program:

r = float(input("Enter the radius: "))
area = (22 * r * r) / 7
print("The area of the circle is", area)

long.q: Write short notes on 3GL, 4GL and natural language.
long.a:
3GL — procedure oriented. A high level language using simple English and mathematical statements. It is machine independent. It is called procedure oriented because the programmer must specify the working procedure in detail — you say how to get the result as well as what it should be. Examples: BASIC, FORTRAN, PASCAL, C, C++.

4GL — problem oriented. A non-procedural language: you say what output you want, without describing how to produce it. Easier still to write and debug, good for web-based software, and machine independent — though execution is slower and hardware-oriented software is hard to write. Examples: Visual Basic, C#, PHP.

5GL — natural language. Uses ordinary sentences and graphical tools, so instructions look like normal communication. It is still in development. It would be the easiest of all to write, but it still needs translating into object code, and it is poor at hardware-oriented work.

long.q: Programming questions 1–15 from Exercise 7B.
long.a:
1. Display a welcome message.

print("Hello, welcome to Python programming!")

2. Greet the user by name.

name = input("Enter your name: ")
print(f"Hello, {name}! Welcome!")

3. Assign a string and a number, then print both.

greeting = "Namaste"
age = 15
print(greeting)
print(age)

8. Minor, adult or senior.

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
if age < 18:
    print("You are a minor")
elif age <= 65:
    print("You are an adult")
else:
    print("You are a senior")

9. Print the numbers 1 to 5.

for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)

10. Print the even numbers up to 100.

for i in range(2, 101, 2):
    print(i, end=" ")
print()

11. Keep asking until the password is right.

password = ""
while password != "python123":
    password = input("Enter the password: ")
print("Access granted")

12. A list of three colours, printed with a for loop.

colours = ["red", "blue", "green"]
for colour in colours:
    print(colour)

13. A dictionary, printed key by key.

person = {
    "name": "Sita",
    "age": 15,
    "favorite_color": "blue"
}
for key in person:
    print(key, "->", person[key])

14. Uppercase, lowercase and centred.

word = input("Enter a word: ")
print(word.upper())
print(word.lower())
print(word.center(20, "*"))

15. Sum a list, and find a square root.

import math

numbers = [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]
print("Sum =", sum(numbers))

n = float(input("Enter a number: "))
print("Square root =", math.sqrt(n))

long.q: Practical exercises: the worked programs.
long.a:
Simple interest. SI = (P × R × T) / 100

P = float(input("Enter principal: "))
R = float(input("Enter rate: "))
T = float(input("Enter time: "))

SI = (P * R * T) / 100
print(f"The simple interest is {SI}.")

Multiplication table up to 10.

n = int(input("Enter a number: "))
for i in range(1, 11):
    print(f"{n} x {i} = {n * i}")

Factorial of a number.

n = int(input("Enter a number: "))
factorial = 1
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    factorial *= i
print(f"The factorial of {n} is {factorial}.")

Celsius to Fahrenheit. F = (C × 9/5) + 32

C = float(input("Enter temperature in Celsius: "))
F = (C * 9 / 5) + 32
print(f"{C} degrees Celsius is {F} degrees Fahrenheit.")

Palindrome checker. The slice [::-1] walks the string backwards.

word = input("Enter a word or number: ")
if word == word[::-1]:
    print(f"{word} is a palindrome.")
else:
    print(f"{word} is not a palindrome.")

Prime number check. Testing divisors only up to the square root is enough, and makes the program fast.

import math

n = int(input("Enter a number: "))

if n < 2:
    print(f"{n} is not prime.")
else:
    prime = True
    for i in range(2, int(math.sqrt(n)) + 1):
        if n % i == 0:
            prime = False
            break
    if prime:
        print(f"{n} is prime.")
    else:
        print(f"{n} is not prime.")

programming.q: Write a program to display the message: "Hello, welcome to Python programming!"
programming.a:
A single print() is all this needs — it shows whatever is inside the brackets on the screen.

print("Hello, welcome to Python programming!")

programming.q: Write a program that asks the user for their name and then prints a greeting message using an f-string, such as "Hello, [name]! Welcome!"
programming.a:
input() collects the name and stores it in the variable name. The f-string then drops that value straight into the sentence — the f before the quotes and the braces {name} are what make it work.

name = input("Enter your name: ")
print(f"Hello, {name}! Welcome!")

programming.q: Create a program where you: assign a string value to a variable called greeting; assign a number to a variable called age; print both variables.
programming.a:
Two variables, each holding a different data type — greeting holds text and age holds a whole number. Python works out the type from the value you give it, so no declaration is needed.

greeting = "Namaste"
age = 15
print(greeting)
print(age)

programming.q: Write a program that takes a string input from the user, converts it to an integer, and adds 10 to it. Print the result.
programming.a:
input() always gives you text, so adding 10 to it directly would join the two together rather than add them. int() converts the text to a whole number first — that conversion is the whole point of the exercise.

num_str = input("Enter a number: ")
num_int = int(num_str)
result = num_int + 10
print(result)

programming.q: Write a program to calculate the sum, difference, and product of two numbers (use variables a and b).
programming.a:
Three arithmetic operators: + for the sum, - for the difference and * for the product.

a = 10
b = 4
print("Sum      =", a + b)
print("Difference =", a - b)
print("Product  =", a * b)

programming.q: Create a program that checks if a number is greater than 10 and less than 20 using a logical operator.
programming.a:
The and operator joins the two comparisons, so the message prints only when both are true. With or it would print when either one was.

number = 15
if number > 10 and number < 20:
    print("The number is between 10 and 20.")
else:
    print("The number is not between 10 and 20.")

programming.q: Write a program that asks the user for a number and prints whether it is positive, negative, or zero.
programming.a:
There are three outcomes, so this needs if, elif and else. The zero case matters — it is neither positive nor negative, and checking it last with else catches it cleanly.

num = int(input("Enter a number: "))
if num > 0:
    print("The number is positive.")
elif num < 0:
    print("The number is negative.")
else:
    print("The number is zero.")

programming.q: Write a program that takes a user's age and prints: "You are a minor" if age is less than 18, "You are an adult" if age is between 18 and 65, "You are a senior" if age is above 65.
programming.a:
The conditions are checked in order, and Python stops at the first one that matches. So by the time we reach the elif, the age is already known to be 18 or more — which is why testing only the upper bound is enough.

age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
if age < 18:
    print("You are a minor")
elif age <= 65:
    print("You are an adult")
else:
    print("You are a senior")

programming.q: Write a for loop that prints the numbers from 1 to 5.
programming.a:
range(1, 6) produces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The second number is where the range stops, and it is never included — a detail worth remembering, because range(1, 5) would give only four numbers.

for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)

programming.q: Write a for loop that prints all the even numbers up to 100.
programming.a:
The third argument of range() is the step. Starting at 2 and stepping by 2 gives every even number, stopping just before 101 — so 100 is included.

for i in range(2, 101, 2):
    print(i, end=" ")
print()

programming.q: Write a while loop that asks the user to enter a password until they enter the correct one (e.g., "python123").
programming.a:
The loop keeps asking while the password is wrong. Setting password to an empty string first guarantees the condition is true the first time, so the prompt appears at least once.

password = ""
while password != "python123":
    password = input("Enter the password: ")
print("Access granted")

programming.q: Create a list of your three favorite colors. Print each color using for loop.
programming.a:
The loop walks through the list and puts each item into the variable colour in turn.

colours = ["red", "blue", "green"]
for colour in colours:
    print(colour)

programming.q: Create a dictionary with keys "name", "age", and "favorite_color". Assign them values and print each key-value pair.
programming.a:
Looping over a dictionary gives you its keys, and person[key] then gives you the matching value.

person = {
    "name": "Sita",
    "age": 15,
    "favorite_color": "blue"
}
for key in person:
    print(key, "->", person[key])

programming.q: Write a program that takes a word from the user and prints it in uppercase, lowercase, and centered within 20 characters.
programming.a:
center(20, "*") pads the word out to 20 characters using asterisks. Change the second argument to a space if you would rather pad with blanks.

word = input("Enter a word: ")
print(word.upper())
print(word.lower())
print(word.center(20, "*"))

programming.q: Write a program that: sums up a list of numbers; finds the square root of a number input by the user.
programming.a:
sum() adds the whole list in one call. math.sqrt() is not built in — it lives in the math module, so that module has to be imported first.

import math

numbers = [4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42]
print("Sum =", sum(numbers))

n = float(input("Enter a number: "))
print("Square root =", math.sqrt(n))

programming.q: Practical 1 — Ask for a first name and last name, then greet the user by both.
programming.a:
Two inputs, joined in an f-string. The space between them in the f-string is just a space in the text — it does not appear on its own.

first = input("Enter your first name: ")
last = input("Enter your last name: ")
print(f"Hello, {first} {last}!")

programming.q: Practical 2 — Store your favourite colour, food and hobby in variables, then print them in a single sentence.
programming.a:
All three go into one sentence through an f-string, which is far easier to read than joining the pieces with +.

colour = "blue"
food = "momo"
hobby = "reading"
print(f"My favourite colour is {colour}, I love eating {food}, and my hobby is {hobby}.")

programming.q: Practical 3 — Ask for two numbers, then calculate the sum, difference, product and quotient.
programming.a:
Four operations on the same pair of numbers. Because the numbers are cast to float, the quotient keeps its decimal part — with whole numbers and / you would still get a decimal, but casting makes the intent clear.

a = float(input("Enter the first number: "))
b = float(input("Enter the second number: "))

print("Sum      =", a + b)
print("Difference =", a - b)
print("Product  =", a * b)
print("Quotient =", a / b)

programming.q: Practical 4 — Even or odd checker.
programming.a:
The modulus operator % gives the remainder after division. Dividing by 2 leaves a remainder of 0 for every even number, so comparing it to 0 settles it.

num = int(input("Enter a number: "))
if num % 2 == 0:
    print(f"{num} is even.")
else:
    print(f"{num} is odd.")

programming.q: Practical 5 — Grade calculator: 90+ A, 80-89 B, 70-79 C, below 70 F.
programming.a:
The chain is checked from the top down, and the first match wins. A mark of 95 never reaches the "B" branch, because "A" was already matched — so the order matters.

marks = int(input("Enter your marks: "))
if marks >= 90:
    grade = "A"
elif marks >= 80:
    grade = "B"
elif marks >= 70:
    grade = "C"
else:
    grade = "F"
print(f"Your grade is {grade}.")

programming.q: Practical 6 — Simple interest calculator: SI = (P x R x T) / 100
programming.a:
The formula translated directly. float is used because money and rates are rarely whole numbers.

P = float(input("Enter principal: "))
R = float(input("Enter rate: "))
T = float(input("Enter time: "))

SI = (P * R * T) / 100
print(f"The simple interest is {SI}.")

programming.q: Practical 7 — Number guessing game against a stored secret number.
programming.a:
The secret is held in a variable and compared with the guess. Using == rather than = is the classic beginner trap here: = assigns, == compares.

secret = 7
guess = int(input("Guess the number: "))
if guess == secret:
    print("Correct! You guessed it.")
else:
    print(f"Wrong. The number was {secret}.")

programming.q: Practical 8 — Multiplication table generator, up to 10.
programming.a:
A loop from 1 to 10, printing the product each time. This is the clearest example of what a loop is for: one line of code producing ten lines of output.

n = int(input("Enter a number: "))
for i in range(1, 11):
    print(f"{n} x {i} = {n * i}")

programming.q: Practical 9 — Counting from 1 to 10 using a while loop.
programming.a:
The counter starts at 1 and the loop runs while it is 10 or less. The line count += 1 is what moves it forward — without it the condition would never become false and the loop would never end.

count = 1
while count <= 10:
    print(count)
    count += 1

programming.q: Practical 10 — Reverse a string entered by the user.
programming.a:
The slice [::-1] walks through the string backwards. The first two positions are empty, meaning "from one end to the other", and -1 is the step going backwards.

text = input("Enter a string: ")
print("Reversed:", text[::-1])

programming.q: Practical 11 — Create a list of five favourite movies and print each with a loop.
programming.a:
Five items in a list, printed one per line by the loop.

movies = ["Chakka Panja", "12 Gaun", "Jwai Saab", "Sathi Ma Timro", "Prem Geet"]
for movie in movies:
    print(movie)

programming.q: Practical 12 — Create a dictionary with name, age and hobby; print each value.
programming.a:
Each value is reached by its key. Unlike a list, a dictionary is not numbered — you look things up by name.

me = {
    "name": "Rabita",
    "age": 15,
    "hobby": "Reading"
}
print(me["name"])
print(me["age"])
print(me["hobby"])

programming.q: Practical 13 — Find the largest of three numbers.
programming.a:
Python has a built-in max(), which is the shortest way. The version below shows the logic explicitly, which is what the exercise is really asking for.

a = int(input("Enter first number: "))
b = int(input("Enter second number: "))
c = int(input("Enter third number: "))

if a >= b and a >= c:
    print(f"The largest is {a}.")
elif b >= c:
    print(f"The largest is {b}.")
else:
    print(f"The largest is {c}.")

# The same job, done with the built-in function:
print("Check:", max(a, b, c))

programming.q: Practical 14 — Convert temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit.
programming.a:
The formula F = (C x 9/5) + 32, translated directly.

C = float(input("Enter temperature in Celsius: "))
F = (C * 9 / 5) + 32
print(f"{C} degrees Celsius is {F} degrees Fahrenheit.")

programming.q: Practical 15 — Rock, paper, scissors game.
programming.a:
random.choice() makes the computer's pick. The rules are worked out with comparisons: scissors beats paper, paper beats rock, and rock beats scissors — anything else is a draw.

import random

choices = ["rock", "paper", "scissors"]
computer = random.choice(choices)
user = input("Enter rock, paper or scissors: ").lower()

print(f"Computer chose {computer}.")

if user == computer:
    print("It is a draw.")
elif (user == "rock" and computer == "scissors") or \
     (user == "paper" and computer == "rock") or \
     (user == "scissors" and computer == "paper"):
    print("You win!")
else:
    print("Computer wins.")

programming.q: Practical 16 — Factorial finder, using a loop.
programming.a:
The factorial of n is n x (n-1) x ... x 1. Starting at 1 and multiplying up through range(1, n + 1) gives the answer. The factorial of 0 is 1, which this handles correctly because an empty range leaves the total at 1.

n = int(input("Enter a number: "))
factorial = 1
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    factorial *= i
print(f"The factorial of {n} is {factorial}.")

programming.q: Practical 17 — Generate the Fibonacci series up to a given number of terms.
programming.a:
Each term is the sum of the two before it. The line a, b = b, a + b updates both at once — Python works out the right-hand side before assigning, which is what makes the swap work.

terms = int(input("How many terms? "))
a, b = 0, 1
for _ in range(terms):
    print(a, end=" ")
    a, b = b, a + b
print()

programming.q: Practical 18 — Palindrome checker (a word or number reading the same both ways).
programming.a:
Compare the input with its reverse. If they match, it is a palindrome — madam and 121 both are.

word = input("Enter a word or number: ")
if word == word[::-1]:
    print(f"{word} is a palindrome.")
else:
    print(f"{word} is not a palindrome.")

programming.q: Practical 19 — Check whether a number is prime.
programming.a:
A prime has no divisor other than 1 and itself. Checking only up to the square root is enough — if no divisor is found by then, there cannot be one above it. That is what keeps the program quick for large numbers.

import math

n = int(input("Enter a number: "))

if n < 2:
    print(f"{n} is not prime.")
else:
    prime = True
    for i in range(2, int(math.sqrt(n)) + 1):
        if n % i == 0:
            prime = False
            break
    if prime:
        print(f"{n} is prime.")
    else:
        print(f"{n} is not prime.")

programming.q: Practical 20 — Password validator: at least 8 characters, containing letters and numbers.
programming.a:
any() with a generator checks whether at least one character meets each condition. len() handles the length rule.

password = input("Enter a password: ")

long_enough = len(password) >= 8
has_letter = any(c.isalpha() for c in password)
has_digit = any(c.isdigit() for c in password)

if long_enough and has_letter and has_digit:
    print("Password is valid.")
else:
    print("Password is not valid.")
    if not long_enough:
        print(" - it must be at least 8 characters long")
    if not has_letter:
        print(" - it must contain a letter")
    if not has_digit:
        print(" - it must contain a number")

practical.q: Search the internet and books, and list the names of different programming languages in use at present.
practical.a:
Group what you find by generation, since that is more useful than a flat list:

Low level — machine code; assembly.

3GL, procedure oriented — C, C++, Java, BASIC, Pascal, Fortran, Cobol.

4GL, problem oriented — PHP, Visual Basic, C#, SQL.

Modern high level — Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Ruby, Go, Rust, Swift, Kotlin, R.

5GL, natural language — still experimental, used mainly in AI and logic programming.

Alongside each name, note what it is mainly used for. Python for data and AI, JavaScript for the web, C for systems and embedded work, SQL for databases. The pattern worth noticing is that languages are chosen to suit the job — which is why this chapter teaches Python rather than claiming it is the only language that matters.

practical.q: Learning Workshop 7 activity: Flowchart and Algorithm Race
practical.a:
Learning outcome: students learn programming logic through hands-on Python activities.

Materials needed: computers with Python installed, printed algorithm and flowchart sheets.

How to run it

1. Give every team the same everyday task — making a cup of tea, finding the largest of three numbers, or deciding whether a student has passed.

2. Each team writes the algorithm in numbered steps and draws the matching flowchart, using the correct shapes: oval for start and stop, parallelogram for input and output, rectangle for a process, diamond for a decision.

3. Teams swap sheets and mark each other's work, looking for a decision with only one exit, a flowchart that cannot be followed top to bottom, or a step that is really two steps.

4. The first team to produce a correct sheet explains it to the class.

What it teaches: planning before coding. A flowchart that cannot be followed will not turn into a working program, and finding that out on paper is far cheaper than finding it out in the editor.

practical.q: Learning Workshop 7 activity: Python Code Fix Challenge
practical.a:
How to run it

1. Prepare several short programs, each with one deliberate fault. Cover the mistakes beginners actually make: a missing colon after an if or for, inconsistent indentation, = where == was meant, a variable used before it is assigned, and a string compared against a number.

2. Teams race to get each program running and producing the right output.

3. A team scores only when it can state what was wrong, not merely that it now works.

4. The first team to fix a program explains the error message to the class.

What it teaches: reading tracebacks. Teach everyone to read the last line first, since that is where the actual message is, and to use the line number as a starting point rather than as the exact location — the mistake is often on the line above.

practical.q: Learning Workshop 7 activity: Python Quick Quiz
practical.a:
How to run it

1. Run a quick-fire round of short questions on syntax and built-in functions — what len() returns, how you start a comment, what input() gives you, how you take the last item of a list, what range(1, 6) produces.

2. Keep the pace high and take answers from the floor rather than in turns, so nobody can opt out.

3. Pause on anything the class gets wrong and clear it up immediately rather than moving on.

What it teaches: recall of the basics under time pressure. Two questions catch almost everyone at first: input() returns a string, so it must be converted before arithmetic, and range(1, 6) stops at 5 because the stop value is excluded.
